And, as my wife learned, if you're in a pub in Žižkov, even the bartender won't let you go until you finally put that beer mat atop your empty mug. --

item.title: What happens when a place has two different names?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.25
Lake Ontario/Lake America: What happens when a place has two different names? Open the same map in the US and Canada and you may see two different names for the same lake. So, who decides what a place is really called? Open Google Maps in Toronto and you may see one name for a place. Open it in New York and you may see another. Increasingly, the map in your pocket can depend on where you're standing. That is what's happening with Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes that lie on the US-Canadian border. After President Trump ordered the US government to rename it "Lake America" following failed trade talks between the two nations this summer, the lake began appearing under different names on different maps. But changing a name on a government database doesn't necessarily change what the rest of the world calls it. From digital maps to tourism organisations and local communities, the Lake Ontario dispute shows how complicated it can be to rename a place – and who ultimately decides which name sticks. Who decides what goes on a map? Unsurprisingly, Canada has not entertained a change. In the US, the modification began with the federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the database used to standardise geographic names for federal use. Trump's executive order required "Lake America" to be added to the system and the former moniker removed. Google reflected the change in line with its long-standing policy of using official government naming sources, meaning US viewers now see "Lake America" while Canadian viewers continue to see "Lake Ontario". Apple Maps has also adopted the new name after pressure from Trump. But private mapping companies are not legally required to follow the federal designation. MapQuest, best known for being one of the earliest digital mapping tools, has refused to adopt the new name – and its refusal subsequently propelled MapQuest to number one overall on Apple's US App Store, with the company saying it had recorded more than 1.5 million installs across the US and Canada since the executive order was issued. "MapQuest focused on maintaining a name that people are familiar with," said Doug Berger, general manager at MapQuest. "When people need directions, they seek familiarity. It was an easy decision." What's in a name? The differing responses show how a federal name change can quickly produce multiple versions of the same geography. Oswego County in New York, which borders the lake, has chosen to retain Lake Ontario in its official and business materials, citing the historical significance of the name and expense to taxpayers and business owners for the cost of rebranding. "In our traditional Seneca language, its name is sga:nyodai:yoh, meaning 'beautiful lake'," said J Conrad Seneca, Seneca Nation President. "To us, Lake Ontario is not a political pawn. It does not separate the countries of the United States and Canada. It is all Indigenous land, which has been occupied by Indigenous people since time immemorial." When two names coexist But beyond the US and Canada, the impact of the name change may be limited. "The naming of bodies of water typically falls within national jurisdictions," explained Taufiq Rahim, senior fellow at non-partisan think tank New America and author of Trump 2.5: A Primer. "While there are international bodies like the IHO [International Hydrographic Organization], they do not have any authority to adjudicate disputes and typically when there is a dispute, two or multiple names can be used." A longstanding example is the dispute over "Persian Gulf" and "Arabian Gulf". Persian Gulf remains the standard name used by the UN, the IHO and most world atlases, while Arab states bordering the waterway – including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman – generally use Arabian Gulf and have encouraged allies to do so as well since the 1960s. More like this: A more recent example is Trump's January 2025 decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America". The new name was adopted on US federal maps and by some digital mapping services, while Mexico and international users continued to encounter "Gulf of Mexico" or both names. In Mobile, Alabama, the National Maritime Museum of the Gulf of Mexico had only recently spent nearly $100,000 (£74,000) rebranding when the federal name changed, leaving it with a newly minted identity tied to a now-disputed place name. At the time, its director told BBC Travel that another name change would require "a complete redo of the entire museum" and that she would follow the lead of city officials. Its website now identifies it simply as the National Maritime Museum of the Gulf. A similar issue is now playing out on the US side of Lake Ontario. The Lake Ontario National Marine Sanctuary, a federally designated protected area covering 1,722 sq miles (4,460 sq km) of waters and lakebed along the eastern New York shoreline, is retaining its name. The National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration, which comanages the sanctuary with New York State, says in a statement that the executive order applies to federal references to the lake itself but did not change the sanctuary's separately designated name. The agency is updating its materials to refer to the lake as "Lake America", while the sanctuary remains the Lake Ontario National Marine Sanctuary. A diplomatic wedge The organisational and financial burden of the name change will likely fall on the United States and its taxpayers. "This adds another unnecessary line to US expenses which in total can exceed hundreds of millions of dollars annually," said Usha Haley, Barton Distinguished Chair in International Business at Wichita State University. "People have to divert time, another important resource, to manage these changes for different audiences." While the change will have practical impacts, it's the symbolic implications that will likely have the most lasting effects. "Geographic naming becomes a proxy for sovereignty and power. It's geopolitical signalling on who controls national and bi-lateral narratives," said Haley. "The downstream symbolic and diplomatic consequences of a name change such as this can be much larger than the immediate commercial calculations." The change is likely to continue the erosion of diplomatic trust between Canada and the US, says Haley, hindering a weakening trading relationship between the two nations. Canada has long been a top destination for US exports, and the third-largest source of US imports, following Mexico and China. She said that symbolic disputes like this can become proxies for larger conflicts. --

item.title: The controversial US art of engraving whale teeth
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.11
Scrimshaw: The controversial art form on the brink of extinction As Moby Dick turns 175, some of the last American scrimshanders grapple with the legacy of maintaining one of the US's oldest art forms. Jade Gotauco spent her childhood among the skeletons of giants. Her father, Chet Gotauco, was a scrimshander – an artist who etched images onto the ivory of hunted whales. In pensive moments, she would slip under the arched jaw of a whale in his Rhode Island garden and sit atop a massive vertebra, watching insects scrabble across the porous bone. "My favourite smell in the world is the sandy aroma of ivory dust," said Gotauco, now an artist herself. Whale teeth adorn the walls of her studio in New Bedford, Massachusetts; she engraves them with nautical scenes in which sperm whales thrash the ocean to foam and whalers hurl barbed harpoons from minute boats. Ask Americans about the cultural legacy of whaling, and many will point to Herman Melville's classic novel Moby Dick, which turns 175 next month. Yet for all the book's brilliance, it's scrimshaw – the practice of artistically carving whale teeth and bones, which is considered one of the US's earliest homegrown art forms – that offers a true insider's view of the industry. Today, there's hardly any of those teeth and bones left on the legal market. Some scrimshanders, including Gotauco, believe the art form should disappear with them. "When the ivory is gone, this is over," she said. Scrimshaw was developed by sailors whose lives unfolded on whaling grounds around the globe as the industry expanded into a 19th-Century behemoth. They strove to depict a culture that, for a few lucrative decades, made New Bedford North America's wealthiest city per capita. "They saw their experiences as important," said Marina Wells, an assistant curator at the New Bedford Whaling Museum, which is home to the largest scrimshaw collection is the world. "You see that in their commemoration of whaling scenes, in all their meticulous detail." Some of the carvings throb with yearning, depicting homey scenes of faraway families. Others capture sailors rowing fragile, open boats dwarfed by the whales they pursued. They're communicating "the dangerous, faraway world of whaling", Wells said. "You have the bloody spouts of the whales after their lungs have been punctured… the intimacy of whalemen interacting with whale bodies that's really hands-on." To modern eyes, the scenes evoke the heartbreaking impacts on species hunted to the brink of extinction; yet the whalers, too, were often broken by the industry. At the Seamen's Bethel, an 1832 mariner's church located across the street from the museum in New Bedford (and which features in the opening chapters of Moby Dick), such risks are on poignant display. Lining its whitewashed sanctuary are marble cenotaphs commemorating those lost at sea. "After fastning to a whale, was carried overboard by a line and drowned," reads the tomb of Captain William Swain. Three sailors from the whaleship Cowper, aged 19, 22 and 24, share another memorial: "All lost by the upsetting of their boat, July 15, 1854, in the Ochotsk Sea." They died as American whaling reached a short-lived fever pitch. In 1857, more than 10,000 men worked aboard New Bedford whaleships, half the city's population at the time. Two years later, petroleum was discovered in Pennsylvania and the ensuing oil rush flooded American cities with kerosene – a comparatively cheap fossil fuel that would eclipse the whale oil used in lamps around the globe. By the turn of the century, American whaling was all but over. Scrimshaw lived on, however. The massive scale of the whaling industry produced a glut of teeth and bones, a byproduct that, at the time, had little commercial value. They gathered dust in attics and warehouses. "When I was a kid they had barrels of whale teeth down at the wharves and sold them for a couple of bucks apiece," recalled Michael Vienneau, a scrimshander on the nearby island of Nantucket, Massachusetts – another onetime whaling hub. Former homes of whaleboat captains surround his small shop, Scrimshander Gallery, in the heart of the island's historic district. A few blocks away is the Nantucket Whaling Museum, whose own significant scrimshaw collection includes pieces by Nantucket whalemen – and famed scrimshanders – Frederick Myrick and Edward Burdett. In the 1960s, scrimshawing surged in popularity, part of a folk-craft revival. (It even got a boost from US President John F Kennedy, an avid collector.) That's when Vienneau got his start, rummaging for cheap whale teeth as a teenager while visiting the island with his family. "Back then, everyone was a scrimshander," he said. "Now I'm one of the last." In part, that's because of the 1973 Endangered Species Act, which tightly restricted the sale of marine ivory. Today, scrimshanders engraving whale teeth and bones must work from the dwindling supply of teeth and bones that remain from before the act was passed – Vienneau has a stash in the back of his shop. "You'll pay several thousand dollars for a raw tooth now," said Vienneau. On a recent afternoon, he was sitting at his workstation squinting at a sperm whale tooth he was engraving with a scene of a sailor brandishing a harpoon at the tail of a diving whale. More teeth were piled in a nearby filing cabinet. His dog, Petey, grabbed a tooth and began to chew on it. Vienneau laughed. "Any dog that gnaws on a sperm whale tooth is a scrimshander's dog," he said, not getting up. As whale teeth grew scarce and expensive, some scrimshanders innovated, carving on cow bones and deer antlers. Even comparatively tooth-rich Vienneau experimented. Once, he flew to Alaska on a tip and spent three days digging a 30,000-year-old mammoth tusk out of permafrost near a remote copper mine. Yet, many purists insist that while such projects are both art and craft, they are not true scrimshaw, since the authentic form relies on the byproducts of historical whaling. Gotauco is one of them. Like some of her peers, she believes this means that scrimshaw is on the brink of extinction. Gotauco works exclusively on pre-1973 ivory and bones. Nearly a century ago, her grandmother emigrated to Boston from Newfoundland, and among her few belongings was a collection of whale teeth and bones she'd inherited from her family of seal hunters, cod fishermen and whalers. That's what Gotauco carves in her New Bedford studio, etching images onto the physical remains of her ancestors' legacy. Along with the whale teeth, Gotauco's grandmother passed along stories of what she said were Mi'kmaq roots. Whales factor into traditional Mi'kmaq stories, and the First Nations community hunted the animals sustainably long before the arrival of Europeans in North America. With her own deep reverence for whales, Gotauco has, at times, felt deeply uneasy about working with ivory. In the years since she learned how to carve scrimshaw by sitting beside her father in his workshop, Gotauco often wondered about the ethics of using materials pulled from the sea with such violence. Commercial whaling was an environmental disaster and a cruelly dangerous job; the beauty of the art form it spurred still catches at her heart. In the end, she embraced it as a form of remembering, calling it "the best way to honour the whales and whalers", albeit one that will likely fade in her lifetime. "When I run out of teeth along with everyone else, I'll raise a cup to the story's end," she said. "May we never get more." --

item.title: Tteokbokki (Spicy Korean Rice Cakes)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.06
Saucy, spicy tteokbokki stars tteok (chewy Korean rice cakes). Stir-frying the rice cakes gives them lightly crisp edges before they simmer in an umami-rich anchovy-kelp dashi spiked with gochujang and gochugaru. A generous amount of onion brings sweetness to balance the chile heat. Bok choy isn’t traditional, but its crisp-tender texture is a welcome counterpoint to all that chew. Odeng (Korean fish cakes) adds another bouncy texture, though you can leave it out. Hard-boiled eggs round things out and are particularly good dragged through the spicy sauce. Tteokbokki FAQs What kind of rice cakes should I use for tteokbokki? Look for cylindrical Korean rice cakes, sometimes labeled tteok or tteokbokki tteok. This recipe calls for the approximately 2½"-long variety, cut in half on a diagonal. Look for them in the freezer section at Korean and other East Asian grocery stores. Or online at sites like Weee! How spicy is this tteokbokki? This version is quite spicy, with heat from both gochujang and gochugaru. If you’re sensitive to spice, you can omit the gochugaru (Korean chile flakes), as some readers have done successfully. Keep in mind that the heat level of gochujang (fermented chile paste) varies by brand. What makes tteokbokki sweet? Tteokbokki recipes often balance their chile heat with sweetness. While some versions use sugar or rice syrup, this recipe relies on a generous amount of cooked onion to sweeten the sauce. Do I need fish cakes to make tteokbokki? No. Korean fish cakes, or odeng, are a common addition and bring a pleasantly bouncy texture, but they’re optional here. The anchovy-kelp broth provides plenty of savory depth without them. Recipe information - Total Time 45 minutes - Yield 6 servings Ingredients ¼ 3 1 8 8 ⅔ 2 1 ¼ 1 1 2 3 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Bring ¼ small onion, thinly sliced, 3 medium-large dried anchovies, one 2x2" piece dried kombu, 2 garlic cloves, smashed, and 3½ cups water to a boil in a small pot or large saucepan. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer at least 15 minutes and up to 45 minutes (the longer the stock simmers, the more flavor it will have). Step 2Strain stock through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; discard solids. Return stock to pot and reheat over medium. Add 8 oz. assorted frozen odeng (Korean fish cakes), bring to a simmer, and cook until just heated through, about 5 minutes. Step 3Meanwhile, mix together ⅔ cup gochujang (Korean hot pepper paste), 2 Tbsp. soy sauce, and 1 Tbsp. gochugaru (coarse Korean red pepper powder) in a small bowl. Step 4Heat ¼ cup vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. cylindrical Korean rice cakes (about 2½" long), cut in half crosswise on a diagonal, and cook, turning occasionally, until crisp, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 2 large onions, thinly sliced, and remaining 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; cook, stirring, until softened, about 2 minutes. Add gochujang mixture and cook, stirring occasionally, until combined and fragrant, about 1 minute more. Step 5Add fish cakes and 2½ cups stock to rice cake mixture and stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until sauce is thickened and rice cakes are tender, about 5 minutes. Step 6Add 1 medium head of bok choy, stems cut into ¼" pieces, leaves cut into 1" pieces, and 1 scallion, thinly sliced on a diagonal, and toss to combine, adding more stock by the tablespoon to thin if needed. Cook, tossing occasionally, until bok choy is wilted, about 2 minutes. Step 7Transfer tteokbokki to a platter. Top with 3 large eggs, hard-boiled, halved lengthwise, 2 Tbsp. toasted sesame seeds, crushed, and remaining 1 scallion, thinly sliced on a diagonal. Editor’s note: This recipe was first published July 2019; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more recipes with gochujang →

item.title: Onigiri (Japanese Rice Balls)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.58
Stuffed with savory fillings and wrapped in crisp nori, Japanese rice balls called onigiri are made for eating on the go. A convenience-store staple in Japan, they’re just as handy tucked into a lunch box or picnic basket. The key to onigiri that hold their shape is properly cooked Japanese short-grain rice. Rinsing and soaking the rice helps it cook evenly; shaping it while still slightly warm helps the grains stick together. Use damp, salted hands to prevent sticking—no rice cooker or onigiri mold required. This version offers three fillings: creamy tuna mayo, tart and salty umeboshi (pickled plums), or spicy kimchi. Once you’ve got the technique down, feel free to experiment with cooked salmon, spicy tuna, cod roe, leftover chicken salad, or crab meat. Just avoid anything too wet, which can make the rice balls difficult to shape. Onigiri FAQs What kind of rice is best for onigiri? Japanese short-grain rice, often labeled sushi rice at US supermarkets, is the best choice. When cooked, the grains cling together enough for the onigiri to hold their shape. Long-grain rice, such as jasmine or basmati, won’t hold together as well. How do you keep onigiri from falling apart? Shape the onigiri while the rice is still warm, using firm but gentle pressure to pack the grains together. Keep the remaining rice covered as you work so it doesn’t cool or dry out, and wet your hands with the salted water in the recipe to prevent sticking. What can you put inside onigiri? This recipe offers options including tuna mayo, umeboshi, and kimchi, but cooked salmon, spicy tuna, cod roe, leftover chicken salad, or crab meat are all fair game. Whatever you choose, avoid excessively wet fillings, which can make the onigiri harder to shape. Can you make onigiri ahead of time? Yes. These onigiri can be made up to two days ahead. Wrap each one tightly and refrigerate. For crisp nori, leave it off until you’re ready to eat; otherwise it will soften as it absorbs moisture from the rice. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 10 minutes (plus soaking) - Yield Makes 12–16 Ingredients 2 3 1 2 1 4 ⅓ ¾ ¼ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place 2 cups sushi rice in a large bowl and pour in cold water to cover by 2"–3". Gently swish around with your hands to rinse, then drain. Repeat process until water is almost clear (about 3 more times). Pour cold water over rice to cover by 1" and let soak 30 minutes (this will help the grains cook more evenly). Drain well in a fine-mesh sieve. Step 2Combine rice and 2½ cups water in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring occasionally. Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer until water is absorbed, 12–14 minutes. Remove from heat and let rice sit (still covered) 15 minutes. This will allow rice to steam and become tender. Uncover and gently fluff rice with a fork. Let sit until cool enough to handle but still warm. Step 3Meanwhile, cut three 8½x7½" toasted nori sheets into 3x1¼" strips with kitchen shears; set aside. Step 4Prepare the fillings. Mix one 5-oz. can tuna, drained, 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and 1 tsp. soy sauce in a small bowl to combine. Place 4 umeboshi (Japanese pickled plums) on a cutting board. Working 1 at a time, press a chef’s knife against fruit until pit is exposed; pull out and discard. Set fruit aside (no need to chop). Working over the sink and using your hands, squeeze liquid out of ⅓ cup Napa cabbage kimchi; chop into small pieces. Step 5Place 1 cup water in a small bowl and stir in ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Dip your hands into salted water, then scoop a little less than ⅓ cup rice into 1 hand. Form into a thick disk 3"–4" in diameter (keep remaining rice in pot covered). Create a small indentation in the center and add 1–2 tsp. tuna mixture or kimchi or a whole umeboshi. Mold rice up and over filling to create a sphere (filling should not be visible), then press firmly with index finger and thumb to form into a triangle. Place on cutting board or a baking sheet. Repeat with remaining rice and fillings, dipping your hands in salt water each time. (You’ll have extra tuna—save it for making a tuna salad sandwich or spooning onto crackers.) Step 6Place ¼ cup furikake or toasted sesame seeds on a small plate. Wrap bottom of each onigiri with a strip of reserved nori, then roll remaining exposed sides of onigiri in furikake. Do Ahead: Onigiri can be made 2 days ahead. Wrap tightly and chill. Editor’s note: This onigiri recipe was first published in September 2020. Head this way for our editors’ favorite ways to use leftover rice →

item.title: 31 Best Butternut Squash Recipes
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.32
Butternut squash is a seasonal favorite for a reason. It’s subtly sweet, easy to find, and versatile enough for everything from soups and pastas to salads and breakfast muffins. Where pumpkin spice lattes signal the arrival of fall, butternut squash quietly defines fall cooking. For the easiest preparation, roast cubed squash (pre-prepped store-bought squash is fine!) until browned and tender; puréed squash—even canned—is especially good in soups and sauces. Its sweetness plays well with sage and brown butter, chile, coconut, hearty greens, and plenty of cheese. Below, find our favorite butternut squash recipes, from cozy orzo with fried sage to crispy phyllo pie and savory-sweet tarte Tatin. What is the best way to cook butternut squash? The best is subjective, but roasting is certainly one of the easiest ways to cook butternut squash—and one of the best for bringing out its natural sweetness. For our go-to method, peel and seed the squash, cut it into 1½" pieces, and toss with olive oil, kosher salt, and black pepper. Roast at 450°F for 35–45 minutes, until browned, tender, and easily pierced with a fork. You can also roast butternut squash whole, simmer it for soup, or shred it for quicker cooking. Do you have to peel butternut squash before cooking it? Not always. Butternut squash skin is edible, but depending on the specific squash, it might be papery or leathery. For that reason, many cooks opt to peel the squash before cooking. If you love squash skin or plan to blitz the whole thing up for soup, feel free to leave it on. If roasting the squash whole or in halves, leave the skin on and scoop out the tender flesh after cooking. Can you eat butternut squash raw? What flavors go well with butternut squash? This gourd has range: Butternut squash pairs especially well with brown butter, sage, maple, nutmeg, coconut, chile, hearty greens, and salty cheeses like Parmesan and goat cheese. Its mild sweetness can handle warm spices and rich, savory flavors without getting lost. How do you buy and store butternut squash? Look for a butternut squash that feels heavy for its size, with hard skin free of bruises or mold. A squash with a thick neck and smaller bulb will have a smaller seed cavity—and more usable flesh. Store whole butternut squash in a cool, dark place, where it can keep for a month or longer; peeled or cut squash should be tightly covered and refrigerated for up to five days.

item.title: Sweet and Tangy Collard Greens
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.68
Collard greens have deep roots in Southern cooking. They’re a fixture on New Year’s Day, when eating greens is said to bring prosperity in the year ahead. Chef Julia Sullivan of Henrietta Red in Nashville serves them alongside black-eyed peas every January 1. “It’s something my mom has always done, and I think my grandparents, too,” she says. “It’s a superstitious thing.” Sullivan’s collard greens get their savory, subtly smoky flavor from bacon, onion, garlic, and red pepper flakes. They simmer until silky-tender in just under an hour, then get a sweet-tart finish from apple cider vinegar and a little sugar. This recipe intentionally leans tangy. If you like your collard greens less acidic, start with 2 Tbsp. vinegar instead of the full ¼ cup, then add more to taste. Collard greens FAQs How do you clean and prep collard greens? Remove the tough center ribs and stems. Next, stack the leaves, roll them up, and slice them crosswise into 1"-thick strips. Dunk the prepped collard greens into a large bowl (or sink!) filled with water. Swish the leaves around to loosen the grit and let them sit for a few minutes. Remove the greens from their container (don’t pour them out or the grit will get back on the leaves) and shake to remove excess liquid. There is no need to dry the collard greens for this recipe; a little bit of water helps them steam and wilt down. Why do you add vinegar to collard greens? Vinegar balances collard greens’ earthy, slightly bitter flavor and cuts through the richness of the bacon and broth. Adding it near the end of cooking keeps its flavor bright. This recipe calls for ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, but you can start with half that amount and adjust to taste. Can I make these collard greens without bacon? Yes. The bacon is optional, so you can simply leave it out, or trade it for beef or turkey bacon. For vegetarian collard greens, also swap the chicken broth for water or vegetable broth and add savory depth with a spoonful of miso paste. What other types of greens work with this recipe? Any sturdy cooking greens can work here, but expect differences in flavor and cooking time. Mustard greens and turnip greens are equally beloved in the South; either will make a slightly sharper, more peppery batch of greens. Kale is also a fine alternative. More delicate Swiss chard will become tender much faster, so reduce the cooking time accordingly. Recipe information - Total Time 55 minutes - Yield 8 servings Ingredients 3 4 1 4 1 3 3 ¼ 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 4 oz. slab bacon, finely chopped, if using, and cook, stirring occasionally, until some fat begins to collect in pot and bacon starts to look shiny, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, and cook, stirring occasionally, until golden and softened, 5–7 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Step 2Add 3 lb. collard greens (about 3 bunches), ribs and stems removed, leaves sliced crosswise 1" thick, to pot a large handful at a time, letting greens wilt slightly after each addition before adding more. Add 3 cups low-sodium chicken broth or water, bring to a simmer, and cook, stirring often, until greens are wilted and have lost about half of their volume, about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low, partially cover pot, and simmer gently, stirring occasionally, until greens are tender and liquid is almost completely evaporated, 25–30 minutes. Step 3Stir ¼ cup apple cider vinegar and 2 tsp. sugar into collard greens and cook until sugar dissolves, about 1 minute; season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Editor’s note: This recipe for collard greens was first published in our December 2017 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more ideas for your New Year’s table →

item.title: Cottage Cheese Lasagna
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.68
Cottage cheese lasagna skeptics, hear us out. Unlike ricotta, which can turn chalky, small-curd, whole-milk cottage cheese stays moist through the long bake. And when mixed with nutty Parmesan, melty Fontina, eggs, and garlic, it makes an exceptionally creamy lasagna filling. A combination of ground beef and hot Italian sausage brings plenty of flavor and richness to the meat sauce, while tomato paste and Worcestershire sauce give canned tomatoes long-simmered depth without the long simmer. Keep the sauce loose: That extra moisture is what cooks the regular dried lasagna noodles right in the baking dish. (Yep, no boiling required.) This may not be nonna’s classic (we’ve got BA’s Best Lasagna for that), but it’s deeply savory, exceptionally cheesy, and considerably easier to assemble. Cottage cheese lasagna FAQs What kind of cottage cheese should I use? Whole-milk cottage cheese is nonnegotiable. Lighter versions can make the lasagna watery and less flavorful. We prefer small-curd for texture, but large-curd works just fine if that’s what you have. Read more about our staff favorite cottage cheese brand: Do you have to boil lasagna noodles before baking? Regular dried lasagna noodles go directly into the baking dish—no boiling or soaking required. The relatively loose tomato sauce provides enough moisture to cook the noodles until al dente as the lasagna bakes. Can I make cottage cheese lasagna ahead of time? Yes. The baked lasagna can be refrigerated for up to 2 days. Let it cool completely, cover loosely with foil, and reheat, covered, in a 325° oven for 30–45 minutes, or until warmed through. You can also make the meat sauce up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate it in an airtight container; there’s no need to reheat it before assembling the lasagna, but you may need to add a few minutes to the baking time. You can also freeze the assembled, unbaked lasagna for up to 2 months. Thaw in the refrigerator overnight and then bake as directed. Can I use ground turkey? Absolutely. Swap the ground beef for ground dark meat turkey and the pork sausage for Italian-style turkey sausage. Because poultry is leaner, add an extra drizzle of olive oil if the pan looks dry. Recipe information - Total Time 2 hours (plus sitting time) - Yield 8–12 servings Ingredients 1 1 8 2 8 3 2 1 1 ¼ 1 2 6 12 2 24 12 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. ground beef (20% fat) and 8 oz. hot Italian sausage, casings removed, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until well browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer meat to a medium bowl, leaving fat behind. Step 2Add 2 large onions, finely chopped, 6 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to same pot; if pot looks dry, add up to 1 Tbsp. more oil. Cook, stirring often, until onions are translucent and golden around the edges, 8–10 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste and 1 Tbsp. dried oregano; cook, stirring constantly, until paste is brick red and beginning to stick to bottom of pot, 5–8 minutes. Return meat to pot. Step 3Add one 28-oz. can plus one 14.5-oz. can crushed tomatoes, ¼ cup Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper to pot. Bring to a simmer, stirring occasionally and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pot. Remove from heat and stir in 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Taste tomato sauce and season with more salt if needed. Step 4Toss 12 oz. Fontina cheese, grated (about 3 cups), and remaining 4 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 2 cups), in a large bowl to combine; measure out 1 cup cheese and set aside for topping. Add 2 large eggs, 24 oz. whole-milk cottage cheese, and remaining 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper to remaining cheese in bowl. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon until combined. Step 5Arrange 3 regular dried lasagna noodles in a single layer in a 13x9" baking dish. (If noodles are long, arrange parallel to long sides of baking dish; if noodles are short, arrange parallel to short sides of baking dish. Don’t worry about any gaps—noodles will swell as they cook.) Spread 1½ cups tomato sauce over noodles. Scatter one third of Fontina mixture evenly over sauce (mixture will be stiff; use hands to break off small pieces and scatter over sauce). Starting with another layer of noodles, repeat process, creating 4 layers of noodles in total and ending with a layer of tomato sauce. Top lasagna with reserved cheese. Step 6Place baking dish on a large rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake lasagna until sauce is bubbling around the edges, top is golden brown, and noodles are al dente (insert a skewer into center of lasagna to check), 75–85 minutes. Let sit at least 15 minutes and up to 45 minutes before serving. Do Ahead: Lasagna can be baked 2 days ahead. Let cool completely; cover loosely with foil and chill. Reheat, covered, in a 325° oven until warmed through, 30–45 minutes. Editor’s note: This cottage cheese lasagna recipe was first printed in September 2023. It has been updated for style.

item.title: The Great Date Boom is Here
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.92
There's nothing the internet loves more than a trendy ingredient. A few years ago, tinned fish became the It girl of the proverbial pantry, inspiring folks to swap their cheese boards for brinier, braver "seacuteries." Then cottage cheese blew up. Creators on TikTok and Reels proved that the creamy breakfast staple could be whipped, baked, blended, braised, and even frozen and churned for a delicious, protein-packed snack. Now, in 2026, we've seemingly reached peak pickle, with pickle-flavored everything from lip balms to (yes, even) lube. But the newest snack darling is one of the oldest ingredients in the world: the date. We saw it firsthand during Pantry Awards judging, when date-based products started landing in our submissions pile in numbers we hadn't seen before. These fiber-filled fruits are having a moment, in new and unexpected ways. Sour date snacks, date-sweetened boxed cakes, date-based candies and syrups, even the world's first soft drink made from dates—the primordial fruit is being reimagined for modern times, and people love it. "Consumers are starting to see dates as more than just a traditional dried fruit," says Amanda Sains-Harris, vice president of marketing for the date-based snack brand Joolies. Sains-Harris explains that the date boom has been a long time coming: Dates have been gaining popularity on social media and at industry trade shows for years. Now the fruits are flying off shelves. The category is up 24.1 percent in conventional grocery channels through June 2026, she says, citing point-of-sale data from the market-intelligence platform SPINS. As with cottage-cheese ice cream and tinned-fish cheese boards, folks seem to be looking for a healthy snack that still tastes good. Cardboard protein bars and chemical-tasting sodas are a thing of the past. "[Dates] check a lot of boxes without feeling overly engineered," Sains-Harris says. "Consumers also don't necessarily want to choose between better-for-you and indulgent anymore. They want both. Dates naturally live in that sweet spot." Grace Finerman founded Date Smarter!, which makes decadent chocolate-covered date caramels (and won one of our 2026 Pantry Awards, BTW). She agrees that consumers are seeking out healthier alternatives to sugary snacks—but they don't want zero-sugar, either. "Five years ago people were really turning to stevia," Finerman says. "I think the pendulum has kind of switched to people now wanting not cane sugar, but something sweet that's not processed." Despite their sticky sweetness, she says, dates are naturally low-glycemic. They're also high in fiber (6.7 to 8 grams per 100 grams), which is a tempting proposition in the age of GLP-1s and fiber-maxxing. And they make great fuel, especially when filled with protein-packed nut butters. "We actually have a large customer base of endurance athletes, professional and collegiate athletes, and overall fitness enthusiasts," says Sophia Karbowski, co-founder of Realsy, which specializes in date snacks stuffed with different nut butters. "The natural combination of carbs, sugar, and fiber in dates—plus a bit of added protein and fat from the natural nut butter filling—is the perfect source of clean energy athletes are looking for." Dates are also incredibly versatile, which makes them attractive to brands, too. On their own, the dried fruits are indulgent. But wrap 'em in bacon or stuff 'em with something sweet, and they're practically heaven. Since they're so sticky, they make excellent binders. Mashed together à la the viral peanut butter date bark that's taken over TikTok, or blended into a paste, they hold nuts, fruits, and other ingredients together. And when they're dried and powdered, they make an excellent refined-sugar substitute in baking mixes, syrups, and more. "We [Date Smarter!] use date powder, which is when you take a date that's dehydrated and run it through a processor," says Finerman. "We make all our caramel with that." Food trends come and go, but these brands are all betting that dates are here to stay (and given that they've been around since literally Mesopotamia, we think so, too). Karbowski expects to see dates on labels across the whole grocery store, from beverages to baking mixes. Sains-Harris wants to push the boundaries of where the fruits can go, and she's already getting creative: In May 2026, Joolies launched Date Sours, which swap the traditional buttery fillings for flavors like sour blue raspberry and cherry cola. "We always say dates are 'the original palm tree candy,'" says Sains-Harris. "And I think they're finally getting the spotlight they deserve." Whatever happens, we're here for it.

item.title: 5 Easy Ways Our Editors Turn Store-Bought Gnocchi Into Dinner
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.39
Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month it’s all about shelf-stable gnocchi. You would never expect an unassuming pouch of store-bought gnocchi, tucked tautly in plastic, to be good. But it is! The little potato dumplings have a pleasantly chew and just enough earthy savoriness to make them feel like more than a pantry fallback. The trick is how it’s made. Most shelf-stable gnocchi starts with dehydrated potato flakes, which give each dumpling a consistent texture and make the product stable enough to be stashed away in your pantry. A clever little bit of food engineering. And there’s no shortage of ways to put this ingredient to work. Stir-fry gnocchi in a hot skillet until they crisp up. Plop them into creamy sauces, where they bob along like buoys. Roast them alongside veg for a one-and-done dinner. There’s a whole lot this humble little pouch can do. Read on for how our editors cook with store-bought gnocchi at home. This Crispy Gnocchi Caprese is a staple in my household. Oddly enough, the last time I made it, I could only find the mini shelf-stable gnocchi in my grocery store. Who knew that even existed? Not me. Because of their small size, the little dots of pasta cooked up quicker than the standard ones, which means dinner was ready in no time. I used a haul of Sun Golds and cherry tomatoes, plus balls of mozzarella and torn basil dressed in bracing vinegar and fruity olive oil. Shoveling into my mouth with a spoon was the only correct way to eat. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking I love busting out shelf-stable gnocchi anytime I need to round out a meal with a carb and don’t want to make rice or pasta. While boiling them and tossing them in sauce is great, I also like to roast them on a sheet-pan so the outside gets crisp while the centers stay pillowy. You don’t have to schlep out a pot, don’t have to wait for water to boil, and you can snuggle them up next to proteins and veggies so everything cooks at once. My current favorite combo is sausage and broccoli rabe; the fat from the sausage sizzles the pasta while the broccoli rabe adds a peppery bite. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor I bought my first package of shelf-stable gnocchi to make a sheet-pan recipe that everyone in the office couldn’t stop talking about. And wow did it upend everything I’d assumed about the premade pasta. It now ends up in my shopping cart more often than not. But what a revelation trying former staffer Kendra Vaculin’s Gnocchi-Leek Soup With Greens still was. So enchanted by the crispy texture the oven provided, I’d entirely missed out on the plushy goodness of these little dumplings in soup. They’re the perfect addition to this weeknight-friendly dinner, adding heft and chew to an otherwise bright meal. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor Many, if not most, of my meals during the week are sheet-pan dinners. I love being able to toss something in the oven, then forget about it. Store-bought gnocchi is perfect for this treatment, and you don’t even need a recipe. Just preheat the oven to 400° or 425°. Dump a bag of gnocchi onto a sheet pan along with your vegetable of choice; say, broccoli florets, chopped bell peppers and onions, or halved brussels sprouts. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and sprinkle of salt and pepper. Roast until the gnocchi are browned and the vegetables are tender. Add some melty cheese on top—funky raclette is my vote here. Keep baking (or even broil) until the cheese melts into gooey puddles. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director The first time I consumed vacuum-packed gnocchi was in 2022 when deputy food editor Hana Asbrink developed her recipe for Sheet-Pan Gnocchi With Soy-Dressed Mushrooms. I was taken aback. These little nondescript nubbins were…good?! A few months later, it was again Hana who introduced another new-to-me food, rosé tteokbokki. Completely smitten by this stew, I started to think about what I could use in place of the tteok, an ingredient my colleagues and I love very much, but can’t always find in every grocery store. The answer, it turns out, is a pouch of gnocchi. They’re doughy and dense, but in this recipe, that’s a good thing. As the gnocchi cook, their starch gently thickens the auburn sauce, and they soften into a comforting bite. —Shilpa Uskokovic, senior Test Kitchen editor

item.title: HexClad Pans Are Not Worth the Money
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.20
Odds are you’ve encountered a HexClad pan before. Even before Gordon Ramsay’s $100 million cash infusion in 2024, the company had successfully wheatpasted its products across the internet with targeted ads and promotional partnerships with food influencers (and most recently I learned, in the Love Island villa). When people find out that I test cookware for a living, I get more questions about HexClad cookware than anything else I cover—by a lot. So I’m writing this stand-alone review. To lay my biases out there: I’m not a fan of nonstick cookware. When I have to test it for my job, I provide several addendums outlining my issues with nonstick cookware—its relatively short lifespan, the way nonstick’s ubiquity prevents people from learning proper cooking technique—and the alternatives I think you should buy instead. Still, as is true with HexClad or any other piece of nonstick cookware, I evaluate these products relative to each other to determine what the best nonstick pans out there are—if you absolutely insist on purchasing one. Which brings me back to HexClad. I’ve cooked with the brand’s pans several times myself—initially several years ago with its original PTFE pans and more recently with the ceramic nonstick versions that replaced them. Here’s what I will say. How HexClad pans differ from other types of nonstick cookware HexClad belongs to an increasingly popular niche in the cookware ecosystem known as “hybrid cookware.” These pans differ from conventional, smooth nonstick by having a textured surface with raised stainless-steel “peaks” and coated nonstick “valleys.” According to HexClad, this pattern provides “a durable surface” that protects the ceramic nonstick coating in the pans depressions. If you’re using a metal spatula for example (one of the cardinal sins of cooking with nonstick pans), the raised peaks will keep the spatula from scraping the nonstick valleys. The brand’s nonstick surfaces are similar to what you’ll find with other ceramic nonstick cookware lines. While companies like to boast about the proprietary ceramic nonstick formulas, almost all variations of the material are manufactured using the same sol-gel process. On the About page of its website, HexClad claims that its cookware “brings together the performance of stainless steel, the durability of cast iron, and the convenience of nonstick.” They also offer a lifetime warranty (however it only covers factory defects). The brand also claims that “HexClad products are made to last a lifetime.” I will get into my issue with these claims below, but these statements run counter to fundamental realities about the science of ceramic nonstick cooking surfaces. What it’s like cooking with HexClad Nonstick pans are great at first impressions, so it didn’t surprise me that these pans deliver on their slippery promises fresh out of the box. I ran the skillet and a saucepan through our standard testing procedure and yes—they did okay. - The pans imparted a nice sear on chicken thighs and released with ease. - Crepes and pancakes release from the surface without resistance, and despite the textured surface, left no weird pattern. - The performance faltered slightly with sunny-side up and scrambled eggs. The first few eggs came off fine with some batches leaving bits of egg residue on the pan. - The saucepan failed to charm me. The textured surface made whisking things like custard or béchamel irritating as the whisk repeatedly snagged on the textured surface. The texture was more nuisance than asset here. Overall, our whole testing team agrees that nonstick surfaces are superfluous when applied to pans other than skillets or sauté pans. Design wise, the pans aren’t too heavy and have nice handles. As to why they have nonstick coating on the bottom of the pan, where it is in direct contact with the heat source…beats me. Bottom line, I’d say these pans when compared to other types of nonstick cookware, are fine. However, I do have some serious issues with HexClad specifically pertaining to how long it claims its pans last. How does HexClad’s performance stand up over time? Dissatisfied HexClad customers have filled internet forums with their complaints about the pans’ longevity and quality, lamenting how eggs and other foods started sticking after just months—sometimes weeks—of regular use. I experienced the same degree of sticking when I cooked with a year-ish-old HexClad set. This isn’t unique to HexClad: All ceramic nonstick coatings degrade over time because of the fundamental nature of the material itself. I spoke with Rob Macfarlane, a professor of metallurgy and materials science at MIT about the limitations of ceramic nonstick. As he explained it, ceramic nonstick coatings are often silica-based sol-gels, a solution of tiny silica particles that fill the metal pan’s microscopically rough surface texture and create a smoother, slick surface. However, these coatings are quite brittle. Repeated heating and cooling will cause small fractures in this coating to develop due to thermal expansion and contraction. As fractures accumulate over time, surface friction increases, reducing the nonstick qualities of the pan. This is why consistently used nonstick pans have a lifespan of one to two years. While you can still cook with them, the continued deterioration of their coatings will lead to chipping and diminishing performance. Translation: The act of cooking itself will cause any ceramic pan to deteriorate over time. But now I need to shift focus to another claim HexClad makes, which is that in order to maintain their nonstick qualities, HexClad pans must be seasoned with neutral oil and left over medium heat. Seasoning. A nonstick pan. You know about seasoning. It’s the thing you have to do to prime your cast-iron and carbon steel cookware. It’s the thing that people complain about. It’s the thing that pushes people to opt for nonstick coatings in the first place. I find HexClad’s suggestion to oil their pans before use obnoxious for multiple reasons. First, it negates the whole low-maintenance value proposition that makes nonstick cookware attractive to so many people. Second, you can’t truly season the surface of a HexClad pan. Neither its stainless-steel peaks nor its ceramic nonstick valleys will develop a seasoning in the same way a carbon steel or cast-iron pan would. When you oil a pan made from one of those materials and subject it to high heat, the oil breaks down and forms a layer of polymerized fat that bonds to the porous metal cooking surfaces. This seasoning repels moisture and prevents food from sticking at a molecular level. This process cannot take place on a ceramic nonstick surface, full stop. While it is technically possible to develop a short-term layer of polymerized fat on a stainless-steel surface, you can not maintain and develop it long-term. Why? Stainless steel is a significantly smoother material, making it more difficult for polymerized fat to adhere to its surface. Additionally, the metal has a non reactive layer of chromium oxide that further inhibits the strong chemical bond necessary for an actual seasoning to develop. If you’re like, “Wait, what about the gunk on my stainless-steel pans?” Well, unpolymerized fat and other food molecules can certainly accumulate on a stainless-steel pan, but this makes your pan more sticky, not less (and is also gross!) It would be one thing if HexClad were to say that you must re-season the pan each time, (which is basically just oiling a pan, which is basically step one of cooking.) Yet the care instructions state, “over the first few weeks of use, your HexClad Hybrid cookware will perform better as it re-seasons from the fats in the food you are cooking.” Okay, so let's not use the term seasoning. HexClad is still advising you to pretreat your pan with fat prior to cooking, the same way you would to turn a stainless-steel surface nonstick. And if a HexClad pan requires the same amount of care and prep as a stainless-steel, cast-iron, or carbon steel pan, I don’t see any point in purchasing HexClad over these other, more durable materials. To the credit of HexClad and other brands making nonstick cookware, I think consumers have naive expectations for these products. Sticking is typically a consequence of improper cooking technique, and a nonstick surface of any kind can only do so much to prevent it. The temperature of a pan, the amount of oil used, and timing, all factor into how or why food sticks. Even with the nonstickiest of nonstick pans, you can still end up with stuck-on food if you aren’t mindful of what you’re doing. Is HexClad worth the money? It would be one thing if these pans were some budget line, but they are marketed as a premium product at premium prices. The 12-inch fry pan sans lid costs $179. For context, an All-Clad pan of the same size goes for $160. The difference is that All-Clad is the standard bearer for professional-quality stainless-steel cookware, with a reputation for longevity backed by decades of use in tens of thousands of kitchens across the country. If after all this you’re still like “Hmph! I want a textured pan, I don’t care what you say!” Fine, but Oxo, GreenPan, and Zwilling all make cheaper versions—so go nuts, pal. The verdict Don’t blow big money on a pans that won’t last. Simply accepting that, sometimes, things will stick while you’re learning to cook will set you up better in the long run. And if you want the convenience of a nonstick surface, at least go for one that doesn’t insist that you use and treat it exactly like the pans they claim to innovate upon. I review nonstick pans because it’s my job, but I have always and will continue to advocate for the alternatives that get better with time, see here, or here, or here.

item.title: Everything is a Luxury Item Now
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.14
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the rise of AI-made reservations. We must address one oft-ignored issue that’s become too acute to overlook: Whoever is in charge of wine at Trader Joe’s needs a wellness check. I’m seeing apple pie wine. I’m seeing pumpkin spice chardonnay. I’m concerned and I want to help. This week chef Daniel Humm of Eleven Madison Park fame entered the consumer packaged goods (CPG) game. His new product is called Riff, a line of boxed pasta dishes that come with seasoning mixes and crunchy toppings, plus suggestions on each box for how you can incorporate fresh ingredients. (Riffs—get it?) Also important: 13,000 cases later, the CDC has announced the Cyclospora outbreak is over. Phew! One less concern among the many other food safety issues currently unfolding—like “small stones and other hard objects” in ice cream. Also in this week’s Open Tab: why every food item seems like it’s a luxury item, Chipotle’s shiny new partnership with Palantir, China’s blueberry scam, and the legacy of Prince’s favorite cheesecake. The era of expensive everything A burger at DC’s Le Diplomate will set you back $29—more than twice what it cost 13 years ago, as The Washington Post reports. In New York, Gigi’s set off a wave of menu pricing discourse with a $77 roast chicken, they’re doing $100 hot dogs in Florida, and across the country, prices at McDonald’s have doubled over the last decade—even as serving sizes have gotten smaller. Why is everything so much more expensive now? The answer is multifaceted: The war in Iran is skyrocketing fuel prices which, in turn, has a profound impact on global food systems, plus inflation is rising steeply—hence this week’s Fed rate bump—and, finally, restaurants’ supply, labor, and utility costs are still rising. A lot of restaurant items are priced as luxuries, but our sense of luxury has also skewed in recent years. Caviar, once rarified, is now par for the course. Wagyu beef, a high-end, hard-to-source import years ago, is on countless menus at all price points. For $158—that’s two roast chickens at Gigi’s—you can indulge in an all-you-can-eat Wagyu and seafood experience, in fact. All this means diners will learn to be more discerning. With prices like these, determining which meals warrant this kind of spending is all the more important. Why is Chipotle working with Palantir? What’s the opposite of a joint slay? Whatever that term might be, that’s how I’d describe an international fast-casual restaurant chain partnering with a multibillion dollar tech giant hell-bent on destroying every last scrap of data privacy for normal people. I am talking, as you may have guessed, about the new collab between Chipotle and Palantir. Palantir, which has been contracted to work with ICE to track migrants’ movements, will be working with Chipotle on a food safety risk platform—essentially a means to try to reduce the number of food safety incidents at the chain’s locations. “The platform brings key information together in one place, enabling our teams to more effectively identify trends, prioritize follow-up, and make proactive, data-informed decisions,” Laurie Schalow, Chipotle’s chief corporate affairs and food safety officer, in a statement to Wired. Will all of this actually result in greater food safety at Chipotle or is this simply a scheme to collect data on your burrito order? Well, reader, at this juncture it’s hard to say. Approximately a decade and a half ago, the fruit giant Driscoll entered the Chinese market to make blueberries happen, bringing in growing technology to lay claim to the best blueberries with the best genetics, according to The Wall Street Journal. By 2025, Chinese production of blueberries doubled that of the US. But Driscoll wasn’t the only one cashing in on the blueberry rush. Chinese business owners allegedly copied those blueberry-growing technologies, and some even stole Driscoll’s copyrighted blueberry varieties. The blueberry market in China is booming, but Driscoll has filed more than 20 lawsuits (and won two) seeking damages against Chinese companies, according to WSJ’s report. Vanessa Drews started making cheesecakes just for the love of the game—a cheesecake-head, if you will. That all changed when Prince (yes, that Prince) developed a taste for Drews’s desserts. Last September, she opened up a brick-and-mortar shop four miles from the late icon’s Paisley Park home, where she serves up the same Prince-approved recipes. Read on to discover the rest of Drews’s story.

item.title: Prince's Favorite Cheesecake Delivers the Funk
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.13
About 20 miles southwest of downtown Minneapolis, in the small town of Excelsior, a curiously named business sits wedged in a strip mall among a taqueria, a nail salon, and a pet groomer. Wander inside and you might think you’re in a museum dedicated to Prince, the Minneapolis-born musical genius who lived just four miles south of here at his private home and recording studio complex, Paisley Park. The purple walls are dotted with photos of the homegrown superstar, who passed away 10 years ago this year. The business may double as a de facto homage to the self-proclaimed Purple Yoda, but it’s actually one of the hottest bakeries in the Midwest. Welcome to Cheesecake Funk. When owner Vanessa Drews opened the cheesecake bakery in September 2025, it quickly became the talk of the baked good loving Twin Cities. And the Prince connection goes far beyond the bakery’s purple walls. But for lovers of all things sweet and creamy, Cheesecake Funk is today a veritable mecca for those in the know. Dig, if you will, the superlative turtle cheesecake laden with rich dark chocolate, gooey caramel, and crunchy toasted pecans, with a crispy bottom crust. The exact recipe for that crust is a secret, but Drews admits to using cinnamon and a healthy portion of brown butter. It’s a masterpiece of contrasting textures and layered flavors, which perhaps explains why it’s Cheesecake Funk’s best seller. For Drews, a single Black mother of two, it all started back in 2002 when she was still a hobby baker. A lifelong lover of cheesecakes, she baked them for family and friends who began requesting them for every party and holiday gathering. “I started tweaking the recipe over time, mixing the crust with brown butter, adding cinnamon here and there,” Drews says. At the time she was working a day job as a senior paralegal and making cheesecake in her free time. But money was tight, and she picked up a part-time gig selling merchandise at Paisley Park on the occasional evenings that Prince threw open-to-the-public parties. One day in 2013, she showed up with a cheesecake. “Prince always had band members and other employees coming here from other parts of the country and the world,” Drews recalls. “So, I put the cheesecake in the fridge with a note saying that anyone was welcome to a piece. I wanted to provide some good food for them and say: ‘Welcome to Minnesota.’” Stocking the fridge with cheesecake became a ritual. Soon Drews noticed the speed with which her cheesecakes were devoured. Who could be responsible? And then, scrolling through the social media site formerly known as Twitter, a particular post caught her attention: A meme of two monkeys trying to resuscitate a fellow simian that featured the words, “The moment you find out somebody ate the last piece of Vanessa’s cheesecake.” It was uploaded from an account managed by Prince. “I thought: ‘Oh my God, I’m the Vanessa he’s referring to!’” she says. “I was euphoric." Prince began calling her edible handiwork “cheesecake funk,” often including the phrase on invitations to parties at Paisley Park, writing “HELPYOSELFTOSOMECHEESECAKEFUNK.” After that, at Paisley Park parties, Prince would occasionally walk by Drews and, with his trademark smirk, say, “What’s for dessert, Vanessa?” before walking away. (This anecdote may surprise Prince fans—there’s a common misconception that he was 100% vegan. Not so, at least when it came to cheesecake.) While Prince’s endorsement certainly boosted her confidence, she didn’t feel ready to quit her job and become a full-time baker. But then, a big break: In 2019, a friend of a friend offered a bite of Drews’s cheesecake to Kam Talebi, founder and CEO of Kaskaid Hospitality, the Twin Cities–based enterprise with 18 restaurants nationwide. He loved it enough to put it on the dessert menu of the Eden Prairie location of Crave American Kitchen & Sushi Bar, a small chain of restaurants scattered across the Midwest. “A few months later, Kam called me and he said, ‘You’d better prepare for volume. I’m adding your cheesecake to all eight Twin Cities locations of Crave,’” Drews recounts. “I remember sitting at my desk at the law office and thinking, Oh my gosh! Is this really happening?” She decided to pull the proverbial trigger. Drews dipped into some of her 401(k) plan to buy baking equipment and set up shop in a rented hotel kitchen. Fast-forward to September 2025, when she opened a bakery near her home in Excelsior, using the moniker Prince came up with, Cheesecake Funk. Prince’s favorite variety, turtle, is decidedly bold, but there are no wallflowers among the 17-plus flavors on offer at any given time, many of them seasonal. This past summer’s flavor, lingonberry, was appropriately Minnesotan given the state’s large population of people with Scandinavian heritage, and it was enough of a hit that Drews added it to the permanent menu. “It’s very tart, but has bursts of sweetness, similar to strawberry,” Drews says. “It’s just really refreshing and light, perfect for summer.” As the weather shifts, it’s on to the next: The current fall seasonal flavors include a deceptively simple apple cheesecake topped with stewed fruit laced with cinnamon. These days, one has ample options when seeking Cheesecake Funk products in the Twin Cities. In downtown Minneapolis, stop by Union Rooftop, Brit’s Pub, Butcher’s Table, Wood + Paddle, or one of a handful of locations of Crave in and around the Twin Cities, or even Paisley Park. Or you can go to the original Cheesecake Funk in Excelsior and say hello to Drews. Prince fans have begun stopping there on their way to or from Paisley Park. “The other day I had a couple from Germany, and this afternoon, these sweet ladies came in from the Netherlands,” Drews says. “People come to find me because they appreciate Prince.” “I’m so thankful to him,” she continues. “Prince is like the gift that keeps on giving.”

item.title: Disneyland Discount Tickets: September 2026 Guide
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.72
You just can’t argue with that Disney magic. Whether you’re a Disney adult or a begrudging occasional visitor, at some point throughout the day, a little bit of Disney dust will hit you. Maybe it’s the fireworks, or the rides, or the many, many Disney-shaped food items. If not that, it might be seeing the excitement on kids’ faces when they run into a princess, Avenger, or cartoon character IRL. I’m no Disney evangelist, but I would say that if you can’t have fun at a theme park, consider looking inward. (And okay, as a former resident of both California and Florida, I have spent more than my fair share of time at the parks on both coasts.) All that aside, trips to the parks are expensive, so if you’re here to find ways to save, I get it—below, find all the current discounts and promotions to be aware of before planning your next trip to Disneyland. Disneyland discounts for Magic Key holders For the uninitiated, annual passholders are called Magic Key holders, and they can pop in and out of Disneyland as they please (with some terms and conditions in there). Through September 7, these theme park enthusiasts can save up to 20% on select Standard and Premium room types at premium Disneyland Resort hotels. The offer is tailored to Sunday through Thursday night stays at Disney’s Grand Californian Hotel & Spa, Disneyland Hotel, The Villas at Disneyland Hotel, and Pixar Place Hotel. Of note, you must present a valid active Magic Key pass at check-in to secure the discounted rate. Disneyland discounts for military members Savings are available on an ongoing basis for active-duty and retired US military personnel, including the National Guard, Reservists, the US Coast Guard, the US Space Force, the Commissioned Corps of the Public Health Service (PHS), and the Commissioned Corps of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Tickets start at $98 for kids of these travelers and $104 for adults purchasing a one-day, one-park ticket. These tickets may not be combined with other ticket discounts or promotions, and cannot be sold or transferred. Locals get discounted Disney tickets for as little as $71 Through October 8, 2026, Anaheim, California, residents can purchase one-day passes for as little as $71. This is valid for any day visit taken by October 8. Proof of eligible residency, including a valid government-issued photo ID, is required for both purchase and admission. Save on multi-day Disneyland tickets While going to the parks for just one day is the most cost-effective option, your per-day cost does go down when you opt for multi-day tickets instead. For example, a one-day ticket will run you between $104 and $224 based on the date you select. If you go for two days, your price per day starts at $168; for three days, it drops to $142 and up per day; for four days, from $120 per day; and for five days, from $104 per day. A few things to note: Disneyland is much smaller than Disney World, with just two parks, so it is possible to cover a good amount of ground in a single day. However, especially if you’re coming from out of town, you may want a few days there so there’s less pressure to squeeze every ride and meal into a single day. There’s also the question of purchasing one-park-per-day tickets or upgrading to a Park Hopper ticket (an extra $100 per day). If you’re visiting for just one day, I’d suggest the Park Hopper ticket so you get to experience both parks. For multi-day trips, it really comes down to preference; you’ll want to decide between chunking out your park visits or having the freedom to roam back and forth between parks throughout the day (which, size-wise, is definitely doable). Save on food, merchandise, and add-ons with Disneyland discounts beyond tickets Tickets are one thing, but once you’re inside the park, it’s easy to rack up charges on dining, souvenirs, and add-on experiences. If you’re concerned about sticking to a budget, there are a few surefire ways to cut costs. For one, take a look at the gift card section next time you're at Target, Costco, or Sam’s Club, as they sometimes sell discounted Disney Gift Cards. If you’re interested in an additional credit card, new Disney Inspire Visa Card holders can earn up to $500 in the form of a $300 eGift to spend at the park and a $200 statement credit after you spend $1,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. You’ll also earn Disney Rewards Dollars on all card purchases, including: - 10% on card purchases made directly with Disney+, Hulu, and Stream.ESPN.com - 3% on card purchases at gas stations and most Disney US locations - 2% on card purchases at grocery stores and restaurants - 1% on all other card purchases When it comes to food, placing mobile orders via the Disneyland App can help you track food spending more easily and find quick options in place of more expensive sit-down meals. Lastly, consider dining off-property or at Downtown Disney to curb costs. On my last visit to Disneyland, I stayed right across the street from the entrance at Park Vue Inn—the proximity was amazing, and it had a pool and hot tub. Rates start at $229 a night, and rooms with kitchenettes are available, which make coming back midday to prep meals a breeze. item.title: The Best Time to Visit Greece For Island-Hopping, Fewer Crowds, and Ideal Temperatures
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.50
Many people travel to Greece to spend time along its coast or on one of its myriad islands—a holiday destination that leaves salt on your skin. And there's good reason to come for that alone, although it gives little sense of a country that is roughly 80 percent mountainous. Beyond the beach there are farming villages where a scenic adventure can segue into local wine and seasonal, farm-to-table food. Some places are worth visiting for a particular occasion: the grape harvest, or an Orthodox feast that brings a village’s scattered families home. Naturally, the best time to visit Greece depends on which of those pleasures you want to build a trip around. An Easter visit calls for early hotel reservations, while an island holiday late in the year needs a close look at ferry schedules and hotel closing dates. For help with those choices, we draw on recommendations from Curated Greece co-founders Vasilis Sarmantas and Seetha Ramanathan, along with Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist Ronnie Liadis of Liadis Travel. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. When is the best month to travel to Greece? September is the best month for a first visit to Greece that combines Athens with an island. The sea has had all summer to warm up, and ferries still serve the main routes frequently. Sarmantas and Ramanathan recommend it for beach holidays with fewer crowds than midsummer: In the Cyclades, the Aegean island group that includes Mykonos and Santorini, the most sought-after hotels remain busy well into the month of September, and sometimes even October. Late May to early June is these experts' other preferred window, near the start of a beach season —which generally lasts until early October. Liadis favors May for wildflowers and comfortable weather, though the sea can feel cool this time of year. The water is warmest from July to September, Sarmantas and Ramanathan told us. April and May are good months to visit Greece for sightseeing. Cooler weather lets you linger at exposed sites such as the Acropolis, the ancient hilltop citadel of Athens, and the open-air theater at Epidaurus on the Peloponnese peninsula southwest of Athens. For a trip in late October, look to Athens or larger southern islands such as Crete and Rhodes, where more hotels stay open year-round. On smaller resort islands, check hotel closing dates alongside ferry schedules before settling on a destination. What is the temperature in Greece by month? July and August are the hottest months, but keep in mind that an Athens forecast tells you little about a village high in the Pindus mountains of the northern mainland. The table below gives a broad seasonal guide using historical monthly averages for five destinations: Athens, the northern city of Thessaloniki, Corfu Town, Heraklion (on Crete), and Rhodes Town. Each range spans the lowest and highest city average in that group. These are benchmarks, so individual days, especially during heat waves, can be considerably hotter. | Month | Typical daytime high | Typical overnight low | |---|---|---| | January | 49–60°F | 34–48°F | | February | 52–60°F | 36–48°F | | March | 58–62°F | 40–50°F | | April | 66–68°F | 46–55°F | | May | 74–79°F | 54–60°F | | June | 81–88°F | 61–68°F | | July | 84–92°F | 65–72°F | | August | 83–92°F | 65–73°F | | September | 80–85°F | 59–69°F | | October | 70–76°F | 51–62°F | | November | 60–68°F | 44–56°F | | December | 52–63°F | 37–51°F | In summer, plan archaeological visits for the earliest entry time available, and check the site’s hours that morning since extreme heat can bring abrupt closures. The EU’s Copernicus climate service recorded extreme heat stress in parts of Greece during summer 2025. Hot, dry, and windy conditions also raise wildfire risk: consult Civil Protection’s daily risk map before a rural excursion and follow local restrictions and any 112 evacuation alerts. Keep in mind that a clear sky does not guarantee a smooth ferry crossing. The meltemi, a northerly wind over the Aegean, can take the edge off a hot beach afternoon while roughening the sea enough to disrupt ferries. When strong winds are forecast, confirm your sailing with the operator before heading to the port. What is the cheapest time to go to Greece? November through March is generally the cheapest time to go to Greece (apart from Christmas and New Year’s). Sarmantas and Ramanathan put the potential savings on international flights at 30 to 50 percent of high season's prices. In Athens and Thessaloniki, that lower hotel bill still comes with plenty to do: Museums stay open and neighborhood restaurants have local regulars to feed through winter. On the islands, check what will be open around your hotel, since many resorts close from roughly November to April. For an island holiday, compare May with late September and early October, when rates can ease before seasonal businesses close. Check the connections while you compare hotels. An extra flight or an overnight stay between ferries can easily absorb what you saved on the room. Orthodox Easter fills rooms in places known for their Holy Week traditions, and its date may differ from Western Easter. Keep an eye on those dates, and if they align with your travel plans, book early and plan to arrive before the weekend. On Good Friday, worshippers follow an epitaphios, a flower-covered bier representing Christ’s tomb, through the streets. The mood changes at midnight on Holy Saturday, when candles are lit to cries of Christos Anesti, “Christ is risen.” By Sunday, families are gathering around tables of roast lamb. In Corfu, the island’s philharmonics, or local brass bands, accompany the Good Friday processions. At 11 a.m. on Holy Saturday, residents drop botides, large clay pots, from balconies. An Easter Sunday arrival would miss both. Patmos, in the eastern Aegean, draws pilgrims to the cave where tradition places St. John’s writing of Revelation. During Holy Week, the abbot of the Monastery of St. John washes the feet of 12 monks in the square of Chora, the island’s capital, reenacting Christ’s gesture to his disciples. In the Peloponnese town of Leonidio, the midnight Resurrection service is the moment to be there, as illuminated paper balloons rise from parishes across town. When is peak season in Greece? July and August are the busiest and most expensive months, although the folks from Curated Greece say the broader high season now extends from early June into mid- or late September. This is when island travelers have the fullest choice of hotels and ferry departures. Book ahead for a particular room or sailing, especially if your dates leave little room to adjust. Around August 15, Greece’s own summer holidays add to the international rush. The Feast of the Dormition, known as Dekapentavgoustos and often called “summer Easter,” commemorates the Virgin Mary’s death. Many families return to their home villages, while pilgrims sail to the Cycladic island of Tinos to visit the revered icon at the Church of Panagia Evangelistria. Some make the ascent from the port on their knees. At village panigiria, the communal feasts held for religious holidays, music, and dancing continue long after church. These homecomings help explain why a ferry can be full even when its destination is absent from the usual resort itineraries. If you want to visit such destinations, book your ferry tickets as soon as the relevant schedule is available, particularly if you need space for a car. How many days are enough for a trip to Greece? If you’re visiting Greece for the first time, try to go for about seven nights for a mix of city and island experiences. “With a week, you can comfortably explore Athens in two or three days, spend a couple of days on one or two islands like Santorini for iconic views or Mykonos for beach time and night life, and possibly include a day trip to a key mainland cultural site like Delphi or Meteora,” as suggested by Sarmantas and Ramanathan. If you have extra time, an additional stop on the mainland or another island, such as Crete or the Peloponnese, can provide further depth, from archaeological wonders to beautiful natural landscapes. Liadis offers a helpful reminder about factoring in travel time: “I don’t recommend less than three nights on any island because a good part of the time is spent transferring from island to island. There are flights that connect to the islands via Athens, but the ferry system is reliable and convenient.” What is the nicest part of Greece to visit? For a first visit, Crete can fill a week without another ferry crossing. Of its two main cities, Heraklion puts you near Knossos, the Bronze Age Minoan palace, while Chania gives easier access to the western beaches and White Mountains. Either lets you combine the coast with lunches in mountain villages, though trying to cover both ends of Greece’s largest island leaves too much of the week to driving. In the village of Elos near Chania, chestnut celebrations in late October or early November put roasted nuts and sweets preserved in syrup on the table.
