In the Cyclades, decide how much of the holiday you want to spend looking at the sea and how much in it. Santorini’s caldera hotels overlook a sea-filled volcanic basin with steep shores, so the famous view does not come with a long sandy beach below. For that, consider Naxos, where inland farming villages also give you reasons to venture away from the coast. On nearby Paros, look around the fishing village of Naoussa for restaurants and hotels within reach of the beach. May and early fall allow more comfortable exploring, with warmer water at the later end of the season. Corfu, in the Ionian Sea, is a good option if you don't want to rely solely on the beach because there is a substantial town to explore. Centuries of Venetian rule shaped its old streets and its cooking. Order pastitsada, meat in a spiced tomato sauce served with pasta, for a sense of how that history survives at lunch. On Kefalonia, another Ionian island, more of the holiday involves driving through mountain country to reach the next cove, so it is a better choice when beach weather is the priority. Spring and fall are good times for a road trip through the Peloponnese. Stay in the harbor town of Nafplio for visits to Mycenae, a Bronze Age citadel, and the theater at Epidaurus. From there, head south toward the Mani peninsula’s stone tower houses or inland to mountainous Arcadia. Here, the roughly 47-mile Menalon Trail connects villages in eight sections of varying difficulty—the stage between Stemnitsa and Dimitsana, for example, follows old mule tracks past cliffside monasteries above the Lousios River and is demanding. Choose your section based on local advice rather than assuming that any village-to-village walk will be gentle. In central Greece, Athenians spend ski weekends in Arachova, a mountain town below Parnassos Ski Centre. Its tavernas serve grilled formaela, the peppery local cheese made from sheep’s or goat’s milk. Farther south in Arcadia, the village of Vytina puts the eight slopes of Mainalo Ski Centre within reach of a village stay. The nearby MANNA hotel occupies a restored 1929 sanatorium, surrounded by fir trees at about 3,900 feet. The forest also merits a visit after the spring or autumn rains, when local guides lead mushroom hunts. Snow has become less dependable in Greece’s mountains, so check lift conditions close to departure and choose bookings you can change. Zagori, in the mountainous Epirus region of northwestern Greece, deserves several days on foot. Its UNESCO-listed landscape includes stone villages connected by old paths and arched bridges, with forests around the Vikos Gorge that turn color in autumn. The stone staircase into Vradeto was the village’s only approach until 1973. Walking it makes the region’s former isolation easier to grasp, and the route can continue to the Beloi viewpoint above the gorge. The village of Aristi is a convenient base near the Voidomatis River, while Papigo gives access to hikes in the Tymfi mountains. Save high routes for snow-free conditions and ask locally about trails after rain. For a fall trip built around wine, start in Thessaloniki and explore the vineyards of Macedonia in northern Greece. The Naoussa here is a wine town, distinct from its namesake on Paros, and the surrounding vineyards grow the red grape Xinomavro. The Kir-Yianni wine estate offers tastings and vineyard tours year-round by reservation. For a harvest visit, ask the estate when it expects to pick before booking your dates. The timing can differ by several weeks between vineyards, even in the same year. Do Americans need a visa for Greece? US tourists can visit Greece without a visa for up to 90 days in any 180-day period, counting time spent elsewhere in the Schengen Area toward the same limit. According to the Department of State, the passport must be valid for at least three months beyond departure, with a blank page available for each stamp. ETIAS, the European Union’s planned travel authorization for visa-exempt visitors, is not yet operating and is not accepting applications. Its timetable has changed, so check the official EU site before departure for the launch date and any new requirements. Plan your stay • Where to Eat, Stay, and Play in Athens: From modern art galleries and tsipouro bars to traditional live-music rebetadikos for dancing the night away, • The Best Airbnbs in Santorini: Where to rent for a private slice of the Greek Island this summer. • A ‘Mamma Mia’–Inspired Packing List for Greece: Flowy white dresses, linen skirts, and overalls included. • 11 Best Hotels in Mykonos: Smart, stylish, and supremely laidback places to stay.

item.title: The Most Remote Places on Earth You Can Actually Visit
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.24
Reaching the most remote places on Earth takes more than just a plane ticket—it takes patience, endurance, and often a string of connections that make the arrival feel like an achievement in itself. These are places where airports are rare, ships arrive only a handful of times a year, and the communities you meet are outnumbered by wildlife. What they offer in return is a kind of distance that feels almost impossible in the modern world—skies free of light pollution, landscapes shaped by extremes, and the rare quiet that comes from being far beyond the usual travel circuit. Why do we seek remoteness? Journeys to places like these are rarely simple, but that difficulty is part of the allure. They remind us what travel feels like when the destination is hard-won, when the act of arriving carries its own reward. In the Kerguelen Islands, there are no hotels or tour buses, only wind, sea, and wildlife. In Russia's Oymyakon, for example, just stepping outside is an act of endurance. And on South Georgia, hundreds of thousands of penguins gather on beaches once scarred by whaling. In a world where so much feels accessible, true remoteness has become rare. These are the most remote places on Earth that shift our sense of scale and remind us that there are still corners of this planet where distance is intact. Kerguelen Islands, Southern Indian Ocean Nicknamed the “Desolation Islands,” this French territory sits marooned in the southern Indian Ocean, approximately 1,865 miles from Madagascar. Few places feel so utterly cut off. Volcanic cliffs plunge into storm-lashed seas, while king penguins and elephant seals crowd the beaches in their thousands. Nobody lives here permanently—only rotating teams of scientists, engineers, and unconventional travelers. What surrounds you is a world sculpted by wind, sea, and stone, where humanity has left little mark. How to get there: The French supply vessel Marion Dufresne II sails from Réunion Island several times a year. The voyage takes around six days. Quttinirpaaq National Park, Canada On the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, just shy of 500 miles from the North Pole, Quttinirpaaq lives up to its Inuktitut name: “top of the world.” It is a place of extremes—glaciers stretch for miles, jagged peaks rise from polar deserts, and the summer sun never sets. Muskoxen graze the tundra, Arctic wolves hunt in silence, and traces of ancient Inuit encampments remind you how long people have endured at this latitude. Few visitors make it here, but those who do find a landscape that feels infinite. How to get there: Travel first to Resolute Bay in Nunavut, then connect by charter plane to Tanquary Fiord, open only in the summer months. Ittoqqortoormiit, Greenland Few places capture the human will to survive like Ittoqqortoormiit, a settlement of around 450 people perched at the edge of Scoresby Sound, the world's largest fjord system. Wooden houses painted red, blue, and yellow dot the snowy cliffs, while rhythms of life here still follow the seasons: hunting and fishing sustain families, sled dogs line the streets, and in winter the sea ice seals the town off from the outside world completely. The surrounding waters carry drifting icebergs, and it's not unusual to see polar bears wandering the coast. How to get there: Reachable by helicopter from Nerlerit Inaat Airport, itself connected by small aircraft from Reykjavik, Iceland. Longyearbyen, Norway Longyearbyen, in the Svalbard archipelago, is the northernmost town of its size in the world. Despite its isolation, it's surprisingly lived-in, with cafés, a craft brewery, and even a fine-dining restaurant. Beyond town, reindeer roam freely, glaciers carve the landscape, and the Global Seed Vault safeguards the world's crops in a frozen hillside. Here, summers pass in endless daylight; winters in an unbroken stretch of night. How to get there: Daily flights connect Oslo and Tromsø to Svalbard Airport, making it one of the more accessible remote places. South Georgia, South Atlantic Ocean A remote island once known for whaling, South Georgia is now a sanctuary where wildlife has reclaimed the land. More than half a million king penguins gather on its beaches, while elephant seals occupy the shore in extraordinary numbers. Rusting relics of abandoned whaling stations remain, and the grave of polar explorer Ernest Shackleton—the Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer who led three British expeditions to the Antarctic—lies at Grytviken, a pilgrimage for history enthusiasts. After decades of ecological strain, including the introduction of reindeer by whalers, conservation projects are now restoring the island’s native habitats and protecting its fragile ecosystem. How to get there: No airports exist—visitors arrive by expedition ship, usually as part of cruises departing from Ushuaia, Argentina. McMurdo Station, Antarctica On Ross Island, McMurdo Station is the largest research base on the continent, supporting around 1,000 people each summer. It has been the launch point for many of Antarctica’s most important expeditions, from early 20th-century journeys led by Scott and Shackleton to modern scientific studies on climate change and glaciology. The surrounding landscape—glaciers, volcanic peaks, and the vast Ross Ice Shelf—has shaped much of what we know about the polar world. Travelers can’t stay at McMurdo, but expedition cruises to the Ross Sea sometimes include landings nearby, offering the rare chance to stand at the centre of Antarctic exploration. How to get there: Expedition cruises to the Ross Sea depart from New Zealand or Australia, with limited charter flights from Christchurch supporting specialist itineraries. Pitcairn Islands, South Pacific Ocean Home to just under 50 people, the Pitcairn Islands are one of the world’s least populated territories. Settled by the HMS Bounty mutineers in 1790, the community is still made up of their descendants. Life moves at a slow rhythm, shaped by the island’s rugged volcanic terrain and the surrounding Pacific waters. For visitors, the appeal lies in the intimacy: hiking to hidden caves, diving into crystalline waters, and being welcomed by almost every resident. How to get there: Fly to Tahiti, then on to Mangareva in French Polynesia. From there, a supply ship makes the 32-hour crossing to Pitcairn several times a year. Changthang, Ladakh, India High on the Tibetan Plateau, Changthang is a high-altitude desert where the air is thin and the landscape seems endless. Nomadic Changpa herders graze yak and goats across sweeping plains, while saltwater lakes like Tso Moriri and Pangong Tso shimmer beneath snow-capped peaks. Black-necked cranes, wild asses, and even snow leopards are spotted here, adding to its sense of undisturbed isolation. How to get there: Flights run from Delhi to Leh, followed by an overland journey across rugged mountain passes into the plateau. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: How I Travel: Shania Twain Brings Spinach To Her Hotel Rooms
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.49
Most people’s carry-on bags hold items like a sweater, book, tablet, chargers, snacks, maybe hand sanitizer, and an eye mask. Pop music icon Shania Twain is bringing a mini recording studio everywhere she goes. “In my carry-on for many, many years is my Pro Tools set-up for recording,” says Twain. “I do a lot of writing and recording in my hotel rooms, so I bring an Apollo [audio-processing hardware], my microphone, the laptop, all of that.” Her latest album, Little Miss Twain, features songs that she wrote and produced years ago, with themes stretching back to her teen romances. The best-selling country-pop artist of all time, Twain got nostalgic with Condé Nast Traveler about her first business-class flight, which she took after signing her record deal, as well as more recent travel—like her 12-night stint performing with Harry Styles in London at Wembley Stadium this past summer—and shared future trips, like the one she’s plotting to India this winter. Plus, other quirky items on her packing list. Her favorite mode of transportation: If we're speaking about touring, bus is my favorite way to travel. I just love moving into it and then not having to unpack every day. I don't love living out of a suitcase. I like to settle in; that's my thing. I like sleeping in small spaces. Her first flight in business class: It was from Toronto to Nashville, after I signed to my record label. They bought me a business-class ticket. People were still smoking on planes then, and I’m so sensitive to cigarette smoke. I thought ‘gee, if you’re moving up in the world, do you have the right to say, Do you mind?’ I was so perplexed that people could smoke in business class, but that was the way it was. And I remember the food was better. Her packing approach: I'm a good packer, a really good packer. I would say I'm a thoughtful packer, in the sense that I've got a good routine down. I pack in categories: I’ll do the shoes, then jewelry, then pajamas, then underwear and socks. Quite organized. How she passed the time in London between shows this summer: I love London. I love to walk, and London has a lot of really quaint, walkable areas with pubs and cafes and shopping. I love Hyde Park. I've ridden horses and gone to concerts there, and it's all walkable from the hotels. And there's the theaters! This summer, I took advantage of seeing Paddington, which was extraordinary. It was just adorable. The cast is really exceptional. I mean, the story is great—we all know the story—but I just thought the theater was ideal for the intimacy of it. Her favorite places to stop through on tour: Quebec City is a great place for a day off on tour. It’s very Paris-like, this little time capsule—like a little bit of Paris was brought over to Canada. It's so quaint and beautiful, and on the water. Very walkable as well. The part of Canada she wants more tourists to see: I would recommend people visiting Canada see more of where I'm from [in northeastern Ontario], because nature is the most extraordinary. We've got areas where you can go moose watching, for example. You're not in a zoo. You see all these wild animals and it's really beautiful. Her priorities when planning a vacation: Food definitely motivates me when I'm traveling. I need to make sure that I'm going to enjoy the food because, as a vegetarian especially, it can be quite limiting. One of my favorite places to visit and eat as a vacation trip is Egypt, because it gives me everything I need. I like to walk everywhere and see the architecture. That's a big thing for me—to see history on every block. I love ancient history particularly, and the cities and villages that are museums in themselves. And then, like I said, the food. The Lebanese food [in Egypt] is extraordinary for vegetarians. So that's a part of the world that I really love. Why she chose to have a home in Switzerland: I had a language base of French growing up in a bilingual town in Ontario and I wanted to maintain that, which I get to do in Switzerland, living on the French side. Plus, the benefit of being in Switzerland is you have the valley and the lakes below, but then you can just drive up for 20 minutes and be on a glacier. I'll never give up my four seasons—and being Canadian, I love winter. The items she needs in her hotel room: One thing I miss the most when I'm traveling in hotels is not being able to cook. I love to cook so I always make sure that there is a really good blender, and that I have things like raw spinach, avocados, tomatoes, and bread—things that I can put olive oil and salt and pepper on and make my own snack without calling room service. The place she’s never been that she’d like to see next: Even though I’ve been very lucky to travel in my career, there's a lot of places I haven't been. I've never been to India. I've got a trip planned this January to Hyderabad, because I have friends from there. I've heard so much about [the country], and I know so many people that have gone, but this will be my first experience. And don't forget, India has the best vegetarian food!

item.title: These US Airlines Have Mishandled the Most Bags in 2026, According to New Data
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.16
Most travelers have experienced that sinking feeling at baggage claim when the carousel stops and their checked luggage is still nowhere to be seen. While lost or delayed bags are sometimes just an unfortunate part of air travel, there are some airlines that statistically mishandle checked bags more often than others. The situation can be extra frustrating in 2026, as most carriers have significantly raised the cost of checking luggage on domestic and short-haul international routes to an average of $45 for the first bag. Despite the elevated fee, US airlines have collectively mishandled 1,120,760 checked bags in the first six months of 2026, according to new data from the Department of Transportation (DOT). That’s an average of about 0.5 bags mishandled per 100 bags enplaned. Although those numbers can seem shocking, they’re similar to mishandled baggage rates for the same stretch in 2025, which saw an average of 0.52 bags mishandled for every 100 loaded into planes’ cargo holds. If you’d like to avoid your carefully packed luggage being on the wrong side of those statistics, it’s a good idea to know which airlines routinely have the highest rates of mishandled bags. The DOT’s monthly air travel consumer reports compare the 13 largest US airlines and how many bags each carrier mishandles per 100 loaded onto planes. A mishandled bag includes baggage that is lost, delayed, damaged, or stolen. In the first half of 2026, American Airlines had the highest rate of mishandled bags, with an average rate of 0.73 mishandled bags per 100 enplaned, the DOT data shows. Closely following is American’s wholly owned regional subsidiary Envoy Air, which mishandled an average of 0.72 bags per 100 enplaned. United Airlines was next, with a mishandled baggage rate of 0.66 bags per 100 enplaned from January to June 2026. On the flip side, low-cost carrier Allegiant Air had the best baggage handling rate, with just 0.12 bags mishandled per 100 enplaned. Travelers who want to keep close tabs on their checked luggage can put devices like Apple Air Tags into their bags and track them during each stage of the flight. Many airlines now integrate Air Tag data into their baggage tracking process, allowing travelers to share the device location with customer service representatives through their mobile apps. Here’s a look at the DOT’s full US airline rankings for the most mishandled bags per 100 enplaned for the first half of 2026: - American Airlines: 0.73 bags - Envoy Air: 0.72 bags - United Airlines: 0.66 bags - Skywest: 0.55 bags - Republic Airways: 0.53 bags - Alaska Airlines/Hawaiian Airlines: 0.53 bags - Frontier Airlines: 0.51 bags - Spirit Airlines: 0.47 bags - PSA Airlines: 0.44 bags - Delta Air Lines: 0.38 bags - Southwest Airlines: 0.32 bags - JetBlue Airways: 0.31 bags - Allegiant Air: 0.12 bags

item.title: The Best Beaches in Italy, From Sicily to Puglia
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.92
You’d be hard-pressed to find a more quintessential Italian pastime than spending a summer day at the beach—and the best beaches in Italy lend themselves to precisely that kind of leisurely indulgence. The country has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, so you can bet there’s a piece of waterfront for everyone. Some are long, wide strips of sand dotted by neat rows of lounge chairs and umbrellas, while others are rocky inlets or hidden coves reachable only by boat or hike. The list below culls our picks for the best beaches all along the peninsula and on the islands, from Liguria in the north to Sicily in the south, along with tips on where to stay near each. Some are accessible by train or public ferry, while others require a car (road trip, anyone?). Keep in mind that summer (especially July and August) is the high season, so expect beaches to be more crowded than at other times of the year. For fewer crowds, consider shoulder season months like May, early June, and September. Tips for visiting the best beaches in Italy For some expert advice on planning a beach-oriented itinerary in Italy, we tapped Georgia Yuill, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and Butterfield & Robinson’s region director for Italy. Though the best time to visit Italy can vary depending on the type of trip you want to have, a beach vacation warrants some summer vibes—and strategy. “The best time to go to the beaches of Italy are on the weekdays of June, early July, and September,” Yuill says. “Waterfronts in Sardinia and Sicily are particularly lovely in September with the water warmed up over the previous months and visitor numbers low, leaving you with a tranquil and gorgeous setting.” Yuill says the beaches can get crowded on the weekends in June, July, and August, when you’re competing not only with fellow tourists for spots on the sand but also with Italians who are on their own vacations as well. “That said, experiencing the coastline or islands such as Sardinia by gulet or catamaran is an excellent solution to finding quiet inlets and harder-to-reach beaches,” says Yuill. This list features beaches that are free to access, but if you can swing it, private strips of sand at beach clubs are a great option as well. “Not only are they perfect for people-watching, but they provide all the things travelers may not have packed, like umbrellas and lounge chairs,” Yuill says. Plus, families traveling to Italy with kids will especially appreciate the lifeguards on duty. And who can say no to the convenience of showers, changing areas, and eateries? Finally, Yuill suggests choosing an area designated as a Blue Flag Beach, which indicates that it is clean and well cared for from an environmental perspective. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Kris Fordham and Caitlin Morton.

item.title: The Best Things to Do in Monaco—the Crown Jewel of the French Riviera
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.64
Monaco’s ritzy reputation began more than 150 years ago with the debut of the James Bond-famous Belle Époque-style Casino de Monte-Carlo. Throw in a fresco-adorned clifftop palace, the super yacht–lined harbor, and one of the most anticipated events in the luxury sports industry’s social calendar (the Monaco Grand Prix), and it’s no wonder the principality has emerged as a summertime playground for jetsetters and royalty alike. Flanked by the Mediterranean Sea and the French Alps, the petite principality may be the world’s second-smallest state, but with freshly revamped grande dame hotels, a sleek new seaside promenade, and two billion dollar land expansion project Mareterra—which rapidly earned the nickname “world’s most expensive neighborhood”—Monaco is proving it’s more than royals and race cars. There’s also the prestigious Rolex Monte-Carlo Masters tennis tournament—and some seats even come with panoramic Mediterranean Sea views, too. While the principality may claim a few superlatives—with the annual Monaco Yacht Show, the unofficial closer to high season, often touting the world’s priciest super yacht—it’s much more accessible than most travelers realize. And thanks to an uptick in direct seasonal flights, it’s even easier to reach. Here’s where to go and what to do when you get there. Getting there and around The Nice airport is the gateway to the French Riviera, and now you can fly direct year-round from New York (JFK) or Newark with business-class-only La Compagnie; seasonally from Atlanta, Philadelphia, and Washington, DC; or from most major cities in Europe. If you’re taking a train from another part of France or Italy, you’ll have to connect in Nice or the Italian border town of Ventimiglia. From Nice, it’s a 25-minute drive or seven-minute helicopter ride to the principality via Blade. Once you arrive in Monaco, the easiest way to get around is by foot or bus (you can tap a credit card or pay for a ticket onboard). Carshare services like Uber and Bolt will drop you in the principality, but you can’t request a car to take you from Monaco to another destination. You can, however, order a taxi or request one through your hotel and charge it to your room, if you’re staying at one of the Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer properties. The best things to do in Monaco Monaco’s rocky shoreline doesn’t sport the same swaths of sandy beaches as some of its neighbors, which is why so much real estate is dedicated to pools (there’s even an open-air, Olympic-sized saltwater pool on the port). Sunbathe along the waterfront solarium that's the Côte d'Azur version of Scandinavia's floating saunas, or set off on a half-day whale-watching safari around the coast to spot migrating fin and sperm whales. While Cannes is defined by La Croisette and Nice’s pebble-strewn shores are bordered by the Promenade des Anglais, Monaco’s main beachside stretch, the crescent-shaped sliver Larvotto, recently received a modern makeover helmed by Renzo Piano. A handful of beach clubs and restaurants spill out along the palm-fringed promenade. For a more subdued scene than Saint-Tropez that’s every bit as glamorous, sprawl on a floral-patterned sunbed (a nod to the 1960s-era motif designed for Princess Grace) at La Rose des Vents’s seasonal, Gucci-themed beach club. If you don’t want to peel yourself away from the plage for lunch (and who could blame you?), you can dine on caviar and king crab tacos (a definite must-order) at your lounger. Across the bay, cliffside La Vigie Zanoni, chef Simone Zanoni’s al fresco Italian eatery, resembles an intimate, unfussy version of Capri. The sweeping views of the principality alone are worth it—and if you’re taking part in a boat day, you can even pull up to the restaurant’s private dock. Rooftop Nikki Beach Monte Carlo’s cabana-clad pool embraces the Riviera’s party-heavy beach club vibes, but for something more understated, cruise over to La Môme Riviera’s rose-striped parasols and Italian restaurant, which hover along the rocks in nearby Roquebrune-Cap-Martin. When you arrive at the private pontoon via boat (Star Boat Luxury offers shuttles departing from Port Hercule), the tucked-away enclave feels like you’ve stumbled upon a private island. Nearby Loulou Pirate is a spruced-up take on a fisherman’s hut and embraces the same barefoot-chic vibe today as when the original locale was a hotspot for the likes of Brigitte Bardot in the 1960s and ‘70s. At Monaco’s newish fashion district, One Monte-Carlo, near the casino, splurge or window shop at designer boutiques like Cartier and Saint Laurent, or sip a glass of champagne under the Art Nouveau-style pavilions at Le Jardin Belle Epoque by Perrier Jouët’s pop-up outside Hôtel Hermitage Monte-Carlo. For vintage and second-hand luxury finds, browse Le Dressing’s two boutiques in the portside La Condamine district. If your trip falls over a Friday, hop on a direct, 30-minute train to Ventimiglia for the open-air weekly market—among the largest in Italy—and pause for lunch at waterfront stalwart Marco Polo 1960. In the evening, catch a performance by the likes of Norah Jones, James Blunt, and John Legend during the Monte-Carlo Summer Festival; take a seat for a classical concert or opera like Carmen at Opéra de Monte-Carlo; or watch a film under the stars at the open-air cinema beneath the Oceanographic Museum. Where to eat and drink The French Riviera is dotted with Michelin-starred restaurants running from the coast up to perched medieval villages like Èze and the neighboring town of Menton, where for the past 20 years Mauro Colagreco’s three-star Mirazur has been as revolutionary for France’s culinary scene as Noma for Denmark’s. Inside Monaco’s covered Condamine market hall in the Place d’Armes square, Colagreco’s Mitron Bakery features a selection of sourdough loaves that are milled and baked daily in Menton. (While the indoor market is closed for construction, vendors are serving from kiosks in the square.) If the weather is nice, head to the smaller port in Fontvieille to Les Perles de Monte-Carlo for platters of freshly shucked oysters and perfectly seasoned sea bass (this place fills up fast, so reserve in advance). Nearby, the original Beefbar—which has expanded to include a swish collection of restaurants everywhere from Saint-Tropez to luxury cruise ships and private flights—draws a local crowd for lunch (the smash cheeseburger is one of the house favorites). The terrace of Liguria-born Zeffirino is another go-to for its Genovese pesto coating fresh, square-shaped mandilli pasta (even Frank Sinatra was a fan of the namesake chef Zeffirino’s pesto). At new eco-district Mareterra—where homes and buildings were designed by Renzo Piano, Tadao Ando, and Sir Norman Foster and residents include billionaires and Formula 1 local legend Charles Leclerc—a handful of shops and restaurants have also opened their doors, including London transplant zēphyr, anchored by its own sultry cocktail bar Naked & Famous. Throughout the principality, young chefs are shaking up stuffy fine-dining concepts, replacing decadent, drenched-in-sauce dishes with lighter fare that lets the Riviera’s seasonal ingredients shine. One of the best examples is Blue Bay Marcel Ravin, where subtle flavors of the Caribbean and its distinct spices are infused into the Martinique-born chef’s cuisine. Picture artisanal plates dressed with vanilla sugar cane vinegar and cassava crumble. The open kitchen unfolds into the airy dining room accented by natural materials like sleek wood paneling and coral-inspired screens disguising tables, so they feel more like private booths—but the true showstopper is the seaside terrace, especially at sunset. There’s no shortage of places to see-and-be-seen in the principality, from Roaring Twenties-inspired rooftop restaurant La Môme Monte-Carlo, where a singer serenades tables that peer over the port and Prince’s Palace, to Amazónico, another rooftop setting that overlooks the glistening casino and where entertainment ranges from Bossa Nova and Cuban music to DJs spinning “electro-tropical” beats. Across the square, book dinner at Greek-Mediterranean GAIA, which draws a fashionable crowd of locals and famous faces year-round (discretion is key, so avoid trying to snap shots of F1 drivers). Take a seat in the foliage-filled terrace, which feels plucked out of the Athens Riviera, and sip a selection of expertly curated Greek Assyrtiko wines. Share classic spreads like taramosalata before ordering from the restaurant’s own fish market, where options include carpaccio or ceviche, as well as grilled whole fish with a drizzle of lemon oil. Then, as the evening progresses, join the well-heeled crowd filing into speakeasy-style, members-only lounge NYX. Monaco’s nightlife ranges from bottle service at late-night lounges like velvet-lined SASS CAFE to DJs spinning tribal house beats at nearby COYA Monte-Carlo, a waterfront, Peruvian-fusion eatery with a pisco bar and lounge. (If you’re after a cavernous, late-night club, you’ll find a few of those, too, including Twiga and Jimmy’z Monte-Carlo). For something more lowkey, start or end your evening with apéro (pre-dinner drinks and light bites) or a nightcap under the Eiffel-designed glass dome at Gustave at Hôtel Hermitage or at Hôtel de Paris’s legendary Le Bar Américain, a 1920s-era haunt popular with everyone from Joséphine Baker and Cary Grant to Lady Gaga. Open year-round, jazz, swing, blues, and soul performers entertain every evening and bar snacks include some of the best barbajuans (Swiss chard-filled fritters) in town. Where to stay Monaco’s sprinkling of five-star Belle Époque hotels are huddled around the Carré d’Or (Golden Square), crowned by the historic centerpiece Casino de Monte-Carlo. The independently owned, Jacques Garcia-designed Hôtel Métropole Monte-Carlo boasts designer names like the Spa Métropole by Guerlain and the Karl Lagerfeld-designed Odyssey, an urban rooftop oasis with a heated saltwater pool and Italian poolside restaurant Zia. Reviving Joël Robuchon's longstanding institution, the late chef’s former right hand is at the helm of the namesake, two Michelin-starred Les Ambassadeurs by Christophe Cussac. Jacques Garcia was brought back on board to spearhead the two-year renovation of the restaurant, which features an open-kitchen concept, chef’s table with 360-degree views of the team at work, and cigar lounge in the extended lobby bar, where a trio of museum-worthy pieces by Pablo Picasso, Francis Bacon, and Andy Warhol anchor the space. One other aspect popular with fans of the former Robuchon eatery has also been brought back: the legendary bread and dessert trolleys. Facing the casino, the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo is perhaps the most emblematic of Monaco, and after a multi-year, multimillion-dollar renovation, it’s among the most modern as well. You’ll still see timeless glamour in the gilded dining room of three-star Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse, with its gold leaf-painted frescoes and columns (and Bordeaux-modeled wine cellar lined with more than 350,000 bottles). But with revamped Art Deco rotunda rooms overlooking the super yacht-filled harbor, and the expansive Prince Rainier III Suite, outfitted with a two-level outdoor lounge and infinity pool perched over the casino, rooms not only offer some of the best views, they’re some of the most luxurious in the South of France. The family-friendly Monte-Carlo Bay Hotel & Resort feels like more of a Mediterranean island retreat, with seaside sun beds and beach fare from two Michelin-starred chef Marcel Ravin; Balinese-style beds by the sand-bottom lagoon; and water sports like parasailing and tubing available off the hotel’s pontoon. At the opposite end of the principality, in what’s technically considered France, the terra cotta-colored Monte Carlo Beach exudes retro, 1930s charm with Art Deco, California villa-inspired rooms hugging the coastline, and an Olympic-sized saltwater pool that served as a backdrop for Helmut Newton’s Vogue and Vanity Fair shoots. A perk for guests staying at Monte-Carlo Beach, Hôtel de Paris, and Hôtel Hermitage: access to the pool and private plage at Monte-Carlo Beach Club, which sports a Jacquemus-themed pontoon with matching striped beach beds. For a stay that comes with sky-high rooms showing off sweeping views of the principality, modernist The Maybourne Riviera is perched along the rocky peninsula of Roquebrune-Cap-Martin and features chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s New York transplant, abc kitchens riviera, plus a striking infinity pool suspended nearly a thousand feet above the sea.

item.title: An Art Lover's Guide to the Coastal Michigan City of Saugatuck
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.51
With its thriving arts and culture, rich array of farm experiences, dynamic dining landscape, and long stretches of Lake Michigan soft sand beaches, Saugatuck is Michiganders' scenic Midwest escape with plenty of small-town charm. Together with neighboring towns Douglas and Fennville, the region has become known as the Art Coast, drawing painters, writers, sculptors, and musicians for decades and helping to establish myriad local makers. That ethos has inspired this November’s Art Coast Food & Wine Festival (November 5-7), a three-day celebration of Southwest Michigan’s vibrant food and drink scene. Led by several local chefs (along with a few out-of-towners), the inaugural event will feature talks, demonstrations, and collaboration dinners. It’s just one more reason to plan a trip to the area this fall, when summertime crowds have subsided and autumn colors and flavors are underway. What to do in Saugatuck: Beaches, wineries, and art galleries to know The region’s largest outdoor draw is Oval Beach, recognized as one of the most beautiful beaches in the country. Pack the umbrella and take in the shoreline activities—visitors and locals alike come here for swimming, sunbathing, and rounds of frisbee. A large parking lot is right next to the beach, helping to ensure a smooth transition from vehicle to vacation mode. Taste some wine and enjoy the vineyard views at Modales Wines in Fennville. Owners Jim and Carol Gonzalez opened the winery in 2019 with the mission of making local bottles with sustainable practices and world-class vision. Today, they have been recognized as one of Michigan’s only certified organic wineries, with nearly two dozen bottles on offer. Book a guided tasting to sample through several of them, including favorites like the rose, syrah, and the award-winning Sauvignon Blanc or Gruner Veltliner. Pair it up with any of their onsite snacks (especially the goat’s and cow’s milk cheese spreads from nearby Evergreen Lane Farm & Creamery). Explore the area by water with a Star of Saugatuck cruise, a 90-minute sternwheel ride down the Kalamazoo River and onto Lake Michigan. Enjoy the trip during the daytime, or book a sunset cruise for golden hour photo opps. Near this dock, spot the Saugatuck Chain Ferry, a hand-cranked chain ferry that connects the downtown district to Mount Baldhead Park and Oval Beach (in use since 1838, it is the only remaining chain driven ferry in the country). Discover the area’s rich arts scene with visits to local galleries, including J. Petter, Dune, and Button Gallery. And check the calendar at Saugatuck Center for the Arts for regularly scheduled concerts, author talks, and artist exhibits (including the recent Mother Lake from local artist Bryanna Manning). During warmer months, swing by the parking lot on Fridays for a weekly farmers market. Saugatuck has several wonderful downtown shopping options—visit Brass Anchor for women’s clothing and accessories, Leon Footwear for handcrafted footwear, and The Book Nook for many beach read contenders. Spend some time exploring Lulu Cadieux—housed in a historic bank building, the lifestyle boutique celebrates everyday joys through a culinary learning center and thoughtfully curated retail selection. The shop features items across multiple categories, including home, garden, and beauty, and owner Terry Walker plans frequent trips abroad to procure goods (including vintage apparel and accessories). Guests can learn about different cuisines and techniques with the team’s onsite cooking classes, which take place in a spacious, state-of-the-art kitchen (complete with a beautiful cookbook collection). And those seeking more of the shop’s aesthetic and ethos can stay overnight at The Polo Shed, their private guest house. Located a short distance from the shop, the property sleeps up to 12 and features comforts and charms such as feather chandeliers, a grand piano, a stone fireplace, and a chef’s kitchen. Where to eat and drink in Saugatuck and Douglas Noble Twist Taphouse recently opened in the heart of downtown, bringing with it house-made beer and spirits, local wine, and from-scratch, New Haven-style pizza. An old-world patio with string lighting greets diners, who can start with one of the beers brewed onsite. Pair them up with creative salads or sandwiches (think the PBLT, with pork belly, tomato jam, and arugula), or any of the pizzas (with options like hot honey pepperoni or Michigan mushroom). For decades, locals and visitors have been flocking to Everyday People Café. That popularity is indeed for the food, but also for the restaurant’s other charms—its cozy, lively bar, comfortable dining rooms, and warm, polished hospitality. Menu items span regions and cuisines: roasted salmon with sauce soubise, vadouvan vinaigrette, and pea shoots; miso-sake marinated sea bass with Chinese eggplant and lemon-ginger beurre blanc; pesto pasta with gemelli noodles, teardrop tomatoes, and parmesan. Whatever the creation, the team here excels, wielding a true grasp of balanced, flavorful dishes. House-made desserts like the key lime pie or blueberry crisp (try it a la mode) serve as a rich and comforting finale. Chicago native Melissa Corey moved to Saugatuck and opened Pennyroyal Café and Provisions, where she and her team put forth seasonal, from-scratch dishes celebrating Michigan farms. Book a table for dinner, or visit during daytime hours for billowy blueberry pancakes, hearty breakfast sandwiches, and a popular whitefish melt. Pastries are baked fresh daily and beautifully conceived—a Basque-style cake with a pastry cream center, rotating croissants, and a caprese danish on weekends (a seasonal favorite with marinated tomatoes and herbed chevre). Dine indoors to witness Corey and team at work on the line, or outdoors in the dreamy, lush garden. It is walk-ins only for brunch, so be sure to arrive early—tables here fill up fast (credit the hospitable team and Corey’s impressive titles, including Chopped winner and James Beard Award nominee). Take a 15-minute drive to Fennville for dinner at Salt of the Earth, a local favorite for seasonal, sustainably sourced cooking. Start with the bread board, featuring several house-baked varieties alongside local butter, followed by the pizza. The team features several wood-fired renditions: wild mushroom (with caramelized onions and arugula), short rib (with white cheddar and cream sauce), and vegetable (with zucchini, peppers, and corn). When it’s time for dessert, don’t miss their S’more Cake, complete with a toasted marshmallow, graham cracker crumbs, and milk chocolate pudding. Dining at Bowdie’s Chophouse is at once elegant and unfussy, and a nod to some of the best big city steakhouses around. Settle in with big band swing sounds and a house cocktail, then go big with the steaks—filet mignon, or the bone-in ribeye for two. Accompany it all with a few of the restaurant’s signature sides—sautéed mushrooms, truffle fries, or brussels sprouts and pork belly. Leaving town, stop for a bite at Farmhouse Deli & Pantry, a beloved spot for sandwiches, salads, and baked goods—all made in-house and from scratch with local, seasonal ingredients. Don’t miss the turkey club or BLT, or earlier in the day, the breakfast burrito (with cage free scrambled eggs and local white cheddar). Where to stay in Saugatuck and Douglas, Michigan In business for nearly 20 years, Bella Vita Vacation Rentals has become a trusted resource for Saugatuck-Douglas travelers. The company manages more than 45 boutique rental properties within 10 miles of Saugatuck, many of which are located just footsteps from downtown or the lake. Peruse their range of listings, featuring water views, modern amenities, and pet-friendly options. Those looking for a boutique stay right on the water will find it at Lake Shore Resort. The property makes the most of its idyllic location overlooking Lake Michigan, with kayaks, a private beach, a swimming pool, and firepits for sunset gatherings. A variety of room types are available, and each one includes breakfast and access to other resort amenities, such as bikes and yoga classes. The spacious Cottage is perfect for larger parties—two units can be rented together or separately, and each features two bedrooms, a washer/dryer, walk-in showers, and gas ranges. Keep an eye on their calendar for upcoming events and programming, including occasional collaboration dinners with local partners. What was first built in 1937 as the home of former Saugatuck mayor Frank Wick became The Wickwood Inn in 1981, the town’s first bed-and-breakfast. Originally modeled after London’s Brown’s Hotel, the property recently underwent a redesign by award-winning Soucie Horner Design Collective, resulting in a refined, modern aesthetic. Several luxury suites welcome guests, along with The Bungalow—a three-bedroom retreat with ensuite bathrooms and curated artwork. When you’re not enjoying the comforts of the room, explore the inn’s amenities, including its English gardens, farm-to-table breakfasts, daily social hours, and heated pool.

item.title: 11 Scenic Train Rides in the US Worth Booking for the Views Alone
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.21
Every year, instead of flying home to southeastern Virginia, I always opt to take the train. My journey typically starts in New York, winding down the Northeast Corridor before stopping in Washington, DC. While this busy stretch of track is far from the most scenic train ride in the US, there were still moments when I found my face pressed against the window—like near Havre de Grace, Maryland where the Susquehanna River widens—unable to look away. It was a reminder of how the joys of slow travel can sneak up on you, even in familiar places you may have traveled through countless times before. That said, there are certain train routes in the US with scenery so mesmerizing that they are worth taking for the sights alone. Amtrak, of course, has more than 30 different train routes crisscrossing every US region, from the vast deserts of the Southwest to the sparkling coast of California, and majestic mountain ranges in between. But even more private rail operators in states like Alaska and Hawaii offer their own scenic train rides that shouldn't be overlooked. The challenge, then, becomes picking which train trip to take—and when. Below, we’ve selected 13 of the most scenic train rides in the US that are worth booking for the views alone. This story has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 9 Standout Galapagos Cruises for Sailing the Bucket-List Wildlife Destination
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.20
An extraordinary archipelago 600 miles off the coast of Ecuador, the Galapagos promise a once-in-a-lifetime travel experience—and many agree there's no better way to visit, than by ship. Unlike the typical island-hopping cruise itinerary you'll find elsewhere, Galapagos Island cruises invite travelers to experience some of the most unspoiled environments on earth. The vessels here are small, too—sometimes accommodating as few as 16 passengers. There are no water parks, Broadway-style shows, or casinos on board. Instead, pristine surroundings, uninhabited islands, and rare wildlife are the featured attractions. These cruise itineraries offer the chance to get up close to giant tortoises and playful sea lions, to snorkel among coral and stingrays, and look for rare birds like the blue-footed booby, a species only found in parts of the Pacific Ocean. Leave the logistics to your captain, and let yourself enjoy an incredible adventure of hiking through untouched natural environments or kayaking, paddleboarding, or snorkeling through one of the most interesting parts of the Pacific Ocean. After all, in the Galapagos, animals outnumber people and some of the most interesting scenes are found on the water. Cruises to this remote region usually span about a week and visit multiple islands. And while it is generally an expensive destination, given the hard-to-reach nature of the islands, there are some more affordable ways to cross off this bucket-list trip. Below, we cover nine of the best Galapagos cruises—with options for every type of traveler. The best Galapagos cruise for luxury travelers Ecoventura offers one of the most luxurious—and family-friendly—cruises in the Galapagos. The company operates three expedition yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which can accommodate 20 guests across 10 staterooms. Children six and up are welcome on board, and some staterooms can be connected to create spacious family suites. The crew is the shining star of these yachts, ensuring personalized service, pleasant surprises—like a pirate-themed send-off party to end the trip—and a menu to suit every palate. There’s a breakfast buffet every morning featuring Ecuadorian specialties and international favorites, and a multicourse dinner every night, with plenty of options for vegetarians. Onboard Ecoventura’s yachts, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, snorkeling gear, and zodiacs are on offer. There’s also a hot tub, fitness center, and plenty of outdoor nooks for taking in the unforgettable views. Off the ship, experienced naturalists lead daily excursions to lava fields, scenic viewpoints, idyllic snorkeling spots, and secluded beaches. Even if you're new to watersports like snorkeling, the ship’s patient guides will teach you how to get comfortable in the water so you can enjoy swimming among turtles, fish, and stingrays. The best Galapagos cruise for solo travelers Join a small group of future friends on the Reina Silvia Voyager, G Adventures’ newest catamaran that’s custom-built for sailing the Galapagos. Two of its 10 cabins feature single beds and are reserved for solo travelers. All come with a private bathroom, desk, and a large picture window to frame the pristine Galapagos views beyond. A 10-day itinerary starts and ends in Quito, taking guests on a journey through the Central and East Islands to look for sea lions, iguanas, and a seemingly endless variety of birds. Go kayaking, snorkeling, scuba diving, or paddleboarding—or kick back and relax on the spacious sundeck while enjoying some of the most unspoiled views in the world. There’s a chef on board to ensure you never go hungry, a hot tub to soothe any sore muscles, lots of spaces for socializing when you want to, and a bar that’s perfect for sunset cocktails—with or without your shipmates. The best Galapagos cruise for travelers craving personal space The Celebrity Flora is one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, but don’t expect it to be packed with crowds. While it's about twice the size of the Celebrity Xploration, which also sails to the Galapagos, the Flora carries the same number of people—about 100. The size difference gives the ship a more spacious feel and roomier suites that start at around 224 square feet. Some cabins have floor-to-ceiling windows that open up to make your suite feel like it has a balcony. Others have actual balconies, some as large as 321 square feet. These eco-conscious ships are designed to navigate the most remote parts of the Galapagos Islands. There’s also a retractable marina onboard to make it easier for travelers with mobility issues to get in and out of the vessels ferrying them from ship to shore. The best Galapagos catamaran cruise Avalon Waterways may be better known for its European river cruises, but it also sails the Galapagos Islands, with a chartered luxury catamaran, the Treasure of the Galapagos. The boat can accommodate a maximum of 16 guests and offers a rare amenity in the Galapagos: private balconies. The largest suite comes in at 430 square feet and features not one but two private outdoor spaces. Guests feast on dishes from creative, locally inspired menus featuring seasonal ingredients. There’s also a hot tub and a naturalist on board, and fares include wine with dinner as well as coffee, tea, and water. The best Galapagos cruise for foodies There may be few better places to eat in the Galapagos than The Grill, one of two restaurants on board the Silver Origin, a 100-passenger ship operated by the luxury cruise line Silversea. The Grill serves up premium cuts of meat cooked tableside atop fiery lava stones. Indulge in locally sourced lobster, Andean quinoa, and fresh Galapagos-caught fish. Meals at The Grill are served alfresco, and it’s hard to find a better view for dinner than these natural landscapes. Elsewhere onboard, guests can learn the art of ceviche-making from the ship’s chef and sample Ecuadorian cheese that has been aged in lava tubes. The smallest suites on board are 325 square feet, and many come with balconies. Even the showers offer ocean views, and there’s butler service onboard for anything you might need. While the Silver Origin is another one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, these voyages tend to sell out—book early. The best Galapagos cruise for adventure seekers Sailings on board the La Pinta, operated by Uncruise, are designed for adventurous spirits who also appreciate time to unwind. This isn’t the newest or most luxurious ship sailing the Galapagos, but it’s comfortable, unpretentious, and recently refurbished. Onboard this 48-passenger yacht, you’ll find plenty of gear: kayaks, paddleboards, snorkeling equipment, scuba equipment, and a glass-bottom boat included. The itinerary includes visits to seven islands and islets as well as a visit to the Charles Darwin Research Station. Hike Dragon Hill on Isla Santa Cruz while looking for iguanas and flamingos, paddleboard alongside sea lions at Isla Floreana, or enjoy a stroll along a secluded white-sand beach. If you think cruising isn’t your thing, Uncruise might just change your mind. The best Galapagos cruise for science lovers If ever you’ve wondered what life would be like as a scientist, HX Expeditions has the Galapagos cruise for you. The company operates a Citizen Science Program on board the MS Santa Cruz II, enlisting guests to help with completing research projects. Guests can join onboard researchers in collecting samples, learn to make field observations, and visit the onboard science lab to analyze materials and work with experts to process data. Between following in the footsteps of Charles Darwin, visiting his namesake research station, and working with onboard researchers, this is a vacation where learning is accessible—and prioritized. The best affordable Galapagos cruise For travelers craving the wild majesty of the Galapagos at a more affordable price, Nature Galapagos & Ecuador delivers an authentic, expertly curated experience that doesn’t compromise on adventure nor break the budget. Specializing in small-ship and land-based tours, their budget-class cruises—aboard intimate, 8 to 10-person yachts like the New Flamingo and Merak—offer access to remote islands, expert bilingual naturalist guides, and daily excursions that bring you face-to-face with marine iguanas and Galapagos tortoises. Accommodations are simple but comfortable, with snorkeling gear, meals, and interisland logistics seamlessly included. Expect to spend around $3,000 for a four‑ to five‑night cruise, compared to about $7,600 for a seven-night sailing on G Adventures. The best Galapagos cruise for kids Inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board the National Geographic Gemini, a ship that sails the Galapagos as part of a partnership between Lindblad Expeditions and National Geographic. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board. FAQ: How early should I book a Galapagos cruise? For the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then. Where do I embark on a Galapagos cruise? Getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee). When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands? With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands. Are Galapagos cruises expensive? The Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s. What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise? The Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Paris Wilson.

item.title: The Best Hotels Near the Sphere in Las Vegas
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.14
I’ve been taking trips to Las Vegas since long before the Sphere was there, and half the fun—for me, at least—has always been staying somewhere central in this wonderfully over-the-top city. A good Vegas hotel should make it easy to slip between a long lunch, a pool afternoon, a big dinner, and whatever you’ve got planned after dark without spending precious vacation time stuck in traffic—and since the Sphere opened in September 2023, there’s a new glowing landmark to factor into that equation. The enormous exosphere has become essential to the Vegas skyline, but the real draw is inside: an immersive venue unlike anything else in the city (or the world, really), where the scale of the screen, sound, and space makes going to a show feel like a transformative event. Booking a hotel nearby is ideal if you're eager to be a quick walk or drive from the venue but also want to keep the neon, restaurants, casinos, pools, and beautiful absurdity of the Strip within reach. Whether you’re planning around the event of your dreams or simply want to experience Vegas’s newest and most iconic orb in all its glory, these are the hotels worth checking into less than a 10-minute drive from the Sphere. FAQ: What big shows are coming up at the Sphere? The Sphere’s fall-through-winter calendar is especially stacked: The Eagles return September 18 through January 23, while Metallica takes over October 1 through March 13. The iconic Wizard of Oz experience goes through December 7, and the Backstreet Boys are back for a New Year’s run from December 26 through January 2. Looking ahead, Oprah Winfrey’s AHA live immersive experience will take place April 2 to 4. You can always stay up to date on the Sphere's website. What to know when walking to the Sphere: While an over-20-minute walk might sound daunting to some, walking to the Sphere in Las Vegas is highly efficient via the indoor, climate-controlled pedestrian bridge connected directly to The Venetian Resort. Visitors arriving from other Las Vegas Strip properties should anticipate a 15-to-30-minute walk through connecting hotel corridors or along Sands Avenue. Due to the venue's grand scale and layout, wear comfortable shoes to easily navigate the extensive walkways and stairways. Also remember to pack light before making your way—the Sphere enforces a strict bag size limit of six by six by two inches, and does not have on-site storage facilities. How we choose the best hotels near the Sphere in Las Vegas: Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: Sennheiser Coupon Codes & Discounts | September 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.93
German audio brand Sennheiser has made its mark on all types of travel experiences, from providing the ideal in-flight headphones for the Concorde, to developing microphones favored by artists on stages across the globe, to launching immersive, speakerless audio for vehicles. To put it simply, you can’t travel well without good sound, and if you’re in the market for noise-canceling headphones that’ll get you through that next long-haul flight, this audio brand’s got you covered. Established in 1945, Sennheiser has long been a household name among audiophiles, but has also won the ears of casual listeners. It all began when Dr. Ing. Fritz Sennheiser founded Laboratorium Wennebostel outside of Hanover, which later became Sennheiser Electronic. The first product was the DM 1 microphone, made for Siemens. The company has been credited with creating the world’s first open-back headphones in 1968, and in 1991, it launched the legendary Orpheus electrostatic headphone (whose successor would be the HE 1 in 2015), followed by the Evolution Microphone Series in 1999. The very best in sound technology doesn’t come cheap; if you’d like to shop the Sennheiser brand, read on for the coupon codes, discounts, and free shipping offers to use before making a purchase. Use a Sennheiser coupon code for 10% off your first order If you’re new to the brand, you’re in luck: First-time customers can sign up for the official Sennheiser newsletter to receive an exclusive 10% off coupon for their initial purchase, up to $100. And once you’re subscribed, you can stay informed about new product launches, flash sales, and subscriber-only promotions—all delivered directly to your inbox. Subscribers can also benefit from free shipping on all orders sitewide with no minimum spend, ensuring extra savings on every purchase. Once you sign up, the discount and free shipping will expire by December 31, 2026, so make sure you put it to use before then. Keep an eye out for limited-time offers at Sennheiser Sennheiser is currently offering limited-time discounts on industry-standard gear, including headphones and soundbars—often available without a specific code. Right now, for instance, the AMBEO Soundbar Max Refurbished has been marked down from $2,999 to $1,299.5, rounding out to a total saving of $1,700. This home theater tool will level up how you watch movies, with a 3D audio experience. Students, military members, and first responders can enjoy a 15% discount Sennheiser is committed to honoring those who serve our communities, from students learning how to make music to nurses who commute to work with a pair of headphones. As a gesture of gratitude, the company offers a 15% discount code to military personnel, veterans, government employees, medical professionals, first responders, seniors, students, and teachers. All you have to do is verify your status through ID.me. Once you’ve completed your verification, you’ll be given a unique promo code, which you can enter into the “Discount Code” field when purchasing an item on the Sennheiser site. Unfortunately, this code can’t be combined with other offers. Shop refurbished Sennheiser products at a discount without a code If you don’t mind giving up on that shiny new toy feeling, Sennheiser offers discounts on "like-new" products that have undergone professional inspection, testing, and restoration to meet original performance standards. You can find previous-generation models, open-box items, or cosmetic-blemish products—like the HD 560S or HD 599 headphones—at a fraction of their price. All refurbished products typically come with a warranty, ensuring peace of mind with your purchase, similar to new items. What to do if your Sennheiser coupon code isn’t working If your Sennheiser coupon code isn't working, be sure to check for typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization, as well as any terms and conditions. The 10% newsletter sign-up promo code, for instance, is capped at a $100 discount and limited to first-time users only. You can also try clearing your browser’s cache and cookies, or switching devices or browsers. When all else fails, Sennheiser's Consumer Experience team is there to help.

item.title: This Dual-Voltage Hair Dryer Is Actually Lightweight and Compact Enough to Pack
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.93
I envy my friends who arrive at the airport with nothing but a slim carry-on in tow. I, on the other hand, check a bag every time. And yes, I do overpack, but I really try not to; by the time I lay all my hair tools on one side of my suitcase, it's halfway full. So, I accepted the fact that I'll never be a carry-on-only traveler a long time ago. But recently, I got my hands on Dyson's new Supersonic travel hair dryer—and for the first time, I might actually be able to save some space in my suitcase. Dyson's latest hair tool is specifically designed with travelers in mind—it's 32% smaller and 25% lighter than the brand's OG best-selling Supersonic hair dryer, meaning it can be tucked away in the corner of a suitcase or pocket of a weekender bag with ease. I've had the Dyson Airwrap for years, and don't get me wrong, it's great—but between the long barrel, the multiple attachments, and the thick cord, it's usually way too bulky for me to pack. When I'm traveling, I want something easy, fuss-free, and overpacker-friendly. On a recent bachelorette trip to Rosemary Beach, Florida, I easily packed my Dyson Supersonic travel hair dryer in my suitcase. And because my friends and I were staying in an Airbnb, a hair dryer wasn't provided, so it was even more important that I bring one. If you, like me, are tired of filling up the majority of your suitcase by packing a bulky hair dryer or styling system, Dyson's new travel tool is worth checking out. I had two main concerns when the hair tool arrived. First, is it actually smaller and lighter than your average hair dryer? And yes, it absolutely is. It's really not much bigger than my iPhone, and takes up a fraction of the space in my bag that my Airwrap does. Second, I wanted to know if it actually worked as well as other Dyson hair tools—or if this smaller version would mean I sacrificed power. Within seconds of turning it on, I could tell this mini hair dryer packed a serious punch. It heats up in seconds and has just as much strength as my full-size Dyson Airwrap. The major pro for this travel hair dryer is that it's dual voltage, meaning you can safely use it in outlets abroad too—unlike the Dyson Airwrap and original Supersonic hair dryer. I love knowing I can take this tool anywhere, whether I'm at home in New Jersey or traveling to Europe. I also love the look of it sitting on a hotel bathroom counter. It's so simple and sleek—and the slim barrel is easy to grip and hold while drying. Its design is simple: There's a button to turn it on and off, a button to control the three heat settings, and another for its two speeds. I have long hair, and the Dyson can fully dry it in about 10 minutes—even when it's sopping wet right out of the shower. It also leaves my hair with a glossy, shiny finish—unlike the hair dryer usually found at hotels that can sometimes leave my hair feeling dry and brittle. I like that the cable length is shorter than most tools (it's only 6.5 feet, compared to the original model that is 8.6 feet). It also comes with a Styling Concentrator, a small attachment that helps prevent frizz and leaves your hair a little smoother. Another cool perk is that it's compatible with attachments for the original Supersonic hair dryer, so you don't have to buy additional parts if you want to mix and match. My only gripe with this hair tool is the price. $300 for a hair dryer is expensive—a lot pricier than others I've used in the past. But it does work way better than any hair dryer I've tried before and is much lighter and smaller. Given its compact size, impressive power, and dual-voltage capabilities, I say it's worth it. I originally got this hair dryer with only travel in mind. But for the past two months, it's been my go-to hair tool, even when I'm home. Call me lazy, but it's so much easier to pull this thing out than my bulkier Airwrap to dry my hair. I recommend Dyson's new hair dryer for any frequent travelers looking for something compact, lightweight, and dual voltage. Or anyone wanting a go-to hair dryer that's less bulky but works just as well as larger hair tools on the market (perfect for those with limited storage space in their bathroom). Whether I'm packing for a two-week trip overseas or a quick weekend escape, you'll definitely find this small-but-mighty hair tool in my bag.

item.title: The Most Comfortable Travel Pants That Aren’t Sweats or Leggings
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.78
When I travel, I want to be comfortable—but not at the cost of looking put together. There’s a time and a place for sweatpants (and yes, we’ve all boarded a flight in them), but I’d argue the best travel pants are something more versatile: soft enough for a six-hour flight, stretchy enough for a spontaneous sprint to the gate, breathable enough for wandering a new city, and spruced up enough to wear straight to dinner. That sweet spot is something many of us editors at Condé Nast Traveler think about—and, frankly, obsess over. The good news is that there are plenty of options beyond your standard jogger. Think jeans with just the right amount of give, yoga pants that pass surprisingly well as trousers, lightweight utility pants with room to roam, and clever, packable styles designed for staying put in your suitcase until you need them again for the flight home. Our editors have tested dozens of travel pants in cities all across the globe—and some really stand out for comfort, versatility, and style. Below, the tried-and-true travel pants we recommend wearing on the plane and long after you land. Dress pants Spanx's Ponte pants feature a high-rise waistband with comfortable, built-in compression, offering a flattering silhouette. Commerce director Madison Flager recommends this pair for work trips, and loves how the wide-leg design balances structure and roominess. Available in petite, regular, and tall inseams, they accommodate a range of heights, enhancing fit and ease. The fabric is stretchy yet firm and resistant to wrinkles, making these pants a functional choice for all kinds of elevated travel outfits. Thanks to their soft, menswear-inspired fabric and a partially elastic waistband, transportation and travel news editor Hannah Towey says this pair of pants from Abercrombie feels “basically like sweatpants.” The pleating details and low-rise, tailored cut flatter curves, while the wide-leg design ensures breathability. The pockets add utility for holding onto travel essentials, and their ability to retain their shape and resist wrinkles makes them suitable for all sorts of run and play. Utility pants The Prana Halle pants are commerce writer Jessica Sulima's go-to for trips that involve anything mildly outdoorsy. According to Sulima, they're great on a hike (and can be rolled up and pinned at the calf once you start to sweat), but are also water-repellant, which makes them a great thing to pack in case of unexpected rain. “I find the low-rise bootcut to be incredibly flattering, which makes me feel better about wearing them on a plane or train,” says Sulima. “Plus, they pack light, compared to more cargo-style hiking pants on the market.” Pull-on pants Made from a viscose and recycled nylon blend, these pants combine structure with stretch, offering a flattering kick flare and pull-on elastic waistband for comfort and ease. Senior features editor Rebecca Misner calls them indestructible: “I think you can basically set them on fire and then still wear them,” she says. Their durability is key for frequent travelers—and despite the elevated price, they’re a reliable investment thanks to the softness, stretch, and structure of the fabric. The tailored silhouette can also be dressed up or down, making the pants ideal for transitioning between travel, work, or play. With soft cotton, an elasticized waist with drawcords, and an easy pull-on structure, this Gap pair could appeal to just about anyone. “These pants are currently working overtime for me as both my go-to flight pants, and maternity pants," says global social director Mercedes Bleth. She's taken them all over the globe—all the way from NYC to Saudi Arabia then Atlanta, on a road trip to Maine, and beyond. And throughout Bleth's pregnancy, she has prioritized buying things that she'll be able to wear long after her bump disappears. “These pants have been, and will continue to be, my go-to when I need of something structured and cute, but also incredibly comfortable,” she says. Global digital director Arati Menon's travel rule is simple: Pick clothes that have room to stretch or settle into (she's notorious for pretzeling her body into a tight economy seat). “Comfort doesn’t have to be at odds with style—I like to play with form and volume, and these balloon pants do just the trick.” According to Menon, who gets plenty of compliments on them in the airport, the pair is perfect with an oversized cotton or poplin shirt (Arket and Dissh are her favorites) and perhaps a more fitted ribbed tank. Flager lived in these linen pants this past summer—and loved them so much that she bought them in both brown and black. “They’re just such a great travel day pant; they're more put together than sweats or joggers, but not at all constrictive,” says Flager. They may be leaving her regular rotation as the weather cools down, but she's already looking forward to pulling them out again for December trips to Jamaica and Florida. Comfortable jeans After years of testing and reviewing travel pants, I can confidently say: Silver Jeans knows how to do denim for the road right. I’m wearing these bad boys as I write this, and I wouldn't trade this pair of jeans for the world. I have shown them said world, though—flying across time zones, navigating cramped cabins, and living out of carry-ons. Through it all, they have proven to be the ultimate classic-but-comfy, wear-them-all-day pants. Unlike poorly made stretch jeans that sag at the knees and waist by day two, these snap right back to a tailored silhouette every single time. And after around two years of owning them, they still look like premium, structured denim on the outside, while keeping a remarkably soft, zero-friction feel (that–I'll say it—replicates that of sweatpants). I also bought them in a black colorway and they've held up beautifully after months of constant wear. For a vintage-inspired fit that doesn't sacrifice comfort, these Gap jeans are Towey's most recent travel companion. For her, they passed what might just be the most ultimate test: a red-eye flight. She flew from NYC to Portugal, and thanks to their ultra-soft, non-stretch denim—it was a comfortable ride. “They doubled as pajamas, but were still stylish enough to arrive in Europe and walk around until hotel check-in,” says Towey. “And the low rise really makes room just in case you bloat when traveling, which is another big plus!” I'm no stranger to Just Black Denim. With a fair price point, spruced up stretchy denim, and versatile styles, the brand has been one of my favorites since first introduced to me two years ago. These are one of the newer pairs I love for short flights, days that turn into nights out, and weekend road trips from NYC. While the high-waisted style sometimes leads the fabric to ride up (hence why they are better for short flights), they are more comfortable and stretchy than every other pair of high-waisted pants I own. You can’t go wrong with its classic light wash color, and the fact that they fold down super thin is such a satisfying win. As a 5'3" girlie, finding jeans that elongate your legs is rare. But when I pair these with a slight platform Chelsea boot? Instant legs for days. I’ve already gotten so many compliments on them. These soft, stretchy jeans from Halara offer high-waist support and a flattering fit without waistband pinching or digging, crucial for extended wear during flights or road trips. Loved and recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, she says the pants are basically pajamas masked in a dark-wash denim design complete with a stylish cuffed hem. Kenny has worn them extensively without any loss in quality, and mentions that she always receives compliments on them. Bleth praises these jeans for being “so comfortable,” likening them to sweatpants but with denim durability. The low-rise, baggy fit allows for unrestricted movement, making them ideal for airport navigation or long drives. The medium wash is versatile, pairing easily with multiple travel outfits, reducing packing needs. Levi’s signature craftsmanship ensures longevity and fabric resilience, essential for frequent travelers who want classic, reliable denim that doesn’t sacrifice comfort. Yoga pants Commerce writer Charley Ward is a big fan of Sisterly Tribe, and its pants in this gorgeous espresso color are no different. Made from a soft, organic cotton blend—they have just the right amount of stretch while maintaining a flattering lift and hold. “They’re very long (as you’d expect from a Scandi brand, frankly)—but as a result, deliver a nice leg-elongating silhouette that works equally for Pilates as long travel days,” says Ward. One of her favorite features is the folded waistband, which can be adjusted (and according to Ward, cradles your stomach gently for an enhancing effect), not to mention the subtle embroidered detail that coyly completes the look. “These are the ultimate comfy-but-still-smart choice—I’ve even worn them to the office, and received compliments on them at that,” says Ward. Set Active's Luxform leggings have been a longtime favorite of Kenny's: “They're seriously the most buttery-soft yet compressive pair I've ever worn,” she says. She first got her hands on the straight-leg version earlier these year, and they've since become her go-to travel pant. “I've worn them on early morning flights, long hours driving in the car, and most recently, during a 10-hour delay at the airport,” says Kenny. “They look just as a good with a crewneck or plain white tee for a travel day as they do with a sports bra for a yoga class.” What she loves most is how smoothing they are—according to Kenny, they hug you in all the right places while still giving room to stretch. And while the straight-leg fit makes them feel a little more elevated than a regular pair of leggings, their comfort level is reportedly just the same.
