This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 14 Airbnbs for Appreciating Fall Foliage Across the US
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.65
If you’re lucky enough to live in a pocket of the US that showcases the change of seasons, there’s something special about rushing to take it all in before it’s gone. The colors of fall slip away before you know it, and now’s the time to book that last-minute autumnal trip somewhere in the woods. Thanks to the remote nature of many Airbnbs, the ones below are perfectly set up to catch the leaves changing all around the country. While the golden mosaics of fall are often associated with the East Coast, the Airbnbs on this list span from your classic New England cabins to off-grid ranches in the Colorado backcountry. Many of these properties boast floor-to-ceiling windows that bring hues of gold, purple, green, and orange straight into your home, plus luxe amenities like barrel saunas and hot tubs. Whether you want to cozy up by the fireplace with a great read or embark on a brisk morning walk with a cup of coffee in hand, these Airbnbs inspire all kinds of seasonal fantasies. These listings were chosen by our editors based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. - Number of guests: 2 Bed & bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Sauna, firepit, hot tubThere are a number of ways to unwind at this cozy, hillside cabin, including soaking in the hot tub, sweating it out in the sauna, or swinging near the outdoor firepit in a pair of hanging egg chairs. You’ll have everything you need to cook at home, from a blender to an air fryer, and you can enjoy your meals at the windowside table that looks out into the surrounding wilderness. Just be warned: At sunrise, you might hear the sounds of a rooster crowing to really get you in the countryside spirit. Location: Navron, Pennsylvania Things to do nearby: Money Rocks County Park, Welsh Mountain Scenic Overlook, Shady Maple Smorgasbord - Number of guests: 4 Bed & bath: 1 bedroom, 2 baths Why we love it: Furnished outdoor deck with grill and firepit, movie projector, seven acres of landWhile some of us are content with the annual pumpkin spice latte to ring in the season, others need a trip to a full-blown glass tree house chalet in the Berkshires. For the latter crowd, book here to curl up before the floating, wood-burning fireplace to really kick off a cozy fall. The multiple floor-to-ceiling windows that look out on the surrounding woods and fern-covered hillside let you feel like you're in the colorful trees, too. This home has one bedroom, but there's a daybed in the living area that lets you squeeze up to four people. (I'd recommend this spot for a couple, though, since there's not much privacy when sleeping in the nearly wall-less living room.) Location: Otis, Massachusetts Things to do nearby: Otis Ridge ski resort, Bob's Way hiking trail, Knox Trail Inn restaurant - Number of guests: 8 Bed & bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms Why we love it: Hot tub, fireplace, deck and patioIs there anywhere more famous for fall foliage than Stowe? Just off Route 100, a highway renowned for its spectacular, kaleidoscopic fall hues, lies this adorable A-frame called the Canopy House. The rustic, bohemian home offers three bedrooms, an outdoor hot tub that fits six, and an upper deck for views of the backyard's fall foliage. The Wi-Fi is guaranteed to be strong and speedy, making this a solid option for remote work. Or better yet, let those powerful megabits fuel your own personal writing retreat. Location: Stowe, Vermont Things to do nearby: Stowe Mountain Resort, Idletyme brewery, Gold Brook Falls - Number of guests: 4 Bed & bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Indoor fireplace, balcony, bathtubIf you stare at this Maine tree house long enough, you’ll notice that it’s fox-shaped—and if you’ve got the kids in tow, you can make a game of spotting the woodsy mascot as you make your way through the home. The owners of this quirky one-bedroom have carefully considered every design element, from the hunter green kitchen cabinets to the copper and gold finishes. The “ears” upstairs, with their vaulted ceilings and triangular windows, are arguably the best place to gaze at the surrounding foliage. Best of all? You’re within walking distance of Bradbury Mountain State Park, which comes alive with color in mid-October. Location: Pownal, Maine Things to do nearby: Dorothy's Sugar House, Pineland Farms, Maine Beer Company - Number of guests: 8 Bed & bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Private tennis courts, Swedish sauna, rafts and stand-up paddleboardsLocated in the heart of the Catskills, this woodsy Alpine chalet-style lake house sleeps eight and is the ultimate group mountain retreat. Highlights of the forested outdoor property include a floating dock on the lake, stand-up paddleboards, a shaded patio with a firepit, and spacious Adirondack chairs—ideal for posting up in with a glass of wine at sunset while you soak up the fall foliage views. Inside, standout details include a farmhouse-style dining table, a floor-to-ceiling stone fireplace with logs provided, a fully stocked kitchen, and a balcony. For more of Traveler's favorite Airbnbs within driving distance of New York City, dig into our ultimate Airbnb guide. Location: Hunter, New York Things to do nearby: Windham Mountain, Kaaterskill Falls, Tannersville - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Private deck, firepit, wooded bathhouseIf you’re dreaming of truly unplugging this fall, look no further than this off-grid tree house nestled in the Catskills. The views of unspoiled wilderness are so good, you might not even notice the lack of electricity or Wi-Fi. For a total forest immersion, hot showers and rooms with toilets are located a two-minute walk from your cabin in the custom timber bathhouse (don’t worry, you can connect to Wi-Fi here if you need). This retreat proves all you really need is a king-size bed and some good windows to live in luxury. Location: Lanesville, New York Things to do nearby: Huckleberry Trail, Tannersville Bike Path, Kaaterskill Wild Forest - Number of guests: 4 Bed & bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Movie theater–grade projector, dedicated workspace, king-size canopy bedThe tall stands of maple, pear, apple, and cherry trees that surround this renovated 1800s carriage house burst into fiery oranges and reds this time of year—perfect for an October or November visit when the colors reach their peaks. If you’re lucky, you might spot a hot-air balloon gliding onto the grass in a landing field behind the property, or a bright fox dashing across the lawn. Inside the house, which comfortably sleeps four people, there's a movie theater–like setup for do-nothing nights in, cathedral ceilings, exposed beams, and floor-to-ceiling windows. Location: Flemington, New Jersey Things to do nearby: Round Valley Reservoir, Flemington Diner, Hilltop Reserve hiking trail - Number of guests: 4 Bed & bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, private patio and backyard, barbecueEach fall, Estes Park basks in the glow of saffron- and amber-hued Aspen trees that grow in groves all over the Rocky Mountains. And you can experience the very best of it—without the crowds—from this off-grid, backcountry cabin. The owner of this two-bedroom (both queens) used to run an outfitting business from the property, which means he can lead you to virtually uncharted trails, whether you’re hiking, motorcycling, or mountain biking. Feel free to bring your own horse too. Location: Estes Park, Colorado Things to do nearby: Kruger Rock Trailhead, Twin Owls Steakhouse, Lily Lake - Number of guests: 6 Bed & bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Solar power, pet-friendly, smart TVs, and Roku in both bedroomsThe Northeast can't take all of the credit for fall views. New Mexico is just as radiant this time of year, and especially so in Taos. The town is home to the Enchanted Circle Scenic Byway, where brilliant yellow trees sprout among evergreen pines all over the mountains. This sustainable smart house sleeps six and makes the perfect home base, as the byway's out loop is just 10 minutes away. It’s solar-powered, runs completely off rainwater, and welcomes pets. Plus, the Rio Grande Del Norte National Monument—a 242,555-acre area of public lands—is walkable from the backyard. Location: Taos, New Mexico Things to do nearby: Taos Brewery, Rio Grande del Norte National Monument, Millicent Rogers Museum - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, 1 bath Why we love it: Private trails, hot tub, cold plungeLocated on a private ridge near the Georgia-Tennessee border, this Tennessee cabin is all clean lines and natural light. It’s hard to say where’s best to take in the golden view—from the living room’s floor-to-ceiling windows, the outdoor deck, or the shared sauna. Guests also have access to an observation tower for optimal leaf peeping, plus a number of private hiking trails dotted across the property. The host notes, “Adventure is close, but the ridge stays quiet.” Location: Old Fort, Tennessee Things to do nearby: Parksville Lake, Conasauga Park, Ocoee Winery - Number of guests: 4 Bed & bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Firepit, smart TV, in-unit washer/dryerThis historic cabin is located only seven miles from the Blue Ridge Parkway, a scenic drive through the Appalachian Mountains connecting Shenandoah National Park and Great Smoky Mountains National Park. It’s a great nesting ground after days spent outdoors exploring the soaring mountains of Asheville. Exposed wooden beams accent the house, with rustic-chic elements throughout, like rocking chairs on the porch, barn doors in the kitchen, and an adorable writing desk positioned next to a window that overlooks the mountains. Location: Weaverville, North Carolina Things to do nearby: Big Ivy Trailhead, Douglas Falls, Pisgah National Forest - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Hot tub, cold plunge, barrel saunaJust a 15-minute drive to Shenandoah National Park, this two-level cabin in Luray, Virginia, offers breathtaking views of the foliage surrounding the Blue Ridge Mountains. Both bedrooms come equipped with king-size beds, while the spa-inspired bathroom features heated floors and a shower with five different massaging heads. The outdoor offerings are just as good: On the ground level, there’s a cedar hot tub and cold plunge where you can take in the autumnal views, and upstairs, find a barrel sauna and firepit for warming up (firewood provided!). Location: Luray, Virginia Things to do nearby: Shenandoah National Park, Lake Arrowhead, Meadow Spring Trail - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 3 beds, 1 bath Why we love it: Record player, private riverside trails, Morso woodstoveLocated on the banks of Washington’s White Salmon River, this gorgeous retreat features a large, open kitchen with a Morso woodstove, a cozy living room stocked with a record player and board games, and two bedrooms—one with a king-size bed and the other with two singles. There are private riverside trails surrounding the property, so you can spend your days taking in the fresh Pacific Northwest air, all while appreciating nature’s changing colors. Location: White Salmon, Washington Things to do nearby: Buck Creek Trailhead, Steelhead Falls, South Hill Winery - Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 6 beds, 3 baths Why we love it: Japanese-inspired wet room, in-unit washer/dryer, record playerLocated just 30 minutes out from Sun Valley, this Idaho retreat gives you access to all kinds of outdoor adventures, from fly-fishing to mountain biking. It’s plopped right in front of the Big Wood River, and you might even spot some elk herds while enjoying your morning coffee on the back porch. The real star of the show, though, is the expansive wet room in the primary suite, featuring Brazilian walnut walls and a freestanding tub. Location: Bellevue, Idaho Things to do nearby: O’Donnell Park, Silver Creek Preserve, Sun Valley This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Meredith Carey.

item.title: When Is Prime Big Deal Days? Here's Everything Travelers Need to Know About the Fall Sale
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.46
Another Amazon Prime Day is just around the corner, and I already have a shopping cart full of wish-listed items I'm hoping to save on. I usually wait for Prime Big Deal Days to stock up on my favorite home and beauty essentials—and this year, I might even try to get a head start on some holiday gifts before all the chaos of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. After all, Amazon tends to offer its steepest discounts during its twice-a-year mega sale. In years past, I've scored on trending shoes, hard-shell luggage, and electronics for up to 50% off. And since Amazon just announced the dates for this year's highly anticipated Prime Day, let this be your sign to start thinking about what you need to restock and which big-ticket items it might be time to buy (hello, Ōura Ring 5). Prime members are guaranteed to find deals across all major categories, including clothing and shoes, luggage, tech, premium beauty and skincare, outdoor gear, and home goods. Below, I'm breaking down everything there is to know so far about Prime Big Deal Days 2026. Plus, I've listed out some deals running on Amazon right now, so you can start shopping—and saving—early. What is Prime Day? In case you're not familiar with Amazon's best sale of the year, let's get you up to speed: Prime Day is an annual savings event where thousands of products are marked down for a limited time. Prime members will have the chance to save up to 60% off best-selling gear, trending apparel, and so much more. Historically, Prime Day runs in July—but for the past few years, Amazon has been offering a similar sale in October, giving eager shoppers yet another chance to save big. Electronics and home goods tend to be the most popular—and most heavily discounted—items during these Prime Day events, but we typically also see great deals on clothing and shoes, luggage, beauty products, outdoor gear, and travel essentials. When is Prime Day? Amazon finally announced the dates for its fall sale. This year, Prime Big Deal Days will run from Tuesday, October 6, through Wednesday, October 7, 2026. This makes right now a great time to start thinking about which items you hope to see on sale and start building your wish list. Do I have to be an Amazon Prime member to shop the sales? Yes, to take advantage of the limited-time mega sale, you must be a Prime member. Not only do members get access to Prime Day deals, but they also earn free two-day shipping all year long. A Prime membership costs $139 annually or $15 per month. If you're on the fence about joining, sign up for a free 30-day trial. What did our readers buy most last Prime Day? Need some inspo on what to add to your shopping cart ahead of Prime Day 2026? Say no more—check below to see what CN Traveler readers bought most during Amazon's July sale. First and foremost, Away luggage was very popular—and for good reason. The brand's lightweight suitcases are some of our editors' all-time favorite carry-ons and checked bags to travel with. Our readers also picked up a bunch of in-flight essentials, from comfy eye masks to neck pillows (these must-haves can make even the longest flights in economy a little bit more bearable!). In addition, comfortable sneakers, trendy jelly flats, Levi's jeans, portable steamers, and the viral Ōura Ring were big hits among our readers. What early sales can I shop now? We're still a few weeks away from Prime Big Deal Days, but Amazon has plenty of great deals running right now worth checking out. From Bagsmart's top-selling toiletry bag to noise-canceling headphones from Beats, there are already plenty of discounted travel essentials marked down. Also on sale: expandable carry-ons and luggage sets from Samsonite, as well as some travel backpacks and duffel bags. Discounted sneakers, Chelsea boots, and workout sets are all up for grabs too. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 20% Off Away Promo Code | September 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.38
It’s no secret that Away is one of our team's favorite luggage brands. With its thoughtfully designed suitcases and sleek essentials, the brand has become synonymous with effortless movement, whether you’re heading out on a quick city escape or a long-haul adventure. If you’ve been waiting to invest in your next travel companion, know that verified Away promo codes can help you save on signature styles—from up to $100 off select luggage bundles to 20% off sale items. Whether you’re planning a cross-country road trip or a flight abroad, these savings make it easier to pack stylishly and travel smarter. Adding to the lineup, Away launched a highly anticipated, kid-friendly partnership with Toy Story 5. This exclusive collection features sweet, colorful, and durable luggage, backpacks, and packing cubes inspired by beloved characters like Woody, Buzz Lightyear, Jessie, and the Little Green Men. When you introduce a friend to the brand, they’ll receive $40 off their first purchase of $125 or more—and once their order is complete, you’ll get $40 off your next one, too. The best part? You can earn up to $200 in rewards by referring as many as five friends. To claim the offer, your friend simply uses your referral link to visit Away’s Get Rewarded page, where a unique code appears to apply at checkout. The discount is valid on suitcases and bags only, making it an ideal way to refresh your own travel setup while helping someone else discover the quality and design that make Away a go-to for savvy travelers. Shop Away Luggage pieces under $300 and family travel essentials Away proves that great design and thoughtful functionality don’t have to come at a steep price. The brand’s lineup of best-selling luggage under $300 includes sleek staples like The Carry-On ($275) and The Bigger Carry-On ($295)—lightweight, durable pieces that glide effortlessly through terminals and tuck neatly into overhead bins. You can explore more travel-ready finds in Away’s Under $300 collection. For families, Away’s Family Travel collection makes group trips easier with space-maximizing suitcases, kids’ luggage, diaper bags, crossbody bags, and even pet carriers. Larger pieces like The Medium Flex and The Trunk offer extra capacity and deep compartments, perfect for storing everyone’s essentials in one place. Free shipping, a lifetime warranty, and more reasons to love Away Away’s appeal goes beyond its minimalist design—it’s the thoughtful details that make the brand a trusted travel companion. Orders over $100 ship free, and if something isn’t quite right, you can return or exchange unused items within 100 days, either online or at one of Away’s 17 stores. And with Shop Pay, you can choose interest-free installments to make investing in quality gear a little easier. What to do if your Away promo code is not working If your Away promo code isn't working at checkout, don't panic—there are a few simple things you can do. item.title: Madewell Promo Codes for September 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.33
To master the art of travel fashion is to keep a uniform—an arsenal of well-made basics that can be mixed and matched depending on the climate, mode of transport, and itinerary. Enter Madewell, a purveyor of perfect T-shirts, vintage-inspired denim, and leather goods since 2006. Whether you need a versatile button-down that can double as a dinner top and beach cover-up, or a do-it-all tote that serves as your personal item, Madewell is stocked with your travel essentials—the pieces you pack again and again. If J.Crew is the preppy girl boss, Madewell is her artsy younger sister. The brand’s history actually dates back to 1937 in New Bedford, Massachusetts, where it started out as a workwear company, producing heavy duty denim overalls and corduroy-lined jackets until its closing in 1989. Mickey Drexler, former CEO of J.Crew, acquired the name and logo in 2004, relaunching Madewell two years later. Since then, the brand has launched a menswear line and collaborated with style icons like Alexa Chung and Dakota Fanning. Whether you’re looking to become a Madewell Insider, or simply take advantage of the brand’s student discount, there’s always a promotion in store. Below, the best Madewell promo codes to take advantage of now. Get a Madewell coupon code on your first order when you sign up to be an Insider Customers new to Madewell’s Insider program can get $10 off a single purchase of $75 or more when they join and sign up for texts. Beyond that initial purchase, there will be plenty more ways to make use of the loyalty program, which guarantees everything from free shipping and access to bi-annual Insider Event sales events to a $25 off birthday gift and complimentary jean hems. You’ll earn 1 point for every $1 that you spend, and for every 250 points, you’ll get $10 off. It’s free to sign up, and if you end up becoming a really serious Madewell shopper, you might even reach Star (spend $500+) or Icon (spend $1000) status, leading to even more perks, like free returns and expedited shipping. Get a $20 Madewell discount code when you refer a friend Once you’ve hopped on the Insider train, get your friends involved with a unique referral link. With the Give $20, Get $20 offer, you’ll receive your own $20 Madewell voucher once your friend signs up for the Insider program and completes a purchase. Save up to 78% without a promo code in the Madewell sale this fall Elevate your fall wardrobe with a little help from the Madewell sale, with markdowns up to 78%, including this chic Smocked Boatneck top. Madewell T-shirts are the kinds of basics you’ll want to stock up on, and the Relaxed Tee in Vintage Jersey is currently discounted in select colors (trust me, they’ll only get better in the wash). If you're looking for your next vacation outfit, the classic Pencil jean, currently 59% off, is perfect for pairing with the Straight-Hem linen shirt, currently 49% off in the color Ivory Linen. Additionally, the retailer is offering discounts on bundles, perfect for saving on your favorite essentials. When you choose three pairs of socks for instance, you'll get 25% off (the Ribbed Crew socks are a godsend for wearing loafers sans blisters). The same goes for three T-shirts or tank tops—there are so many styles to mix and match with, whether you're after the '90s Shell Tank or the Perfect Crewneck. The Insiders Event: an extra 25% off everything without a promo code Twice a year, Madewell hosts an Insiders Event that marks (nearly) everything down 25%. The sale is open to Insiders only, so make sure you sign up for the program. Discounts apply to women’s and men’s styles and include everything from the best-selling Devon pants to Rugby shirts. You can participate in the sales event both in stores and online. Get a $20 Madewell discount code when you refer a friend Once you’ve hopped on the Insider train, get your friends involved with a unique referral link. With the Give $20, Get $20 offer, you’ll receive your own $20 Madewell voucher once your friend signs up for the Insider program and completes a purchase. Select customers can receive a 15% discount code As a thank you for their service, Madewell offers a 15% discount to first responders, medical professionals, and military personnel; teachers and college students get a break too. For in-store purchases, simply flash your ID at checkout, and if you’re buying online, verify via SheerID. Your discount will be valid for one year (after which you’ll just need to renew) and applied to eligible items in your cart, no promo code needed. Trade in an old pair of jeans for a $20 discount off new Madewell denim In a commitment to sustainability—and a nod to the idea that clothes made well are ripe for reuse—the brand will offer $20 off a pair of Madewell jeans when you trade in an old pair, no matter the brand. Simply drop your old jeans off at a store, where they’ll be resold or recycled via Cotton's Blue Jeans Go Green program, or trade in from home via ThredUp—print out a free shipping label, load up your package (you can also include clothing), and you’ll receive the $20 off for every pair of jeans you send, plus shopping credit for anything else that sells within the listing window. How to fix a Madewell promo code that’s not working If your Madewell coupon code isn't working, be sure to check for typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization. You should also check the details of the promo code to ensure it's still active and hasn't expired. Some discount codes have a minimum spend requirement, so make sure your cart meets any necessary criteria to qualify. You can also try clearing your browser’s cache and cookies, or switching devices or browsers. If all else fails, the Madewell team is there to help.

item.title: 29 Best Hotels in Miami (2026), From Key Biscayne to Wynwood
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.13
Once dominated by pastel Art Deco and late-night bass, the best hotels in Miami have evolved into an eclectic, high-design, sprawling ecosystem. Beyond the legendary oceanfront icons of South Beach lie moody art-filled sanctuaries, discreet European-style retreats, and soaring glass towers anchored in the cosmopolitan energy of Brickell. Luckily, when it comes to picking the right one, towering Downtown Miami and iconic Miami Beach alike have a wide variety of top-tier accommodations for every need (and bank account). City-loving travelers will be pleasantly surprised by the sophisticated hotels in Miami’s dense urban core. Beach-goers can look forward to thousands of square feet of pristine beach to enjoy at a number of oceanfront resorts. Whether you are chasing Damien Hirst gold, rooftop bars, or pristine (and velvet-rope-free) beaches, here are the absolute best places to check in right now. Our top picks: - Best overall: 1 Hotel South Beach - Best for beach access: Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club - Most romantic: Faena Hotel Miami Beach - Best for families: Loews Miami Beach Hotel - Best for first-timers: Andaz Miami Beach by Hyatt - Read Full ReviewAfter a six-year closure and a $100 million restoration, the Delano Miami Beach returns knowing exactly what made it legendary in the first place: design, drama, and glamor with a sense of place. Elastic Architects resisted turning the hotel into a museum of its former selves, instead weaving together restored favorites like the Rose Bar with guestrooms that feel warmer and more inviting than before, especially the two-story Poolside Bungalows just steps from the hotel's iconic pool. In the Delano’s third incarnation, one of Miami Beach's best beach-and-pool scenes returns (both cocktail- and kid-friendly this go’round), paired with high profile restaurants by Paris Society, namely Gigi Rigolatto and Mimi Kakushi, where locals often outnumber overnight guests. Add Café Delano's irresistible pistachio croissants, heartfelt service, an immaculate art collection, and members programming open to hotel guests, and the Delano once again is all the hype on South Beach. - Read Full ReviewA crisp, minimalist European import that seamlessly blends modern corporate cool with Miami's vibrant rooftop culture all while being tucked away on a quiet leafy street in Brickell’s bustling neighborhood. The 275 rooms here are a calm and cool retreat from Miami’s loud and frenetic downtown. Spacious and flooded with natural light, thanks to floor-to-ceiling windows, the rooms lean into a soothing palette of cool grays, warm wood accents, and pops of yellow. Brickell’s glittering skyline envelopes this high-rise and, depending on where your room is situated, you can catch a glimpse of Biscayne Bay or the lush Simpson Park that cuts through a swath of downtown. Bathrooms are streamlined and modern with expansive glass walk-in showers and all rooms include Lavazza coffee makers and mini-fridges. - Read Full ReviewArriving at the Surfcomber feels a bit like hopscotching through Miami Beach history. The hotel's Collins Avenue neighbors—The Sagamore, National, SLS, among others—line the street in linen white. Not one to break dress code, the Surfcomber's façade is also marked by sharp lines; a dramatic, semicircle driveway to coast into; and smooth, matte-white walls—a fitting canvas for the party lights that paint the South Beach streets neon. With 186 rooms, there is a box-of-chocolates variety of accommodations to choose from, whether you're a solo traveler just looking for a place to settle at night, or you're looking to really treat yourself by booking an oceanfront suite with your own private balcony. All rooms come with luxury Atelier Bloem bath products, and keep to a generally neutral palette to keep the attention on the view from your room. A visit to the pool and backyard space is just about necessary when it comes to staying at the Surfcomber. Be amazed by the difference the distance of the lobby can make between the bass-boosted streets and the secluded beach bar and stunning pool—go ahead, rent that cabana. - Read Full ReviewUnframed, Autograph Collection signals a fun, cutting-edge design chapter for Miami Beach—with bold, curvy architecture and easygoing spaces that invite you to stay a while. Behind its sculptural façade, you’ll find plush rooms, a rooftop pool for lingering, and a French Riviera–inspired dining scene that gives the hotel its own personality. It’s a stylish home base for exploring South Beach—close enough to the action, but with plenty of reasons to come back before the night is over. The 149 rooms feel like a cool retreat from the buzz of Miami Beach. Rich velvet headboards, warm wood finishes, and pops of blush and rust make the spaces feel inviting and chic, while details like marble vanities and sleek microcement showers add just the right amount of drama. - Read Full ReviewBlink and you might think you mistakenly hopped a plane to Savannah instead of South Beach: At the northernmost end of Ocean Drive, this hotel’s Florida-Georgia style of architecture sticks out like a colonial masterpiece in a sea of pastel-colored Art Deco gems. While some people head to the neighborhood with only late nights out on their mind, The Betsy attracts a different, more erudite crowd. Yes, they love being in the thick of all that touristy mayhem, but prefer that it not happen right outside their window. And it’s not just the hotel’s quaint façade that seems to attract a different type of South Beach reveler; inside, the public spaces act as a sort of art gallery, with photo exhibitions rotating throughout the year. Rooms are spacious and have mini libraries, writing desks, and oversized marble bathrooms; the hotel also counts two pools and a rooftop ocean deck among its attractions. - Read Full ReviewThe first new hotel to grace South Beach’s storied Española Way in a decade, the enchanting Esme Miami Beach is all about the boutique hotel charms. Rather than replicate the easy, breezy, sand-in-your-toes style of South Beach’s grand dames, this restored enclave (which comprises eight buildings connected by charming paseos) offers a well-placed base from which to explore South Beach. You know you’re in for a unique experience as soon as you walk in the door; the lobby is outfitted with thick crimson carpeting, Moroccan-style benches, and accents of brass and dark green, setting the tone for the Moorish influence on decor throughout the property. The rooftop pool is small but striking (and not really made for anything other than dipping), but it’s a perfect spot for catching sun under the connected peach and white striped daybeds that line the deck. - Read Full ReviewLocated in the trendy Brickell neighborhood, this Four Seasons lets you discover Miami beyond just the beach—without sacrificing those turquoise water views. With a two-acre, palm tree-lined rooftop pool overlooking Biscayne Bay, you can access the best of the city’s vibrant downtown area while still enjoying the tropical relaxation one deserves when vacationing in South Florida. Most of the guests here are well-heeled business travelers, but there were also a fair amount of (well-behaved) young families and friend groups on vacation mode at the property’s sprawling pool facilities. Among Miamians, the hotel is best known for its extravagant Sunday Brunch; all tables become immediately filled with a combination of local residents and hotel guests, a natural overlap felt throughout the property, which is also home to the Four Seasons Residences. - Read Full ReviewJust as he did back in the 1990s with the Delano, Ian Schrager is reinventing the Miami Beach experience with The Edition. Here, every amenity a person could want (or even know was possible) is there for the taking—ice skating rink included—and the hotel has five fabulous drinking and dining options, including Matador Room, Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s innovative Latin fusion restaurant. There’s no detail in the rooms that hasn't been scrutinized in an attempt to exceed guests’ every expectation, and the heavenly, low-slung bed—which sits atop a light oak frame that blends in with the walls, and is topped with a down comforter and pillows—is no exception. - Read Full ReviewThere are two entry points to the Gale: through the high-ceilinged, grand valet on one side, and rose-hued in-house restaurant Casa Gianna on the other. Either route makes for quite the entrance to this sparkling 51-story tower, where glamorous people with things to do come and go at a steady clip. This is an affordable, reliable stay smack dab in the thick of Downtown Miami that feels impenetrably tranquil despite the noise all around. The rooms here mirror the residences in the same building, so you can book a studio, one-bedroom, or two-bedroom ranging from 410 to 910 square feet. Most of these have full kitchens and washer-dryers, so you can really set up shop. Decor is minimal and modern, with black-and-white photography on the walls and furniture in neutral colors. The windows are floor-to-ceiling for the most part, meaning massive Miami views. Take out a bike to Miami Beach—you’ll fly past traffic and will not regret it. - Read Full ReviewThe Ritz-Carlton South Beach, one of a string of hotels on Miami’s destination waterfront, is a refined respite from the area’s pool parties and 'til-the-sun-rises nightlife, while still providing easy access to the city’s best restaurants, a great lobby bar scene, and ocean views. The rooms are crisp and modern, with white walls and linens punctuated by deep cerulean blue furniture—a velvet bed frame, plush chaise—and midcentury-style accents like bronze reading lamps and caned armchairs. In the ocean-view rooms and suites, which make up a majority of the room categories, the brilliant Atlantic out of the window is the real star of the show, just as it should be. Like most Ritz-Carltons, the experience is reliably five-star: service is fantastic, the decor is elevated and modern while nodding to the destination, amenities leave little to be desired, and the location is ideal. - Read Full ReviewThe first hotel to officially open in Wynwood, Miami’s graffiti-clad neighborhood that’s now home to dozens of galleries, shops, and restaurants—the Arlo is an art-filled oasis that seeks to strike a balance between being a splashy getaway and a vibrant urban hotel. The hotel’s aesthetic draws on the neighborhood’s high concentration of street art, with the property's exterior walls featuring works by Miami-based artist Hoxxoh, and 250 pieces of contemporary art positioned throughout the public spaces and guest rooms. There’s an inviting ninth-floor rooftop pool with a cocktail bar and views of the Miami skyline. The hotel also strives to be a hub of activity for its guests with weekly programming like comedy nights, fitness classes, and space devoted to loungey coworking environments with a pool table and a yoga deck. While the hotel is lacking in certain frills (like room service), there are also thoughtful touches like complimentary fortune cookies in the rooms with unique fortunes and bicycles for guests to explore the neighborhood. - Read Full ReviewMiami Beach’s midcentury Art Deco scene may have cemented its place in design history, but today a new, grown-up iteration can be found in the form of The Shelborne By Proper. Guest rooms are reflective of the entire property’s mood: elevated yet easy. My room on the sixth floor featured a partial ocean view, just enough of a glimpse of that turquoise blue water to whet my palate. The room’s design feels calm and grounded, which I owe to the soft, earthy tones and warm, natural textiles. It’s a nice counterbalance to the energetic vibe that Miami Beach naturally offers, a true retreat that feels intentionally devoid of flashy artwork and instead focuses on curved, architectural furnishings that are low-profile and slim. Also noteworthy is that the design is nowhere near that stereotypical Florida coastal-chic image with wooden floors and shiplapped walls. Instead, the rooms are elevated with marble flooring that is warmed up with a textured off-white rug. - Read Full ReviewEven amid the architectural exhibitionism of Miami Beach, the gleaming curved main tower of the 1,500-room Fontainebleau Miami Beach is a knockout. The design of this essentially launched the so-called Miami-Modern style, and the resort dominates its stretch of Miami Beach. It’s a clean and classic escape where contemporary vibes meet retro in a flash of glamour. Although the Fontainebleau has been upgraded at no small expense, guests still feel like they’re part of its storied past. - Read Full ReviewOpened in 2024, this 13-room hotel is nestled inside the four-story landmark Moore building, which also houses a posh coworking space, private club, art gallery, and restaurant on the ground floor. Upon walking inside, you’re immediately struck by the Zaha Hadid site-specific installation Elastika that spans the light-filled atrium connecting the different levels with stretches of web-like material. It’s both cheeky and iconic. The main spot here is Torno Subito, located on the ground floor of the atrium and headed up by famed Italian chef Massimo Bottura and his team. The menu focuses on modern Italian cuisine and includes dishes like Mediterranean Sea Bass stuffed with pork, tiny, handmade tortellini served in a rich Parmigiano broth, and “Oops, I burned the Key lime pie”—a South Florida-inspired reimagining of Bottura's iconic "Oops, I dropped the lemon tart" dessert. Guests of the hotel can also dine on the second-floor balcony restaurant that is part of the members’ club. My lunch there included a delicious hen-of-the-woods mushroom pizza and spicy tuna crispy rice from the sushi bar. During city-wide events like Art Basel and Formula 1, the place is a hive of activity. FAQ: How we choose the best hotels in Miami Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind More Miami recommendations Read our complete Miami travel guide here, which includes: This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 9 Hotels With Indoor Water Parks Worth Planning a Trip Around
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.01
Hotels with indoor water parks have saved more than a few family vacations from the tyranny of the weather forecast. When the main attraction is tucked under a roof, a rainy Saturday or surprise cold snap suddenly matters a lot less. And for anyone traveling with kids, there’s something deeply appealing about checking into a hotel where the day’s biggest activity requires little more planning than putting on a swimsuit and taking the elevator downstairs. I’ve spent years writing about hotels and family travel, and the resorts that stick with me tend to be the ones that make life easier without making the trip feel generic. A great indoor water park does exactly that. Kids get the big-ticket fun of slides, wave pools, and lazy rivers, while parents get a vacation that requires considerably less logistical gymnastics. The best properties go further, pairing all that chlorine-fueled chaos with skiing, horseback riding, mountain adventures, good restaurants, or even a little grown-up downtime. The resorts below are places where the water park can justify the trip, but it doesn’t have to consume it. Read on for the best hotels with indoor water parks in the US. FAQ: What's the best indoor water park resort in the US? For a trip where you want the water park to be the main focus, I'd pick Kalahari Resorts & Conventions in Wisconsin Dells. The town itself is built around water parks, and Kalahari's is 125,000 square feet right now and set to grow another 75,000 when the expansion opens in late October 2026. There's also enough else on the property—restaurants, a spa, shops, an adventure park—that you don't need to leave the premises for a long weekend. If, however, you want mountain time to be part of the trip too, Camelback, Jay Peak, and Boyne Mountain are all solid choices. Which hotel has the biggest indoor water park? Kalahari Resorts & Conventions in Round Rock, Texas, currently boasts America's largest indoor water park resort, at 223,000 square feet. Among the nine listed here, Kalahari Wisconsin Dells and Camelback's Aquatopia are tied at 125,000 square feet. However, Kalahari Wisconsin Dells will pull ahead once its expansion opens in late October 2026. Why pick an indoor water park over an outdoor one? It's simple: It removes the weather variable. A climate-controlled park stays warm through winter, through a rainy spring break, and through a cold fall weekend, so you can book the trip without checking a forecast first. This matters even more at mountain resorts, where a day might start with snow and ski boots and end with a lazy river. Several of these resorts also have outdoor pools that open seasonally, so you're not locked into one or the other. How we choose the best hotels with indoor water parks Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: In the Rainforest of Chilean Patagonia, Pushing My Limits at a Trail Running Retreat
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.01
It’s 3 a.m., zero degrees, and drizzling, and I’m standing in the middle of the Punucapa rainforest in the southern Los Ríos region of Chile, about to go for a run. Back home in my comfortable corner of south east London, with its mere four months of annual sunshine and warmth, I'd become desperate to not be a fair weather runner. But this now seems like a rather extreme approach to my New Year’s resolution to embrace running in the wet and cold. I’m not alone: a canopy of evergreen, moss-covered trees, and a floor of giant Jurassic ferns envelop me along with 80 other runners, all awake and full of adrenaline at this unseemly hour. An Indigenous Mapuche singer’s voice rings out into the silence in an ancestral welcome chant; we are on his people’s land, and he wishes us safe travels as we scale the punishing mountains. Soon, though, it will be just me, my head torch, and the dancing mist as my warm breath rapidly condenses into the pitch black night. Trail running is increasingly evolving from a niche, counter-culture sport that ultra runners do to punish themselves into a mainstream driver for travel. The UTMB Torrencial in Valdivia, Chile started 10 years ago with 300 local runners, and this year welcomed 3,000 people from almost 30 countries; it’s now the biggest trail running event in Latin America. “Valdivia in winter is a good place to learn to love the rain,” head organizer Marcela Escalona promises me the evening before, showing me around the bustling race hub full of warm showers, massage tables, and tasty meals of asado (smoky, grilled meat) for the finishers. “In the quiet of the off-peak season, runners here can enjoy the freedom of the rainforest.” As part of the race’s 900 per cent participation increase in recent years, women like me—new to the sport and running shorter 6km and 12km distances—are the quickest growing group. I could have stuck to the trails on the outskirts of London, but having wanted to explore South America for years and finding myself devastatingly chair-shaped and suffering from the January blues at the top of the year, the invitation to “face one of the darkest nights of the year” in the mud, rain, and cold was exactly the adventure I was looking for. The shortest 6km race seemed achievable; I'd start my trail running journey, unlock South America, and leave the 100km ultra ultra to those impressive, fit individuals I aspire to be. But 24 hours before beginning I was crying on the phone to my girlfriend, chastising myself for being so impulsive. What if I trip and slide down the mountain? What if I’m so slow in the mud they kick me out before I finish? What if I freeze halfway through my run because I’ve not got enough layers? What if all the pro runners laugh at me, a fledgling beginner? And on a deeper level, why do I feel the need to pursue such extremes, rather than being content with my weekly local ParkRun? Fast forward to the horn blowing and I sprint like the proverbial hare. This surprises me, because I’m reliably the tortoise; I run a consistently slow six-and-a-half minute kilometer, but now I’m running it in five. My watch tells me I’ve just run my fastest kilometer ever, and still the other runners are outpacing me. The panic of being left behind kicks in, but the pendulum beam of my head torch lulls me into a slower rhythm, reminding me I didn’t do this to win: I just need to finish. All I can see is mud; my running poles sink a good six inches per stride as I haul myself up the 350 meter ascent. My local “hilly” park maxes out at 50 meters of elevation. In laypeople terms, I’m used to running up a 15-story hill. This is 105 stories, in a place where it rains 10 months of the year, and it’s a total mud pit. I’m one misstep away from sliding down the mountain like I'm on a giant slip and slide. At 1 a.m. that morning I’d woken with my race day alarm to a text from my mother: “Don’t break anything. Love you.” Rousing words as I mentally check my survival thermal blanket, safety whistle, first aid kit, water, and tracking chip are all secure in my running vest in case I hurtle back down to the jungle floor. Before this trip I was on the verge of burnout. My average day involved moving from one screen to the next. My longing to try trail running grew from knowing it would require my full focus to deftly navigate exposed tree roots, intruding branches, slippery rocks and gushing, knee-deep streams: a zone of forced mindfulness. In the peace of the darkness and silence of this ancient temperate rainforest wedged between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes, I’m overcome by a wave of utter bliss. My body is alert but my mind is in nature’s own sound bath. I pause to inhale the sweet balsamic of the Mañío and the pepperiness of the ancient Canelo trees. The Valdivian rainforest has some of the cleanest, freshest air in the world. The only survivor of the last Ice Age, the Los Ríos region is a real dinosaur landscape; a hidden gem of Chile that most travelers skip in favour of the popular San Pedro di Atacama desert in the north or the marvels of Torres del Paine in southern Patagonia. When I finally hit level ground and sturdy gravel, only hundreds of meters from the race’s end, I’m suddenly sad to be finishing. My legs are jelly, but I’m on an endorphin high and want to keep running. Why did I limit myself to 6km? Warm cheers and smiley faces greet me as I finish at 4:25 a.m., yelling “¡Buena! ¡Buena!” I did it; I didn’t fall. I’m almost last, but who cares. I want to keep running. Let me back into that glorious rainforest. At 9 a.m., when most local Valdivians are waking up, I’m soaking in the hot tub of Hotel Puerto del Sur, pisco sour in hand. Looking directly across the Cruces River at the mountain I just scaled, I can see the deep green, conifer shapes of the rainforest. I wonder how those ultra ultra runners are going on their 100km, 18-or-so-hour journeys, almost envious. Another sip and my thoughts melt; the yin and yang of hard trails and cossetting recovery. Re-entering the race hub in my finisher hoodie, other runners look up and nod, silently welcoming me into the tribe. I curiously seek out 100km finishers, wondering how it all began for them. Santiago-based Carlos' first race was 14km: “I cried when I finished 14km and said never again. Then I moved onto 30, 40, 50km races. When I realized I couldn't run a race without crying I decided to keep going: 80 and now to 100km.” What’s the limit, I ask? “Mont-Blanc,” he says with a dogged grin. The hallowed pinnacle of the UTMB World Series, Mont-Blanc, is an astonishing invite-only 174km trail with 9,900 meters of elevation gain through France, Italy, and Switzerland. “One day?” I wonder to myself. Determined to explore more of the Los Ríos region before I head home, I spend a few days in the lap of luxury in the middle of the jungle. A two-hour drive from Valdivia, on the edge of Patagonia, is the 100,000 hectare Unesco-protected biological reserve, Huilo Huilo. Home to some of the rarest animals in the world—Darwin’s frogs, pumas, and the adorable miniature pudu deer—Huilo Huilo also houses three Michelin Guide hotels. I stay in Montaña Mágica, a literal treehouse with a waterfall casually cascading down the side. Going to sleep surrounded by snow-topped volcanoes, with the perfect white noise of a waterfall, watching tall spindly Nothofagus beeches swaying outside my picture-book circular windows, is a magical moment. Over the next few days I mix lounging by the spa and gentle self-guided trails through the jungle with some of the reserve’s winter activities. I continued to pursue Chile’s magnificent extremes by snowmobiling up and snowshoeing down Mocho Choshuenco volcano in the morning and bathing by the side of a ravine in the Rañintulelfu hot springs at sunset. I think back to my nervous beginnings in Chile, fearful of my limitations. Sitting on the edge of my ability expanded my belief of what’s possible—and with mountains, sub-zero temperatures and pouring rain now in my running wheelhouse, the only logical next step is to go further. Huilo Huilo has a 20km trail race in November on the side of the volcano. Maybe this time I can watch the sunrise from the trail, back in flow in the rainforest.

item.title: This sun-soaked destination has been named the best place for a last-minute autumn escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.61
As one record-breaking summer draws to a close and the guarantee of drizzle and plummeting temperatures hangs over us, the prospect of catching some last-minute autumn sunshine is extremely tempting. While there is no shortage of chic winter sun destinations on our radar, whether that’s Christmas in the Caribbean or banishing the January blues along Mexico’s Pacific coast, there’s still time to top up the vitamin D closer to home. But where should we be heading for sun-sure adventures this September and October? According to the number-crunchers at travel insurance site Quotezone.co.uk, Antalya is the best destination for an autumn sun getaway right now. The ancient Turkish city has long been a favourite destination among sun-seekers, with a plethora of sleek hotels and resorts catering to every type of escape along its glittering coast. With some of the best beaches in Turkey, plenty of history to uncover, a lively city centre and natural landscapes beloved by active travellers and adrenaline junkies, it’s the perfect place to don the swimwear one last time. To uncover the dreamiest autumn sun destinations, Quotezone selected ten of the most popular holiday spots in southern Europe and pitted them against each other across several factors. These include the average temperatures in September and October, sunshine hours, rainfall and sea temperature – plus the lowest price for a three-night stay. With an average temperature of 27.6°C, 9.5 sunshine hours and a particularly balmy sea temperature of 27.5°C, Antalya is a clear winner. In second place is the Canary Island of Tenerife, included in the survey as an autonomous community of Spain, with average temperatures of 26.3°C and some of the cheapest stays at £108 for three nights. The Cypriot city of Larnaca is third, also offering 9.5 hours of sunshine, while the largest and most southerly of the Greek islands, Crete, promises an escape from the northern hemisphere’s chill and 24.5°C waters for bathing.

item.title: Where was 'The Dog Stars' filmed? The surprising mountainous hideout that stood in for Canada's peaks
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.91
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Dog Stars filmed? The year is 2035. Along a mountain range on the south side of Denver, survivors are navigating an unprecedented, post-pandemic world. A deadly flu outbreak has wiped out a vast majority of the human population, and many who have survived remain with a debilitating blood disease. This is the premise of Ridley Scott’s latest blockbuster, starring Jacob Elordi as young pilot Hig, Margaret Qualley as Cima and Josh Brolin as Bangley. While Bangley has no intentions of leaving the efficient homestead he and Hig have settled into, Hig is determined to track down other survivors, frequently embarking on tracking missions alongside his trusty dog, Jasper. As these stories unfold in a post-apocalyptic world far from crumbling metropolises, the natural world plays a major role in Scott’s latest movie. While set in Canada, filming took place in Italy between April and June 2025. “The size and scale of the production footprint in Italy was ideal for what we needed,” says The Dog Stars production designer Chris Seager. “We found a combination of quality locations that could convincingly represent Colorado, while also being relatively close together. This allowed us to work much more efficiently from a production point of view.” “We also considered Canada,” says Chris. “But ultimately Italy offered the best combination of location quality, scale and practical logistics. Being able to concentrate so many of the locations within a manageable area was a huge advantage for the production, helping us maximise our time and resources.” So where exactly did the team set up camp during the epic-scale production? Here, we uncover some of the key locations to keep an eye out for. Cinecittà Studios, Rome While much of The Dog Stars’ cinematography took place beside forests and mountain peaks, Rome’s Cinecittà Studios played a crucial role in the scenes set at Grand Junction Airport. “Cinecittà was amazing,” says Chris. “It quickly became evident that, to achieve the scale and complexity of the effects that Ridley wanted, we needed to work on a soundstage where we could have complete control over the environment.” Chris recalls how the set within Europe’s largest film studio was built in just four weeks. On the studio filming, cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt said, “[Cinecittà Studios] houses Italy’s most modern sound stages. It’s the centre of studio production and is familiar to all local crew. It was the best and most obvious option.” Abruzzo Much filming also took place in Italy’s Abruzzo region. One such apocalyptic scene honed in on the city of Avezzano. Chris says: “One of the biggest and most challenging locations was the petrol station [in Avezzano] where we filmed the city landing sequence – we actually landed the plane in the street! We transformed the location entirely: we trashed the petrol station and the surrounding area to create the sense of a world that had been abandoned and reclaimed by nature. The greens department and the layered set dressing played a huge role in this. “To represent the cycle of life, we created a swimming pool and diving board, which we filled with dead bodies and overgrown vegetation, crocuses growing through the remains. It was a very strong visual expression of the post-apocalyptic, graphic world, but it also presented considerable logistical challenges in terms of access and working within the location.” EUR, Rome The Roman business and residential district of EUR (Esposizione Universale Roma), known for its cultural happenings and Fascist-era architecture, saw the production team set up more post-apocalyptic scenes. “The Roman neighbourhood of EUR stood in for the Denver city hall triage centre where Hig goes to retrieve supplies. It was a challenging place to shoot, as it’s normally a busy city, but the Roman authorities were very helpful in making it happen for us, and it was ultimately one of the most successful sections of the film,” says Erik. Bordano Bordano was an empty field that is used for hang-gliding, so we had to transform the entire site from scratch,” says Chris. “We built nine airplane hangars, Bangley’s house and tower, as well as a number of smaller sheds and a trailer home. We also dressed large quantities of grass and other greenery to make the location feel abandoned and overgrown.” “The whole process took approximately five weeks, which was a very tight turnaround given the scale of the build. The major benefit of working on location was the sheer amount of space and the ability to create the environment at the scale required, rather than being constrained by a studio. It also allowed the buildings, runway and surrounding environment to exist together as one cohesive world, giving the finished locations a greater sense of authenticity and scale.” The Dog Stars is in UK cinemas now

item.title: Where was Youth filmed? Sharon Horgan’s latest divorce comedy embraces the history of London
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.33
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Youth filmed? Sharon Horgan is behind so many TV shows that we know and love, including the darkly funny Bad Sisters, Pulling, Catastrophe, and hilarious Motherland. Shows that will forever remain iconic to audiences around the world. And now, she’s back with her latest project, Youth. The new eight-episode HBO series follows a 50-year-old divorcée (played by Horgan herself) who finds herself single again and searching for love and intimacy, while navigating her career, caring for her elderly parents, and her troubled 18-year-old son (played by Cillian Murphy’s son, Aran). As well as love and divorce, Youth also examines the online influences shaping teenage boys through the character of Alex’s son Ruari, who is struggling emotionally and being fed distorted ideas of masculinity in the digital sphere. The series stars Rupert Friend, Sharlene Whyte, Aran Murphy, and Robbie Gee, with Harriet Walter, Anne Reid, Freddie Fox, and Damian Lewis also appearing in supporting and guest roles throughout the show. Speaking about the inspiration behind her new series, Horgan recently told The Guardian: “When I found myself divorced, I genuinely thought I’d be alone forever. I didn’t even know if I’d ever have sex again. There’s that extreme fear of being alone and being lonely. But at the same time, you think you have a freedom as well. You do suddenly think: ‘My kids have finished school, I’ve got some time to try and get this right.’” Where was Youth filmed? The Old Sessions House, London The physical setting for Horgan’s character Alex’s work is The Old Sessions House, which houses the fictional literary agency Alex is a part of. The Irish Times visited the production set in May 2026 and reported that filming was taking place inside the building. Horgan was there on the day of filming and explained that they were actually shooting in this historic building, rather than merely using it as a photographic exterior. And The Old Sessions House does have a rich literary history. Constructed between 1780 and 1782, the building (named Middlesex Quarter Sessions) served as a courthouse for many years. Its connection to the literary world is that Charles Dickens used this location as the courthouse that Oliver Twist appeared before in his novel. Lucky Cat, Mayfair The HBO trailer also shows Alex appearing to have a work meeting at Gordon Ramsay’s Asian-inspired restaurant, Lucky Cat. The luxury and elegance of the restaurant’s interiors are perhaps a fitting setting to showcase Alex’s professional endeavours in publishing and her desire to progress in her career. Islington, North London Some parts of the more residential scenes of Youth were filmed in the borough of Islington, including Wenlock Road and Union Wharf. Mallorca, Spain There have also been local reports that Youth took to Spanish climates to film parts of the series. According to Majorca Daily Bulletin, Rupert Friend and the production crew were spotted in May 2026 filming in Sant Elm. However, not too much else is known about what scenes were filmed here and how they fit into Youth’s storylines. Youth premieres on HBO on 20 September 2026.

item.title: 12 best islands in Thailand to visit 2026 for honeymooners, families and solo travellers
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.22
The best islands in Thailand evoke images of pristine white sands, rustic-chic beach shacks, and gently swaying hammocks offering views of the turquoise sea and famed rock formations. But with a total of 1,430 islands spread across the Gulf of Thailand and Andaman Sea, not all are born equal. The largest, Phuket, is one of the busiest in terms of travellers, with its own international airport and some of the best hotels in Thailand. Then there are the tiny, off-the-beaten-track gems like Koh Lipe, small enough to explore by foot and only accessible by speedboat or ferry from the Thai mainland. With so many to choose from, one of the best approaches is to base your itinerary on the time of year. Islands off the West Coast such as Phuket, Koh Lanta and Koh Lipe are at their best in December to April, while Koh Samui and Koh Tao off the east coast are ideal for visiting from February to September. There's no need to choose just one island either, with day trips by boat readily available to take you from plush resort to remote islet and back again. Lauren Burvill For inspiration, we round up the best islands in Thai including what they offer and where to stay. Editor's picks of the best islands in Thailand - For families: Koh Samui - For couples: Koh Lipe - For solo travel: Koh Pha Ngan and Koh Phi Phi - For divers and snorkelers: Koh Phi Phi How to travel between islands in Thailand? It depends on what islands you'll be travelling to during your holiday. It is best to take the ferry between islands in Southern Thailands. For example, Phuket (a great starting point) has a daily ferry to Ko Phi Phi that takes anywhere between 45 minutes to an hour plus. There are also some islands like Phuket, Krabi and Koh Samui that can easily be accessed via airplanes too.

item.title: Claude Monet’s most famous paintings are coming to Tate Modern in a major 2027 exhibition
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.21
Culture-loving Londoners have been treated to a string of excellent exhibitions this year. From Queen Elizabeth II: Her Life in Style at The King's Gallery to The Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum, there has been no shortage of showcases to capture our imaginations. As summer draws to a close, more details about the exhibitions we can look forward to next year are emerging. The latest? Tate Modern’s first-ever exhibition focused on the world-renowned work of French painter Claude Monet, of course. Set to open its doors on 25 February 2027 and run until 27 June 2027, the exhibition will feature more than 60 paintings in what’s said to be the UK’s largest presentation of the Impressionist’s work in nearly a decade. Coinciding with the 100th anniversary of Monet’s death, Monet: Painting Time will span masterpieces from the 1870s to the 1920s, tracing the artist’s lifelong entanglement with nature. Highlights to see along the gallery walls will include iconic paintings such as Cathédrale de Rouen, effet de soleil, fin de journée (1892) and a selection of rarely exhibited loans from private collections like Branch of the Seine near Giverny (Sunrise) (1897). In a statement announcing the exhibition, Sasha de Marigny, Anthropic’s chief brand and communications officer, said: "Alive to colour, light, and shimmering motion, Monet uniquely captured a mood and a moment in a world that never held still. A century on, his work asks us to slow down, notice each carefully placed brushstroke and dash of colour, and find the world more vivid for it. Anthropic is proud to support Tate Modern's first solo exhibition dedicated to his work." Monet transformed the way artists painted modern life, capturing the effects of light, atmosphere and time through rapid, expressive brushstrokes. The master artist repeatedly returned to the same subjects, including haystacks, cathedrals, poplars and the Seine, painting them at different times of day and year to reveal nature’s constant transformation. At Giverny, where he settled in 1883, his garden and pond inspired his monumental Water Lily series, which occupied the final three decades of his career. As museums and galleries continue to announce their 2027 programmes, we’re all eyes and ears, anticipating the year’s hottest tickets.

item.title: Inside the secret Yorkshire art walk that’s harder to get into than Glastonbury
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.15
I love walking. As a Cotswolds countryside resident, my once-concrete jaunts across east London have been swapped for crunchy grass stomps through cow-laden fields or floating across rolling hills just out my front door. I also love art. Exhibitions and retrospectives are often what dictate my travels. A recent dash on the Eurostar brought me to a speedy 48-hour whip around the late David Hockney exhibition at the Louis Vuitton Museum in Paris, in between long bistro meals and a snoop around the city’s latest new hotel opening. So when a few art-obsessed friends returned from what they called the most incredible walk of their lives up in the North York Moors, but said that they couldn't really tell me why, I was immediately intrigued. I began researching and uncovered an outdoor art walk where tickets to gain access to were as hard as heading to Glastonbury. The walk is, rather intriguingly, called Hanging Stones. I'd heard about artist Andy Goldsworthy from my mother. The contemporary English land artist has been shaping, morphing and discerningly using his hands to form large scale works using natural materials we might often overlook in everyday life: stones, snow, rock, leaves, iron, twigs, mud and more. One of his most talked-about pieces involved transporting 13 one-tonne snowballs from Scotland and placing them on the streets of London during a hot summer's day. He challenges and inspires conversation about our world and its precious land, and for his ongoing project up in Yorkshire – commissioned by the David Ross Foundation – he shifts the focus to the raw beauty of the Moors. To get tickets, eager hikers need to set reminders to check the website. Slots open at hangingstones.org – it’s currently booked out for the rest of the year, but new releases come out regularly. It costs £10 per adult; under-18s and students go free. There’s a maximum of four groups of six allowed each day. On the day, collect your laminated map and keys from Sevenford House B&B, then head to the Milburn Arms in Rosedale Abbey where the circular walk begins and ends. Allow five to six hours... you’ll need it, and wear proper boots (once you have your slot, I’d advise against trying to change it, so prepare for all weather conditions) and bring your own food and water – there are no facilities en route. My husband and I set off up north for a six-mile hike through farmers' fields and dormant heather hills to to pick up an instruction guide and a set of dangling keys… Here's everything we found along the way. To Goldsworthy, the whole walk is an artwork in itself. There are ten stone outbuildings, some rebuilt from ruin, all immaculately beautiful and each with its own installation inside. The tenth, titled Heygate Thorns, is currently in the works, but there’s a tiny window Goldsworthy left for you to have a special glimpse. My favourite stretch was the uphill push to the furthest point you reach before looping back, which is surrounded by hazy gorse and heather. There’s magic in unlocking giant padlocks and not knowing what’s inside. The signposts felt straight out of Lord of the Rings; little slits of eyes hammered into stone are your earmarks to keep you on your way. Don’t forget to look up. The light can change everything. Goldsworthy makes the mundane something joyful to look at. Perhaps the perfect picnic spot, or keep on pushing to the highest point of the walk for a chapel- like shelter on a particularly blustering day.

item.title: The underrated Devon escape where wild swimming, ancient legends and opulent hotels meet
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.14
My mother's family can trace its history in South Devon to the 13th century, and most of my early memories belong to its beaches. I didn’t form a relationship with Dartmoor until I moved from London to an ancient market town nearby three years ago. Since then, this lonely upland region 2,000 feet above sea level has taught me that bright, beautiful places can also brood. Dartmoor’s 368 square miles are often described as “England’s last wilderness”, yet they are, in fact, a carefully managed palimpsest that has been reimagined for agricultural use since the Bronze Age. Once, gazing over its whaleback ridges from Bone Hill at sunset, a friend compared the landscape to an open wound, the trees long cleared by swaling (an age-old practice that involves burning land each winter for grazing). In 2026, the national park is celebrating its 75th anniversary with festivals and events – though the region’s history stretches back at least 12,000 years, when early humans stripped bilberries from its dripping rainforest, the remnants of which cling on in areas such as Wistman’s Wood and Shaugh Bridge. One of the moor’s most distinctive aspects are the granite tors that crest its outer edges. They were formed when the rock broke up due to freezing and thawing during the Ice Age – which also gouged out the valleys with its monstrous talons – and are the moor’s waymarkers. Their companions under the enormous skies are ponies, buzzards, skylarks and ghosts. Perhaps unsurprisingly, they play a starring role in many folktales too. Old Crockern, the spirit of Dartmoor, slumbers uneasily beneath Crockern Tor, waking occasionally to wreak revenge on humans who pillage his resources for profit alone. About a mile from Hound Tor some see the outline of a giant called Bowerman who was petrified for disturbing a witches’ coven while hunting. And of course, the moor is also the setting for the most famous story in the Sherlock Holmes series, The Hound of the Baskervilles, which is inspired by rumours of a pack of “wisht” (uncanny) hounds said to haunt the region. Although 90 per cent of the land is managed, it would be a mistake to think of Dartmoor as tame. The oozings of the hills around Princetown and Fox Tor Mire are so dangerous that only locals who know the route dare cross. As I watched the Perseid meteor shower last summer, a fog swallowed my tent so completely that I struggled to find it, though the granite boulder I lay on was scarcely 30 feet away. The temperature plummeted and I awoke shivering the next morning to find I could see nothing beyond the pony standing sentinel over my camp. However someone chooses to discover Dartmoor, they will feel the texture of this place in their bones. Those who prefer a bed of organic linen to moss will be pleased to hear that several world-class hotels have sprung up in recent years. The cultural scene is thriving as cosmopolitan makers have relocated to the region, reimagining heritage crafts for a tech-sick generation increasingly curious about the old ways. There are also a host of options for engaging interactively with the landscape. WildWise teaches traditional navigation using natural landmarks, and Emma Cunis, author of Dartmoor Myths and Legends, offers guided hikes to sacred sites under the name Dartmoor’s Daughter. Dartmoor In his 1900 tome A Book of Dartmoor, Sabine Baring-Gould described the moor as the nursery of many Devon rivers: “And what a mother! She sends them forth limpid and pure, full of laughter and leap, of flash and brawl.” Nowhere is this more evident than at Olga Polizzi’s extraordinary Hotel Endsleigh, housed in the Duke of Bedford’s former hunting lodge amid Humphry Repton-designed gardens where running water can be heard in every corner. Cream tea with home-baked scones, served daily on the lawn, is a delight. Near Ugborough, Fowlescombe Farm has 10 nature-inspired suites, many with custom-made furniture. Its regenerative farm supplies an exceptional restaurant overseen by Elly Wentworth that serves heritage breeds such as Manx loaghtan sheep, as well as unusual vegetables including sea kale. For a classic Dartmoor outing, it’s worth drinking in the view from Haytor before heading to The Rugglestone Inn for ales from Dartmoor Brewery. To really feel the landscape, Wilder Sauna at Dartmeet offers a plunge into the River Dart’s numbing waters, or else there’s Chagford’s swimming pool, a heated lido also fed by the river. Established in Saxon times, this stannary town has a stolid exterior, belied by hand-scrawled flyers advertising pagan ceremonies and full-moon circles. In its market square, visitors can find The Dartmoor Shepherd’s dreamy sheepskin homewares, as well as Astor’s Bookshop & Art Materials, which has a secret room filled with magazines. Chagford is also a jumping-off point for the Dartmoor Artisan Trail, which links the workshops of craftspeople, including tanner Jessie Watson Brown and wood turner Sharif Adams, who offers classes in using a traditional pole lathe to make bowls. The trail is curated by local photographer Suzy Bennett and is newly available as a day trip with a guide – a rare opportunity to try disappearing skills while learning about life on the moor. The South Hams Coast As a child I imagined the South Hams were named because the hills that bounce all the way from Plymouth to Dartmouth are shaped like juicy legs of gammon. The word actually derives from “hamm”, the Old English term for valleys hemmed in by tidal estuaries and soaring climbs. Bantham is a privately owned estate with a sweeping surf beach, vineyard and 14th-century pub, The Sloop Inn. Off the shore, tidal Burgh Island is like something from a pirate story with gulls circling the spires of art deco Burgh Island Hotel, a favourite of everyone from Agatha Christie to Winston Churchill. The South West Coast Path unfurls on either side, and it’s a must to start the day with breakfast on the terrace of Bantham Stores while watching the harbour master and his black labrador pootle about the estuary. If the tide is right on the Avon and Erme, it’s possible to hike eight miles to Mothecombe in the south, where The Somewhere Sauna overlooks the water – and an owl box whose inhabitant once departed like a phantom torpedo as I steamed under a harvest moon. The Flete Estate hosts Rootle, a supper club serving hyper-local ingredients such as foraged seaweed in a converted barn. About 20 miles to the southeast is Salcombe with its palm trees and Victorian villas running down to the Kingsbridge Estuary. The town, a favourite with the yachting set (and at its best outside school holidays), mainlines seaside nostalgia, with the pink-and-white-striped awnings of Cranch’s Sweetshop (founded in 1869) stirring beside stylish boutiques such as Busby & Fox and relaxed seafood restaurants including Crab Shed. The top stays are the South Sands Hotel and Gara Rock, reached by catching the wooden ferry to East Portlemouth and continuing for another four miles along the coast path. This magnificently isolated hotel on a knife-edge cliff has an indoor pool that’s a wonderful place from which to watch the English Channel roar. Ashburton and Totnes Perching on Dartmoor’s southern edge is the deeply lovely stannary town of Ashburton. Here streets laid out to a Saxon plan are now home to cool brunch spots such as Rafikis, Emilia – a classic Italian osteria in the old bank with a handwritten menu that changes daily – and about a dozen excellent antiques shops. Entering Catherine Waters Antiques feels like stepping into a Vermeer painting, and The Shambles stocks everything from French linen to Scandinavian silver. It’s always worthwhile stopping by Ashburton Arts Centre: owned and operated by the community, this Grade II-listed Methodist church reverberates with music spanning Javanese gamelan to jazz. Totnes, about eight miles south, has been associated with liberalism since wealthy Americans Dorothy and Leonard Elmhirst purchased the crumbling estate Dartington Hall as a centre for the arts and ecology in 1925. This free-spirited town is home to a clutch of inspiring businesses. Sandridge Barton produces an astonishing selection of wines in a limestone-rich corner of the Dart Valley, including bright, beautiful sparklers with just a hint of Devon hedgerow. St John’s Tavern alumnus Sean Blood oversees excellent restaurant Roam, cooking up bold bistro plates that nod to the Basque Country, yet are sourced hyper-locally from no-dig and regenerative farms. Geetie Singh-Watson’s The Bull Inn, at the crest of the ancient high street, serves seasonal, ethical dishes largely sourced from her husband Guy’s organic Baddaford Farm – which is just down the road – alongside natural wines. The inn’s nine rooms provided a trove of inspiration as I renovated my home, including porcelain lampshades by Pippi & Me and organic bed linen from Greenfibres. It’s the perfect base from which to explore sections of the newly opened South Hams Way, a 100-mile circular hiking trail devised by the local ramblers group that winds through sunken green lanes and up cliffs like sails.

item.title: Where was 'Slow Horses' filmed? 5 London locations to look out for in the Apple TV+ series
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.05
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Slow Horses filmed?
