Now the term has come to span all manner of small hotels in Morocco – from monochrome boutique boltholes for those seeking out new wave aesthetics to celebratory full buyout only 16th century buildings riffing on Japanese design and increasingly, in luxury hotels, an emerging breed of private riad villas. Often fusing modern design with Moroccan motifs and drawing from the rich artisanal heritage of the country, the converted former mansions feature rooms around a pretty flower-draped courtyard, with rooftop dining spaces and, if you are in luck, a mosaic-lined pool to cool off. A stay in one of these storied dwellings can be a more accessible way into stylish slumber than the grand palace hotels – with all the grace but at a fraction of the price – although the lines between the two are becoming increasingly blurred. Marrakech riads are in such high demand that Airbnb recently added them to their search categories, making it even easier to discover these often hidden gems. Here, we spotlight the prettiest riads in Marrakech, from Nobu's grandiose private space to smaller, lesser celebrated homes with just as much charismatic flair. Editor's picks of the best riads in Marrakech - For luxury: Riad Nobu - large groups: Riad Beyond Beautiful - For an afforable stay: - For couples: Riad Melhoun - For families: Riad La Maison - For hotel perks: Riad Melhoun How we choose the best riads in Marrakech We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. item.title: The best villas in Morocco for group getaways in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.40
Glittering Morocco’s diverse landscapes, azure coastlines and breathless, eclectic cityscapes make it an attractive destination to visit year-round and the best villas in Morocco offer an especially memorable way to see it all. There’s no shortage of wonderful hotels, but for a group trip without the crowds, a private villa is best. For families and big groups of friends, they offer the best of both worlds: the privacy and space to settle in on your own terms, often with the pools, sprawling gardens and attentive service you’d expect from a luxury hotel. Around Marrakech in particular, villas offer a chance to dip into the energy of the medina before retreating to a quieter base, with many properties looking towards the peaks of the Atlas Mountains. The bustling capital city has perennial charm, but beyond its walls, there’s so much more to Morocco worth exploring. Whether you’re gearing up for a hiking trip to the Atlas mountains, looking to immerse yourself in the sights and sounds of the buzzy souks or headed out to the coast, there’s a fantastic nearby address to know. Most of our favourite Morocco villas pair idyllic views with in-house chefs, housekeepers and even security staff for a hotel-worthy break in your own space. Below are ten of the best villa rentals in Morocco to know about in 2026. item.title: I visited the ‘Kingdom of Happiness’ to find the secret to joy – here is everything I learnt
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.24
“In your previous life, you were a highly revered scholar,” I am told. Typically, I’d feel smug at this revelation, but I'm getting a strong impression this isn’t a place that welcomes ego. Pangri Zampa Lhakhang, Bhutan’s only college of astrology, is a spiritual site of reflection and insight. Opposite me, one of the college’s most learned monks is reading my astrological charts. He looks at me carefully, as if he can clearly see through my attempts to hide my smugness, before studying the papers spread out before him. “In your next life, you'll be born in the West as a male figure,” the monk nods sagely. I’m less thrilled with this prophecy, but I bow my head in deference. This ancient site, just north of Thimphu, is believed to be the oldest Buddhist monastery in Bhutan. It’s the first of several incredible spiritual sites I'm visiting over the course of a week, on a journey to learn more about how this often-overlooked country is a haven for well-being – and, hopefully, to learn more about the secret to happiness along the way. Over the last 50 years, Bhutan has transformed from a country totally cut off from the rest of the world to one revered for its policies dedicated to preserving nature, culture and spirituality. Until 1974, tourists weren’t allowed into Bhutan. Today, travellers are welcome – at a cost. Current tourist tax sets travellers back $100 (around £73) per day. It’s a major deterrent for many, particularly those looking for quick travel bucket-list ticks. But it succeeds in drawing in those looking for deeper, more rewarding travel – those seeking to learn and embrace what Bhutan has to offer. In the 1970s, the country developed Gross National Happiness, a framework designed to prioritise collective wellbeing over economic success. The results speak for themselves. In 2023, Bhutan moved from an underdeveloped to a developing country. Life expectancy has soared, and poverty has dropped. Education and healthcare are entirely free. Environmental laws such as the mandate for 60 per cent of the country to be forested (a target they smash year after year, with an estimated 71 per cent of Bhutan covered by forest) have resulted in Bhutan becoming the world’s first and only carbon-negative country. Wellness is a key part of Gross National Happiness. But in Bhutan, it’s less about what wellness means, and more about how you apply it. The attitude here is pretty simple: happiness comes first, and everything else will follow. The result is a population that claims to be the happiest in the world. “For us, happiness is fundamentally a state of your mind,” explains Dorji Bidha, a professional guide for travellers in Bhutan. “You need to be happy with what you have.” This attitude is evident everywhere you look – there is gratitude for the environment, an appreciation for community, and a deep respect for one another. At Six Senses Bhutan, we witness this outlook firsthand as we learn about daily Bhutanese customs and pastimes. From archery (the country's national sport) and butter tea rituals to creating mini stupas (or tsa-tsas), activities are designed around connection and spirituality. Each craft and ritual we learn about demonstrates a new way to be more in tune with ourselves, each other, and our surroundings, perfectly balanced. “These things have deeper spiritual meanings, but also a great sense of community and fun,” explains Karun Pourel, the hotel’s sales and marketing executive. It wasn't long before we started noticing this sense of fun at every corner. On the drive from Thimphu to Punakha, we realised there were no traffic lights or road signs anywhere in Bhutan, and no one seemed to be driving faster than 50km/h. As we weaved through mountain passageways and swerved around winding roads hugging hillsides, the only signs we saw read “No hurry no worry”, “Expect the unexpected” or “Mind my curves”. “We love to laugh,” smiles Dorji when I point out the signs. “It’s important to recognise the simple things in life that make you smile.” She points out the window at KFC as we drove through the capital. “See? Here, we have Karma Fried Chicken. Doesn’t it make you smile?” In a place where spirituality reigns supreme, you anticipate a certain level of sobriety as you tour through the country – not puns on Western fast food chains. The next few days are filled with more insight into Bhutanese life. At Happiness Field Village Farmstay in Punakha, we spend evenings gazing at the stars, taking natural dye workshops, and learning about the country’s indigenous species and local wildlife. It's an effective reminder that in order to be happy, one needs to honour everything, from the small herbs growing at our feet, to the vastness of the skies and stars above. These lessons continue as we head east. At Gangtey Lodge, we experience how spirituality and wellness are baked into daily routines. Phobjikha is considered the soul of Bhutan, and right at the valley’s edge sits Gangtey Monastery, one of the country’s two Nyingmapa schools of Buddhism. We meet with the head monk at the school to learn dharma teachings. This school welcomes debate – we discuss various topics from practising compassion, justifying anger and life after death. When it comes to discussing happiness, the general consensus is that it came from within, but it’s like a muscle that needed to be exercised – only then can you appreciate the true nature of happiness. Back at the hotel, I speak to Kinley Dorji, the spa manager, about wellness. “In Bhutan, no one knew what wellness meant before the beginning of tourism here. My parents, and my grandparents, believed in simply being well – being outside, sleeping and eating well. That was it,” she explains. “For health, we use herbs, mushrooms and butter on the skin. And lots of hot stone baths.” Hot stone baths are a traditional spa treatment in Bhutan. Stones are collected from hot springs and used to heat up water, which is in turn infused with local herbs like artemisia to soothe aching muscles after a hard day at work or a pilgrimage to local monasteries. Speaking to Kinley shows me again how wellness and happiness go hand in hand in Bhutan – nature, the environment, and being outside is key for health and living well. Everyone I speak to seemed to genuinely love their work. I ask Dorji about the work-life balance in the country, and she replies with a shrug: “Life is to be lived, not to work. When somebody hustles so much, we remind one another of happiness. We say: ‘What are you doing? Do you know you’re going to die one day?’ People hustle a lot. Why? For what? Live your life and be happy.” “In Bhutan, wellness and spirituality are part of life. We always try to align with nature, not go against it,” explains our yoga instructor at Bhutan Spirit Sanctuary, a Himalayan retreat where holism and tranquillity are key. “Even our hotel faces directly towards the monastery across the valley. Everything is designed with that alignment in mind. Life is combining wellness into every aspect.” Bhutan is gearing up for another wave of hospitality in the coming years. Gelephu Mindfulness City is a project led by the King, a master plan devised to boost Bhutan’s economic status, while embodying the Buddhist values of spirituality, sustainability, culture and wellness. The city will be as vast in size as it is in ambition – three times the size of Singapore. A new international airport is in the works, as well as high-speed railway links to India, plus new healthcare facilities and tech hubs. There will be biodiversity corridors where animals can pass from one mountain to another, and more monuments, monasteries and meditation centres. “Gelephu Mindfulness City is going to be like any other city in the world, but it's going to measure the economic development with the spiritual wellbeing of people,” explains Dorji. “The idea came into being because so many people are driven by capitalism and commercialisation, but they are not taking care of spiritual wellbeing. The king's vision is that we can achieve both. It’s mindful capitalism.” Since the first king of Bhutan came to power in the early 1900s, the royal family has been fiercely protective of its land and people. And the current king and his government have given their people no reason to doubt them yet. There is a mutual respect between the governing body and the Bhutanese citizens – everyone abides by the rules, no one seems discontented, and there is faith and hope in what’s to come. It’s a profound way of life. For such a tiny kingdom, Bhutan surprises me at every turn. Its development is slow, cautious and careful, yet the ambition is unmatched. The number of economic initiatives, purpose-driven projects and dedication to the country’s growth and prosperity are always matched by a consideration of quality of life, and a devotion to the happiness of the people. In my astrology reading on my first day in Bhutan, I'm told I need to be very cautious next year. It’s the year of the sheep, which apparently clashes with my spiritual animal, the hawk. I'm advised to tread carefully and be considerate in my actions. A few months ago, I would have scoffed at this suggestion. But now, armed with everything I’ve learnt on this trip, I know that this prophecy isn’t something to be ignored. It’s not a warning; it’s advice. It turns out the secret to happiness isn’t as complicated as I once thought. It is as simple as paying attention – not just to yourself, but to the ground below your feet and the skies above your head. Next year, when the sheep clashes with the hawk, you'll find me diligently checking which way the wind blows to hang my prayer flags accordingly, gazing up at the stars, and doing as much as I possibly can to live a life that is a little more present, a little more aware and, hopefully, a little happier. Olivia Morelli was a guest of the Department of Tourism Bhutan, in partnership with tour operator The Explorations Company. She travelled from London to Bhutan with Thai Airways and Drukair, travelling via Bangkok and staying at COMO Metropolitan Bangkok.

item.title: Where was ‘MobLand’ filmed? Pierce Brosnan takes us behind the scenes of Season 2
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.14
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was MobLand filmed? Warring families, London gangsters, teetering drug empires… There’s nothing quite like a good crime drama, and MobLand is surely one of the best in recent memory. Season one left us on the edge of our seats, and we’ve been (im)patiently waiting to see what will come of the Harrigans and the Da Souzas ever since. Luckily, the second season promises much of the blood, guts and gore of the first – we spoke to Pierce Brosnan about what it was like returning to Conrad Harrigan, and his favourite places to film Season 2 of Mobland. “When Guy [Ritchie] came to me with this idea two years ago, Helen [Mirren] and I had been working together on The Thursday Murder Club,” Brosnan says. “She said, ‘Do you like it? Are you going to do it?’ I said, 'Yes, I want to go back to London. I want to be back here in this wonderful city where my career started.’ And she said, ‘Okay, good. Well, if you are doing it, I'll do it.' And both of us just jumped right in there. We get on very well together.” Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren play the husband-and-wife duo of Conrad and Maeve Harrigan. They are both totally ruthless, power-hungry and seemingly incapable of empathy – their sole goal is control, and they don’t care who they manipulate, maim or kill along the way, even within their own family. “It was wonderful to go back to Conrad,” he continues. “I enjoy playing this character so much. He's happened at a great time in my life, and to be working with Dame Helen Mirren and this magnificent cast, Tom Hardy and the rest of our company, has been a joy. The writing by Jez Butterworth is so rich and textured and nuanced, and it works on so many different levels. It's like putting on an old coat, really. There's something so familiar about it.” The series takes place mainly in London, depicting mob families as they battle for control over the city's drug scenes. “London is an ever-changing city. Londinium has been the epicentre of many great events historically, culturally, and certainly from the world of the arts and a filmmaker like Guy Ritchie, who he's born of this land and he knows it so well, whether it be the interior life of the city or the countryside. So as a storyteller, he is the perfect gentleman to create this world of MobLand." For the Harrigans, their name and identity is something to be protected at all cost. The way they are viewed and respected, and how they fit into the warring dynasties of London, is of utmost importance. For Brosnan, understanding Conrad’s background and how he became the man he is was a big part of preparing for the role. “I think there's a strong identification for me with Conrad because of being a transplant. I left Ireland when I was 11 years of age – August 12th, 1964. I landed and was rejoined with my mother, and we lived in Putney. So filming in and around London was a lot of fun.” “I didn't do in-depth study or preparation for Conrad, but when I spoke to Guy Ritchie for the first time after reading the initial five episodes, I started talking about the character and where he was from, as a Londoner with an Irish background, because so many Irish folks who live in North or South London have lost their accents. So I was trying to define the character and the accent but he said, look, and this was the phone call, and the first phone call, he said, “Don't worry about it. We'll sort it out on the day. Put it out of your mind.” So I kept it as simple as possible and I more or less made it up on the day.” "These characters that we play – Maeve, Conrad – are these Irish, rebellious outsiders, these from-the-streets folks who have created this wealth of life through really extreme circumstances of violence. They do what certain rich people do in life, whether they be rock stars or artists who become very wealthy – they buy the country estate, but they really know nothing about living in the countryside. So in the series you go from the Cotswolds to the East End of London and back again. It was brilliant.” “I'm as much an audience member as I am a participant. My family love this show; they've never wanted to watch me as much as they do on this show, and so we all celebrate it.” Below, Pierce Brosnan tells us about his favourite places to film Mobland Season 2, from the UK's oldest film studios to the lush lands of the Cotswolds. Where was MobLand Season 2 filmed? Ealing Studios, London “My world consists mainly of Ealing Studios, where we film,” Brosnan says. “Ealing Studios is one of the great bastions of English film work, and it has a whole history of some of the great Ealing comedies.” It opened in 1902 as the UK’s first film studio, and still operates today – making it the UK’s oldest continuously working film studio. Kentish Town, London “Conrad does a scene sequence driving the Bentley around Kentish Town, and I went to drama school up in Chalk Farm, so on that particular day we did a tour of my old haunts. Tom Hardy [who plays Harry Da Souza] and I went to the same drama school – I was many years ahead of him, but we were taught by the same teachers in the world of method acting. It was a drama school called the Drama Centre in Chalk Farm, and I graduated in 76, so I was many, many, many years ahead of Tom. Michael Fassbender and Colin Firth both went there, too. It felt full circle going back, although it was quite weird because I was actually driving the Bentley with a camera truck in front, so I had to be aware and focus because I was actually on the streets and being filmed. Guy Ritchie and all the directors, they make such a feast of the action sequences. I'm very impressed by the driving sequences in MobLand.” Scott’s, Mayfair, London The first scene in season one of MobLand begins in the basement of a glitzy London restaurant, and between scenes at The Midland Grand inside the St Pancras Renaissance Hotel to Loulou’s nightclub in Mayfair, you’d be safe to assume Season 2 will have more high-end London settings, too. “We shoot at Scott's,” Brosnan says. “Maeve and I, we go to meet Serafina [played by Mandeep Dhillon]. And Maeve is all out there. She's all absolutely bedecked like a queen, like an empress. So we shot there, and then we shot down and around Harley Street.” Oxford Stadium, Oxford Season 1 ends with Maeve and Conrad in prison, but Season 2 sees them back in the game – this time, gambling at a local dog track. “Well, the opening scene is at the dog races. So episode one is at the dog races,” Brosnan says. The races are set at White Hart Stadium, a venue that has now been demolished but was once the sport's main track. But the scenes were actually shot in Oxford, at the Oxford Stadium greyhound track on Sandy Lane in Cowley. “That was a wonderful day's work,” adds Pierce. "It was quite spectacular, and it's a major kind of shootout. Blood and guts everywhere." Mallorca, Spain “We go off to Mallorca at one point. I don't think I'm giving anything away by telling you that,” laughs Brosnan. "We had a week in Mallorca, and we stayed at a delightful hotel on the ocean front. It's a gorgeous part of the world. One of the highlights for me was going to Miro's studio [Fundació Miró Mallorca]. I'm a painter, and so seeing the life of the great artist Joan Miró was a highlight for me. The Cotswolds Season 2 sees the Harrigans back in their main residence in the Cotswolds. “It's an absolute joy – everyone loves going to the dear Cotswolds,” says Brosnan. “There folks down there are probably thinking: ‘please no more, please do not show any more of our beautiful landscape!’ We went back to the same house. It's just outside of Bourton-on-the-Water, near Broadway. It really is a lovely time to be there too – we always start this show in November, so we're in the winter months, but to be down in Broadway, near that part of the world at Christmastime is just pure magic.” “My favourite place to stay is the Dormy House in the Cotswolds. It's a beautiful hotel. They look after us so well. It's charming, and you can tramp along and walk across the fields. Stayed at the Soho Farmhouse for a while, too. There are some beautiful walks, and you just get out, and if you feel like you're in the middle of nowhere, it's so stunning around there. We stayed at Estelle Manor, too, which is quite magnificent. It's a beautiful old home and a stately home. Conrad would probably like Estelle Manor. He'd pull up in the Bentley. It's all people who want to be seen and they're all very important, feeling very important. But Dormy House has my heart. I just like it. It's quiet and it's just my speed. It's intimate, small. The food is very good, and the staff are just charming and lovely.” Tyrella Beach, Northern Ireland In December 2025, Belfast Live reported that the cast and crew were seen shooting on Tyrella Beach in County Down, Northern Ireland. “They shot some scenes in Northern Ireland. I didn't shoot anything there, but two of the characters go off to Northern Ireland.” The pictures show Eddie Harrigan and Gina Da Souza walking along the shore. In a production interview, Helen Mirren said that Season 2 will "broaden the landscape out of North London and especially the younger members of the family are seeing that there’s a globalisation element to it.” We see this with the Northern Ireland and Mallorca scenes, but is there scope for a shoot even further afield in future seasons? “Helen and I were just talking about this, actually. We'd love to go to Italy. Helen lives in Puglia, so we've talked about maybe some cross-pollination between families and the mafia. It would be very good. Well, I think Jez and his company of writers have already got season three more or less in the bag. I'm not sure, to tell you the truth, but we haven't seen it, so we never know where it's going. But yes, I would love to continue.”

Naples is finally having its moment, and the spike in foreign tourism has also helped revitalise the city’s hospitality scene. The best way to experience this relatively unsung spot for a few nights? By living like a local in one of the best Airbnbs in Naples. Barbados’s vibrant mix of breathtaking beaches, Colonial-style architecture, botanical gardens and characteristic Caribbean hospitality makes it a natural beacon for those seeking sun, sand, rum punch and a warm island breeze. Despite a slim 21-mile radius, there’s a surprising number of excellent hotels bringing historical charm, plush beds and unrivalled sea views to restore peace to weary travellers. item.title: D.C.’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Started as a Pop-Up
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.53
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings. When chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy opened Alfie’s as a pop-up restaurant in 2016, they didn’t expect the road to a brick-and-mortar location to last nearly a decade. The temporary D.C. location where the duo served northern Thai cuisine to the city’s tight-knit service industry and other regulars was open for just a few months. After that, Ahn and McCoy began operating it as a roving concept all around the world, but now they’re finally returning to D.C. with a permanent venue in Georgetown. Now the team is settled into a new 25-seat venue tucked in an alley off of Georgetown’s M Street serving Thai dishes made with Mid-Atlantic ingredients and natural wine produced just over the river in Virginia. Still, elements of the pop-up — like its run-and-gun service and chalkboard menu that shifts based on what local purveyors have in season — remain. We caught up with McCoy to learn more about how the team has shifted this scrappy pop-up model into a brick-and-mortar concept while keeping that dynamic energy intact. Liz Provencher: Why did you decide to launch Alfie’s in a pop-up format? Alex McCoy: We [already] had a permanent space in Petworth that we were building out [for our brick-and-mortar restaurant]. There was another restaurant space down the street that was slated to be demolished, so we talked to the landlords and they were like, “It’s yours until your space is ready or our project starts.” We thought it was a great opportunity to train our staff, test the food, and work through the menus while our spot was in construction. It was in a quiet part of town, and we just really wanted to have fun with it, but it ended up becoming this cult sensation. We were packed for months in advance. We had Vogue writing about us. Bon Appetit called it one of the top new restaurants in America. But it was really only about six months total that we had the place open, which is kind of wild. We closed the pop-up in 2017. That Petworth space didn’t end up working out for us, so we had to look for a new space. In the meantime, we were doing pop-ups in New York, D.C., London. We spent a lot of time overseas and some of the bigger pop-ups were in London with our buddies at Carousel. In that time, we were always looking for a new venue, and it was the time in Europe that really evolved the brand into what it is now. How did that time on the road shape the concept and operation plan? After COVID… everyone was struggling to try to figure out how to make restaurants work. With operating and staff costs going up, people were coming up with these creative service styles with [fewer] servers and less table service and more QR codes. The math isn’t mathing, you know? It seemed to me that the model should be similar to the way things operate in Europe with these little hole-in-the-wall places in Paris and London. Chefs don’t own six or seven restaurants; they’re in there [in one place] with one or two people. Not only was that the heart and soul of what Alfie’s always was, but it felt to me to be the way forward with the brand. After we did our last pop-up in London, we found this funky little spot in Georgetown, which is a neighborhood that feels the most European of anywhere in D.C. to me. It’s this incredible 25-seat space in an alleyway behind the hustle and bustle of M Street. It’s a little gritty. You step down into the alleyway and you have to dodge cars. It’s a really cool, funky space with a lot of character. So immediately it was like, this is the spot. This encapsulates the vibe and the ambiance and the feeling and the energy of what we’re trying to do. Have things changed since running the restaurant as a pop-up? It’s very much still a pop-up mindset. Justin, myself, and Ian, who is our sous chef, we’re 90 percent of the staff at this restaurant. From a cooking perspective, twenty-five seats is perfect because it gives us this opportunity to really [pore] over small batches of food. If we’re making a curry for the day, we’re [only] making 30 orders. We’re able to look at the menu on a daily basis and assess based on what ingredients come in. If our local fishmonger has five beautiful seabreams that he’s bringing in, we’ll just throw them on the menu because we have that ability to be scrappy and change things up and make adjustments and not have to retrain the staff and everything. That also plays into Thailand’s market culture, which is the ethos of our brand. We want to challenge ourselves to make dishes utilizing what’s available around here: rockfish, soft shell crab, foraged asparagus from the Eastern Shore, morel mushrooms, things like that. Does your drink menu also play off of local ingredients? When you go to France or Italy or another wine-producing region, you go to a bar or restaurant and you’re drinking what was made in the town or right around it. You don’t often see that in D.C., even when Virginia wineries are making spectacular stuff, literally 15 to 20 minutes away by car. The majority of our wines by the glass are from Virginia and we have more than 2,000 local producers by the bottle too. Our bottles, for the most part, are between $35 and $75. We only have a couple that top that. I think a lot of people go out to eat dreading the check. But I want people to come in and just get lost in the experience and not have to worry that they can’t take a chance on something that they haven’t tried before because it’s too expensive. They don’t have to be thinking about the price of everything they’re eating and drinking while they’re here. Alfie’s also has a wine club. How does that work? Alfie’s has always [drawn] a lot of regulars, and we’ve always tried to facilitate this vibe of being your other living room. If you love wine, we want this to be a place that you want to spend a lot of your time and cater that a little bit more. Our wine club has 19 spots, and for a monthly fee of $150, you basically get a rack of your own [in the restaurant]. If you have a great collection at home, you can bring it in. Or if you have specific tastes and things that you enjoy when you come here, we can curate the wine locker for you so you can actually purchase wine at a steep discount that we don’t have on the list. If there are special selections that are too expensive for us to put on the menu, we can get those for you, and you’ll pay 50% less than standard restaurant prices. After releasing the first few days of reservations, you immediately had 700 bookings. Were you expecting that kind of reception? I wouldn’t say I expected anything. [But] I was hoping for it, and I kind of felt it. Sometimes in this industry, you can feel when something is gonna hit. Leading up to [opening] and seeing some of the interest on social media, it seemed like it was gonna go that route so we were trying to plan for it. Alfie’s scratches an itch that [D.C. diners] haven’t been able to scratch at least since 2020. The city is getting burnt out [by] small businesses being replaced by big corporate restaurant group spots, and we’re very much the antithesis of that. You walk in, and Justin and I are in the kitchen, so we can say hi to you and run food to the table. I think it’s a vibe that D.C. hasn’t had in years.

item.title: This Restaurant Rocks (No, Literally)
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.35
A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now. “There’s a rock in the sink!” That was the takeaway last winter after the East Coast contingent of the team that writes this newsletter met for brunch at Flynn McGarry’s stylish, Scandi-inflected Gem Home in lower Manhattan. While the rest of us waited for our plates of Danish breakfast, Francky Knapp had shuffled off to the bathroom, then returned to the table with newfound excitement at this unexpected find. Naturally, I, too, had to see it for myself. The slab of stone occupied the entire industrial-style basin, a patch of rust-colored mineral deposits at its center where the water hit. Weird! I thought, then I put it out of my mind for months. That was until I met a friend for coffee at the location of Rhythm Zero in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, which looks more like a room in an art museum than a coffee shop. There, a large hunk of stone sat in front of a large mirror next to the counter. Yet another imposed itself in the bathroom, positioned between the sink and the toilet, as though natural absorption for dripping hands making the trip to the hand dryer. Two establishments with big decorative rocks: a coincidence, or an affectation? But then, I found myself in Pizza 4P’s, an ambitiously and intricately designed pizza import from Vietnam for which six literal boulders were transported into the restaurant from a stone wholesaler in New Jersey. Now three spots? There’s something going on there. It’s at Pizza 4P’s, which opened this summer in Brooklyn in a high-ceilinged industrial space, where this trend can be found at its extreme. When you open the door, you’re greeted by a host stand in the form of a large, tablelike boulder. The stone, which was forklifted in, was chosen for this usage because of its waist height and the natural notch in its corner, perfect for holding menus. An adjacent stone, lower and smaller, acts as a bench for diners waiting for their table. Four more boulders erupt from the space, forcing the layout of the large dining room into a snaking path. “After we found the stones, we changed the position,” global branding director Kazuya Kubota explained to me over a tour of the space. None have been cut into shape; they have all been chosen for their size and form, and then the restaurant designed around them. Some of the stones sprout thick metal support wires, allowing them to weigh down the wooden frames along the walls that hold hanging plants. The largest stone — at around two tons, toward the center of the dining room, with a table butting up against it — is comparable in weight to the pizza oven, according to Kubota. Along with all the hanging plants, the stones give the otherwise industrial space a semblance of nature, bridging the gap between Brooklyn urbanism and the pastoral settings of the farms listed on the menu. For her rocks, Ivana Somorai, who owns Rhythm Zero, was inspired by the use of natural materials in Japanese design. She told me over email that she also wanted to bring a “natural, unexpected element” into the shop’s interiors. Initially, the Greenpoint location featured several rocks, minimal seating, and a large tangerine tree. When she redesigned the interior — it now features a large couch and more seating — the rocks stayed, mostly because they were too heavy. “I knew they would not be leaving the space for a while,” Somorai wrote. Since then, rocks have become a memorable feature of the cafe. (Every location looks different; all are very stylish, some feature stones.) The one next to the mirror “unexpectedly became a favorite sitting area for our regulars,” Somorai explains. “The rocks began as part of a specific design moment, but they ended up becoming part of the life of the cafe and the way people use the space.” As for why the second rock ended up in the bathroom… well, isn’t that kind of the last thing you’d expect? “I wanted people to be surprised when they opened the door: The bathroom is dark, and then there is this large rock. I wanted them to be like, ‘Why is there a rock here?’” Somorai wrote. (Yes, I had that thought.) I imagine this desire to pique curiosity is part of the rationale at Gem, too. While I couldn’t get ahold of McGarry to know more about the Gem stone [ba-dum-tss], his representative told me via email that, to his recollection, “Gem Home, [the now-closed] Gem Wine, and I think Cove all had/have rocks in their restroom sinks.” This really only opens up more questions though; if only I could have asked them! As for Pizza 4P’s, those big rocks fit into a bigger philosophy. The chain has dozens of locations in different countries. Each location is unique — its art, furniture, and space designed entirely custom (boulders in Brooklyn doesn’t mean stones in Cambodia). Each country is guided by a different theme. In Indonesia, that’s biodiversity; in the United States, it’s the idea of “what the earth told me.” To that end, they thought of the stones like they did ingredients, Kubota explains: The goal is to find something beautiful in nature and then work around it. Alas, on my most recent visit to Rhythm Zero in Greenpoint, the rock outside the bathroom was gone. Apparently, that was part of an even more recent renovation. The rocks were moved to the nearby Transmitter Park. Somorai described it as “where they belong, I guess.”

item.title: The 12 New Cookbooks We Can’t Wait to Cook From This Fall
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.41
We have reached that time of year again. Every good tomato suddenly prompts the pondering: Will this be the last one for the season? The heat begins to give way to crisper breezes, and we start to crave the comfort of windows fogged up from bubbling pots of soup instead of thinking about how to minimize our time in front of a hot stove. The 12 New Cookbooks We Can’t Wait to Cook From This Fall The season’s exciting new releases include Asian American croissants, divorce cooking, Indian street food, foraged treats, and more Luckily, this season’s cookbooks offer many exciting ways to joyously warm ourselves in the kitchen, whether by baking border-traversing croissants and comforting counter cakes, or keeping the stove simmering with Dutch ovens of borscht, beef noodle soup, or budae jjigae. There are diversions from the standard cookbook on this list, too, like a divorce-inspired reflection (in which the essays are just as essential as the recipes) and a treasure trove of a garden almanac that feels like an escape into another world. I’ve compiled 12 selections from the fall cookbook season that have me especially excited to cook and read this fall and winter. Joyce Tang with Soleil Ho Hardie Grant, out now If you feel like everything is an Asian American bakery now, you’re right. In the Bay Area, Bake Sum — with its Spam-musubi-esque croissants and ube pineapple buns — was an early adopter of the current trend, starting as a pandemic pop-up in 2020 before opening its Oakland location the following year. In her colorful and playful new cookbook, chief baking officer Joyce Tang pulls back the curtain on her cuisine-bending treats, like quiche inspired by chawanmushi, the Japanese savory egg custard, and danishes in the style of okonomiyaki and aloo matar, the Indian dish of spiced potatoes and peas. The bakes involving laminated dough are ambitious, weekend-worthy projects, but the book takes a welcomingly progressive approach, easing in novice bakers via puddings and jellies (its first recipe is a simple, anyone-can-do-it microwave mochi) before exploring more advanced techniques in its chapter on cakes, and then making its way to croissants. This is a book for the person who counts big baking projects among their favorite ways to spend the colder months. Carla Lalli Clarkson Potter, out now Lalli, who won audiences over as Carla Lalli Music during her time at Bon Appétit, has catalogued the dissolution of her 24-year marriage in a cookbook. With its reflections on motherhood, identity, and where a background in restaurants fits into those things, Lalli continues the narrative thread of releases like Tanya Bush’s Will This Make Me Happy and Rebecca May Johnson’s Small Fires. That’s to say that you’re here as much for the essays as for the recipes. The latter, including dishes such as “weeknight lamb chop special, for any number” and “quick beans and rice for when the avocado is ripe,” are delightfully loose and flexible. These are realistic suggestions for weeknights when you’re burnt-out, but also for those glorious instances in which you care more about getting yourself on the sand than fussing about what to make for your beach trip (for those instances: peaches with lime and salt).Many of these ideas were birthed during “separation summer,” when Lalli often found herself eating alone after years of cooking for four. These recipes (and the words that accompany them, like a list of things that “made [Lalli] feel free”) will feel useful on bad days, sick days, and anytime you need to give yourself grace, but also whenever you need to be reminded of how much pleasure life offers. Richard Christiansen Chronicle, September 15 Pleasure Principles is the newest book from Richard Christiansen of Flamingo Estate, the Los Angeles-based lifestyle brand so luxurious and sprawling in its ambitions that even Martha Stewart has described it as “over the top.” Pleasure Principles is predictably maximalist; not specifically a cookbook, it feels like picking up a paper trail while exploring the lush thicket of Christiansen’s secret (if oft-Instagrammed) garden. Stories about the building of Christiansen’s property veer into detours about the history of camellia plants and Coco Chanel, interspersed with archival imagery and photos of flora shot in the style of high-fashion editorial. A primer about the vast range of sage plants gives way to a checklist of garden tasks for January, seasonal project ideas (“help build a bird’s nest” or “make a sage tincture”), and recipes for pasta with sage leaves embedded in the dough and vegetable broth featuring lotus petals and dried skullcap. Pleasure Principles feels like an immersive fantasy world: Open up any random page for a little hit of magic, or an escape into Christiansen’s sparkly, greenery-filled universe. It’s a book that’ll make even winter feel vibrant and full of possibility. Meherwan Irani with Jamie Feldmar Ten Speed Press, September 22 This is a book that will make you want to have a party. That’s partially because recipes like the deep-fried, carb-on-carb vada pav and crisp, thin dosa with coconut chutney will feed six or more (and benefit, process-wise, from the economy of scale). It’s also because it feels raucous and alive, full of bright colors, bold typography, and big proclamations, ready for joyful debate. Is vada pav, as Meherwan Irani writes, “without question, the greatest sandwich of all time”? Is this, indeed, as the title suggests, the best Indian cookbook in the world? This is food that makes you want to crowd around a table, tearing off pieces of seekh kebab with fluffy, still-steaming naan and crushing cold beers. Whether Indian street food is, as Irani audaciously claims, the “best food on the planet” remains up for discussion, but for those of us who can’t get to India or to Irani’s lauded North Carolina restaurants Chai Pani and Botiwalla anytime soon, this book is a good way to test that argument. Alexis Nikole Nelson with Jeanelle Hayner Olson S&S/Simon Element, September 22 Alexis Nikole Nelson, also known as Black Forager, is a bright spot in the doom spiral that social media can often be. Nelson is known (and widely loved, picking up nearly 5 million followers on TikTok alone) for her bubbly disposition, whimsical vibe, and clever creations such as syrup infused with pine cones and color-changing pine-needle cookies. She demystifies the vast array of food that you can forage without even having to go deep into the woods, like acorns and the fruit of the linden trees that are abundant in many parts of the United States, and balances practicality, safety, and play in the process. Her long-awaited cookbook gets its name from the catchphrase that ends her videos: “Happy snacking. Don’t die.” With recipes like pickled magnolia flowers, Japanese knotweed granita, and maitake mushroom “steaks,” this book promises to be a guide to seeing even your suburban neighborhood through new eyes. Dona Murad Quadrille, September 22 New York City’s Librae Bakery draws on its owner Dona Murad’s upbringing in Bahrain with an Indian and Portuguese mother and a Bahraini Persian father; her time spent working in Copenhagen with her husband Andre, who is French Moroccan; and her new life in NYC, where Andre grew up. Naturally, the bakery has embraced the language and perspective of “third-culture” cuisine from the start, serving croissants with pistachio frangipane, scented with rose water; morning buns spread with labneh and za’atar; babka with both lemon curd and loomi (black lime); and more. Much of this book requires getting comfortable with Murad’s “mother dough” recipes — like ones for croissant dough, morning buns, and enriched dough — or working with sourdough starter. For those new to these more involved bakes, Murad provides thorough, nicely documented steps and imagery. If you need something easier than croissants, Murad’s cookies and breads, including cleverly topped sheets of focaccia, provide a more approachable entry point. Another book for bakers who don’t turn down a challenge, Librae is also for anyone who respects traditional pastry techniques but wants to push flavors further. Clara Lee and Eddo Kim Workman, October 6 If it can’t still be summer, at least it’s almost soup season. Here, Clara Lee and Eddo Kim break Korean soups into fundamentals — a chart compares the qualities of guk versus tang versus jjigae versus jeongol; the first section of the book is about making broth, then categorizing those soups into applications. There are quick-cooking soups, soups for slower nights, soups for each season, soups that are especially restorative, and soups for sharing; you could spend the entirety of the coming colder months cooking exclusively through this repertoire. If Lee and Kim’s names are familiar, that’s because they ran the cherished San Francisco superette Queens, which closed in 2023 to transition into a line of pantry staples. The shop has been described as “iconoclastic,” representing the new wave of Korean American cuisine. Consider Korean Soups essential for anyone who loves to be cozy, anyone who’s looking to deepen their understanding of Korean home cooking, or anyone who simply needs more ways to use the gochujang they bought for cookies a while ago. Kay Chun Knopf, October 6 Recipe developers I know cite NYT Cooking contributor Kay Chun among their favorite recipe developers, and it’s easy to see why. Her book starts off with snacks and pickles, Chun adding low-lift but flavor-packed flourishes: She quickly marinates sardines to top toast; her calamari gets a gilda-esque zhuzh, skewered with fried peppers and olives. Gather Around My Table delivers on its promise of simple, weeknight-friendly food that doesn’t feel boring, with dishes such as grilled tofu simmered in soy sauce with aromatics, and then given the ssam and taco treatment with both a perilla leaf and a tortilla. Wakame and a shallot vinaigrette featuring grated tomatoes make her green salad livelier and less run-of-the-mill (her mustard vinaigrette, meanwhile, gets amped up by doenjang). I appreciate that Chun gives tofu an entire chapter, too, coaxing even omnivores to employ it more, as in her pork breakfast sausages with crumbled tofu for added moisture and protein. With Gather Around My Table, Chun consistently offers low-effort ways to make familiar dishes more interesting and rewarding. Eric Sze and Elyse Inamine Hardie Grant, October 13 We’ve come full circle: Fusion is good again, or at least so proclaims chef Eric Sze, known for his New York City restaurant Wenwen and the recently closed 886. His debut cookbook Taiwanese?, emphasis on that question mark, is an ode to letting Taiwanese food be fun, free, and a little freaky: His lu rou fan, also known as lo ba beng, the dish of braised pork over rice, includes the “strange addition of peanut butter,” for example. Why the hell not? Especially when Sze has, as documented in the book (with vivid imagery from star photographer Alex Lau), gone on a bonkers crawl of 60-plus bowls of lu rou fan in a single week; he’s earned the right to experiment. Taiwanese? is not the traditionalist’s guide to the cuisine, but anyone who likes seeing the commonalities between disparate cuisines and playing with the boundaries between them will get a kick out of this book, which includes recipes such as seared zhajiang lasagna with pork and octopus, and beef noodle soup burgers. Suffused throughout is an impish irreverence: Sze calls a soup made with yellow-fat chicken, regular chicken, and goth Silkie chicken “diversity chicken soup”; he’s known, at Wenwen, for the “BDSM chicken” (that incredibly involved recipe’s in here, too). Taiwanese? is a good pick for anyone who’s serious about food but also sees some of the self-imposed rules around it as really not that serious, or for anyone who’s got a great relationship with their local butcher. Caroline Schiff Abrams, October 13 This is, as the name would suggest, a book for the daily-3-p.m.-sweet-treat kind of people. But it’s also a book about making baking less annoying and more chill, a boon for anyone who would love baked goods more often but hates the thought of all the fuss. In her new cookbook, beloved New York City pastry chef Caroline Schiff, formerly of Gage & Tollner, assures you that sifting is generally unnecessary, and that your baked goods will probably be fine even if you forgot to bring the eggs to room temperature. Her ideas will appeal to the baker without a dishwasher — her giant chocolate chip cookie dirties one bowl and requires no mixer nor hand beater. It’s also for the snacker who wants to reap as many rewards as possible out of a single burst of effort (see: the black and white coconut macaroons and the cardamom counter cake with chocolate ganache, both of which keep for a week). Schiff describes her lifestyle as one in which “there’s always something sweet in [the] kitchen — no special occasion required,” allowing friends to stop by anytime for cake and tea (and that’s both definitions of the latter). Daily Dessert is a call to be less fussy and to enjoy ourselves more, and who isn’t enticed by that? Alissa Timoshkina Quadrille, October 20 The cozy hits continue, and as someone who prefers to eat most food out of the comforting confines of a bowl, I appreciate Alissa Timoshkina’s commitment to a highly specific pursuit: spoonable food. In Lozhka, you’ll find a tour of Eastern Europe through all things slurpable and scoopable. Much of this is soup or stew, as to be expected, but oh, the variety! Here is Slovak and Belarusian mačanka, a mushroom stew infused with sauerkraut brine (and which Timoshkina serves with lokše, crepes made with mashed potato dough); Armenian lentil soup with the tannic touch of both prunes and walnuts; and so many ways to use millet, barley, and beans (on that note, this is a great book for anyone who is trying to eat more fiber). There are filled dumplings and drop dumplings and steamed bread dumplings! I don’t want to hope for a long winter, but with this book to work through, I also wouldn’t mind it quite as much. Lucas Sin Artisan, October 27 Lucas Sin, the chef formerly of New York City’s Junzi, has always been very good at explaining how to cook; his cooking tutorials via Instagram Stories buoyed me through the early pandemic and taught me techniques I still use today. As a cookbook author, he’s a natural. His first cookbook combines his conversational yet helpfully specific instruction style with his clear passion for Hong Kong’s cha chaan tengs, diners where you’ll find set meals of macaroni in soup, luscious scrambled eggs, and toast. The photography here is gorgeous, indulgent, and transportive, each page a rich text: Sin offers a trove of highly readable little insights, like the backstory as to why roast pork belly and tofu skin over rice became known as “A Man’s Romance” (the answer: a viral, anonymous Hong Kong blog post), cast-iron sizzling pan etiquette, his favorite places in Hong Kong to get the dishes mentioned, and more. Sin is in the process of opening his own cha chaan teng in NYC and is testing out his repertoire of dishes in an extremely popular pop-up; especially for those of us who still haven’t gotten a seat, Cha Chaan Teng is the next best thing.

item.title: Hoy Is Bringing Night-Market Energy to NYC
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.20
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. This is the first installment of our series Getting on the Map, presented by Apple Maps. Over the next three weeks, we’ll be sharing how some of the most creative bars and restaurants are marketing themselves to stand out in a crowded hospitality scene. When I spoke with Cyed Adraincem, he apologized for stumbling over any words; he’d been up at 4 a.m. to wash the sidewalk in front of his forthcoming restaurant. “I wanted to beat all the foot traffic,” he said. Adraincem seems to have brought that same dedication to outfitting Hoy, which will serve Filipino street food in a Manila night-market-like space. Though not yet open, the restaurant has already garnered a lot of attention for its loud and off-kilter aesthetic, smart pop cultural ties, and behind-the-scenes peeks into R&D. I asked him about designing the space, the merch plan, and how opening is going. Mary Anne Porto: Can you tell us about the restaurant concept? Cyed Adraincem: It’s Filipino street food, super fast casual. I’m trying to introduce Filipino food to a broader audience because I feel like we’re underrepresented in New York City. We’ll be serving barbecue skewers, lumpia, and a couple different sandwiches. It’s a pretty simple menu, nothing too fancy, mostly traditional, with chef techniques that we’ve learned over the years. I think the New York dining scene wants something more casual, more affordable right now. They don’t want something pretentious; they just want to eat and have a good drink. The space is based on American diners because I love them. I’ve also been working in cocktail bars for the past seven years. So if you come into the restaurant, it’s kind of a mashup of the two. Those two things [feel similar] to the Manila night market [theme] we’re going for. It’s very high energy; everyone is front-facing; it’s loud and fun. Since everything is counter service, everything is front-facing. The kitchen is open, so I think the energy will keep going throughout the restaurant. We’ll communicate in front of everyone, and it’ll be like a street-market affair. How did you come up with the branding and logo for Hoy? My designer is Kristofferson San Pablo. He’s a Filipino American, and he’s actually my cousin. He’s a well-known artist in LA. We decided on this design based on all the intense fun of a Manila night market. So there are a lot of different colors, a lot of visually stimulating stuff, without being too overwhelming. The pattern on the walls comes from one of the oldest textile patterns in the Philippines. It was an easy choice to showcase our culture in a cool way. [We have] shelves of snacks that are supposed to mimic a sari-sari store in the Philippines. They are usually on every street corner and typically operating right out of the owner’s home, selling an assortment of everyday essentials. Cookbooks [on the shelves were] passed down from my parents. Some of them are very old. They are the baseline of what we will be creating for the restaurant. We also have cookbooks from our local favorites. We tried to stay away from the typical Filipino [branding] stuff, like the star and the sun and barong tagalogs, things that are very obviously Filipino. We wanted to use things like the barrel man, carabao [water buffalo], farmer life, which are a little bit different from the mainstream. I love the barrel man. It’s super Filipino culture. And the other fun part of it is I get to teach people who don’t know about this. These barrel men were made-to-sell souvenirs for poor people to make money. But it’s also how Filipinos act: It’s fun, it’s a gag gift. I also have a bunch of art pieces from different artists around the city and LA as well. We’re going to try to stick with as much Filipino art as we can, but I’m open to [any artists]. As long as it’s local and made with community in mind, I’m happy to support them. Before even opening, you’ve channeled these pop-culture moments through some of your designs, like your Knicks-themed choking sign. How quickly can you and your designer put together this art, and what’s the process like? Everything’s on the fly, baby. Kris’ art is very pop-culture heavy. For him, it’s kind of second nature. I bring things up, and he’s like “Oh yeah, I’ve already been working on something like that.” He keeps up with all of it. He works fast. What merch are you planning to have? A bunch of different things. We entertained the idea of making our own barrel man, or barrel man key chains, and even house slippers. Our standard products we’ll probably carry are shirts, hats, and totes, and we’ll probably cater to the season. As we get open and understand the space better, we’ll start producing more merch. It’s going to be fun, and most of this merch is going to be collaborative with other artists and creatives, too. Some restaurants open with a bare-bones design while they get their footing, then expand into merch as they grow. But it seems like you’re going all-in with your opening, with a very designed space and a merch line. Why did you decide to do that? I’ve been in the industry for almost 17 years. And working in cocktail bars for seven of those, I saw that merch was flying off the shelves. Bartenders were always wearing other bars’ shirts, representing other industry spots. I think more people are wearing clothes that [signify] places that they love. I see Kikkoman jackets and T-shirts from all of my favorite restaurants, and that’s all I wear, too. So I thought it was important to spread the word, and eventually have it as another outlet of revenue. How did you approach the inside of the restaurant? Realistically, [furnishing a restaurant] is a lot of legwork. Everything is so expensive right now. It’s probably the worst time to open a restaurant. So it’s about doing your due diligence and comparing prices. I go to Home Depot, Amazon, The Container Store and see who has the best price, then go from there, so it’s a lot of searching and researching. And everything on the shelves is pretty personal: knickknacks and art from friends and family. We’ll also have a lot of vegetation to try to mimic the tropical Philippines. We made a pot pond out of a large planter pot, and we’re currently growing lemongrass, a calamansi tree, and labuyo chiles in a garden next to the pond. We’re in a corner building, so we get lots of light. We’re going to make a jungle and grow and eat what we can. What’s your path to opening look like right now? We have an issue with our gas firing with the DOB [New York’s Department of Buildings] right now, so we can’t cook onsite until it gets all sorted out. Until then, we decided to open up for the community and have a residency in the space. We’re [hosting] Arellano Pandesal from Queens, which does Filipino pastries, while we do the beverages. We’re also planning to launch a community market place with local vendors and friends and family. It’s a good way to get people in the space and get people excited.

item.title: Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.56
Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Old Raj gin looks like the kind of thing you’d find at the back of your grandfather’s drinks cabinet; its mercantile font and black-and-white portrait of a colonial officer are from another age. Launched in 1972 by Scotland’s oldest independent whisky bottlers, Cadenhead’s, the saffron-laced gin spent decades being resolutely uncool. So I was astonished to find, on a recent trip to New York, that it’s now a cult Martini pour. William Elliott, bar director of Brooklyn’s Maison Premiere, was an early adopter of Old Raj. “We were hunting down obscure, overproof [high abv] gins for a tableside Martini and were struck by its quiet intensity,” he says. “The luxurious application of saffron gives it a tonal and textural quality that was a clear upgrade from the brutishness of most London Dry-style gins.” Old Raj is bottled at two strengths: 46 per cent (Red Label, £30) and a bracing 55 per cent (Blue Label, £34). “The 55 per cent abv version is the must-have,” says Nima Ansari, spirits buyer at Manhattan’s Astor Wines. The fact Old Raj is owned by the company that distils the Campbeltown single malt Springbank is also, he says, a plus for spirits connoisseurs. Blue Label is what they use for Martinis at Maison Premiere and Le Veau d’Or on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. You’ll also see it on the list at Gallaghers Steakhouse, Death & Co and Frenchette, where it’s served in a Martini twist with vermouth and tomato water. “I first came across Old Raj while working at Small Victory in Austin, Texas,” says Jojo Colonna, bar director at Four Horsemen’s buzzing Italian I Cavallini in Brooklyn. If a customer requested Blue Label, he says, “it was a sign of an intentional Martini drinker”. Old-style, high-strength gins have been making a comeback among Martini connoisseurs. “At the higher abv, the spirit holds on to more of those botanical oils and aromas,” says James Stevenson, founder of new Martini bar Brutes of Mayfair, where the house gin is Plymouth Navy Strength (£42), a 57 per cent abv homage to the high-proof gins once drunk by officers in the Royal Navy. “You still get a very dry, clean Martini, but with a much more oily texture, from the gin.” If you’re mixing Martinis with a high-strength gin, “stir with ice for longer than usual to allow for adequate dilution”, advises Kevin Beary, beverage director of Chicago’s Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club. Erik Delanoy of Elder in NYC also recommends using Old Raj Blue Label for a wet Martini with equal parts gin and vermouth. At Three Sheets in Soho, they favour The Botanist’s 50 per cent abv Distiller’s Strength (£42). “It’s still very soft and mellow,” says co-owner Max Venning. “Because it’s higher-proof, you can stir it down for longer and get the Martini really cold, without losing the lovely wild, floral botanicals.” Forget old-school stiffener – it’s now all about soft power. Comments

item.title: Louis Thompson – fashion’s favourite pastry chef
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.21
Louis Thompson – fashion’s favourite pastry chef Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Louis Thompson is sitting in a brightly lit hallway in central London, “wearing my chef whites, which have come straight out of the kitchen”, he says excitedly. He is rakishly handsome and 6ft 2in tall, and his faint Australian accent and youth are evident. His whereabouts – the brightly lit kitchen of Spring, the critically lauded restaurant where he’s freelancing today – are more nondescript. “I’m just piping some chocolate sprinkles, because Spring would never buy chocolate sprinkles,” he jokes. “We make them by hand with beautiful Mexican chilli and vanilla.” Since arriving from his native Melbourne in 2019, 28-year-old Thompson has become one of London’s most in-demand pastry chefs. The month we speak, he’s spent countless hours churning 100 kilos of ice cream for a private summer party at the Serpentine Pavilion, baked three single-layer cakes for the wedding of Quince Bakery founder Anna Higham, and shared a recipe for elderflower fritters with fellow pastry chef Nicola Lamb’s more than 100,000 Substack subscribers. This month he’ll join Helen Goh at Quince Bakery in Islington to discuss her new book, Baking & the Meaning of Life (Murdoch). Pastry cheffing aside, Thompson is a rising model who has worked for Simone Rocha and Stefan Cooke. (He inaugurated the latter’s AW25 collection with a nearly metre-wide cherry and almond cake.) Now, having signed with Next London modelling agency, he hopes to learn from the various creatives in his network. “He just hits the nail on the head every time,” says Stefan Cooke co-founder Jake Burt, who has been serving Thompson’s pastries with black coffee and Marlboro Reds at his cult east London shop Jake’s since 2024. He saw Thompson at a Stefan Cooke event in 2023, which led to the model’s first print campaign, and recruited him to do the cakes. Thompson credits his late father – “a fiercely intelligent man” who received an Order of Australia for his work with marginalised communities – for his love of cooking. At home, food was a “pathway to curiosity and access”, he says. A rhubarb tart became a lesson about rationing in the second world war. Strawberries tossed with heaps of brown sugar and balsamic vinegar taught him to conjure magic from unfussy ingredients. Thompson’s mother, a lecturer in architecture at RMIT University, instilled in him “neatness, care and diligence”, something evidenced in his signature galettes, a traditionally entry-level pastry, which in his hands becomes a Michelin-level dish. Only a few years ago, Thompson was working at a call centre in Melbourne, trying to save money in order to move London to study fashion history and theory at Central Saint Martins. He’d devour cookbooks and stay up until the early hours baking and icing cakes with a colleague to unwind. “What drew me to baking was that it was more process-driven [than cooking],” he says. “In baking, you use raw ingredients combined in a specific way to transform them. The timelines are generally longer and you’re often bringing different elements together.” Thompson baked part-time while juggling his studies. A three-month stint making bagels at a café led to a job at Violet London, the California-style bakery where he learned the art of icing cakes. Three years later, in 2023, he was referred to Spring. The restaurant’s late chef-patron Skye Gyngell – “the most charismatic person I ever met” – praised him for his curiosity. “Food-wise, she definitely taught me subtlety,” Thompson reflects. “As a younger chef, I thought being skilled meant being able to turn the flavour dials up to 100. Skye taught me how to arrange flavour with more harmony.” Back then, it looked as if Thompson would have to choose between food and fashion; today his remit allows him to do both. “It’s simply another form of communication,” he says of his modelling. His ability to straddle both industries is reflective of a time where the worlds of fashion and culinary arts have become closely interlinked. “Combining food and fashion is a way of creating intimacy around something that can otherwise feel quite untouchable,” says cake artist Sophia Stolz, who bakes for brands including Miu Miu, Dior and Gucci. “Food is incredibly universal; luxury fashion is not. Food creates a common ground between a brand and the person experiencing it.” Thompson is content for his two pursuits to keep evolving. “I’ve spent a long time connecting all sorts of random dots,” he says. “Now I’m at a point where those dots and connections form a cohesive web.” Most recently he’s started contributing to AnOther Magazine’s new food column. A commission for American comedian Cole Escola is also on deck. In December, he’ll travel home and host events with local chefs he admires. “I try to sniff out new information wherever it might be,” he says. “I always seek out new experiences – and go into them with openness.” Comments

item.title: Oxbridge’s formal dinners have had a reboot
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.12
Oxbridge’s formal dinners have had a reboot Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Recently I was invited to a formal hall dinner at Worcester College, Oxford. The Provost Lord David Isaac wanted to show me what food at a modern, progressive college looks like. In 2019, in an attempt to be more inclusive, the governing body voted to abolish some of the college’s formal hall traditions. Candlelit, multi-course dinners are a fixture of older universities such as Oxford, Cambridge, Durham and Trinity College Dublin; attendees wear gowns and lounge suits (black tie on Sundays, except for informal dinners), students are required to stand as fellows approach the high table and grace is said. Surprisingly, the undergraduates at Worcester voted overwhelmingly to retain these customs, prompting one Oxford academic to observe that “some of the governing body are more woke than the student community”. Nevertheless, Isaac has been anxious to make the dinners feel more inclusive. A former chair of Stonewall and the Equality and Human Rights Commission, Isaac attended grammar school in Abergavenny before reading law at Trinity Hall, Cambridge. He vividly remembers being served grapefruit on a plate at a formal dinner and having no idea how to eat it. “Given my own background, I’m committed to ensuring that, as an elite institution, we’re not elitist in the type of students we educate. Our undergraduate body is 86 per cent state school students. I also want our food to be high-quality and to reflect everyone’s tastes.” Hence the introduction of meat-free Mondays and 60 per cent of the food being vegan, vegetarian or suitable for other special diets such as halal. As a Cambridge graduate, I am familiar with the formal hall traditions. I can’t say, however, that the meals I consumed as an undergraduate contributed to my love of gastronomy. “The food was execrable,” recalls former Labour party activist and Worcester graduate Lord Richard Faulkner of his experiences in the ’60s. A common complaint with a few notable exceptions: “In my day, Merton College had the best food, which may have contributed to why the Emperor of Japan went there [in the ’80s],” says former head of MI6, Sir Richard Moore. At Worcester, it seems, the British institutional tradition of serving up slop is through. When I dined there, the menu included leek, pea and watercress soup with poached halibut followed by roast guinea fowl ballotine with artichoke purée, wild mushrooms and Madeira sauce and a white chocolate and raspberry tart. The three-course meal cost students £15 (and £18.60 for their guests). Worcester’s formal hall honours the Benedictine traditions on which the college was founded – “studying, living and eating together and being in dialogue”, says Isaac. At a time when just one in three British families eat together each day, there’s surely value in this. Other formal hall traditions such as “sconcing” (a drinking game where students must down a large tankard of ale for breaking certain rules, such as talking about religion or politics) have long been retired. Latin grace, however, still remains. Robin Geddes, an alumnus of St John’s College, Oxford, from the 2010s considers the custom archaic: “I’m sure my classics tutor would be horrified to hear me say that.” Fergus Murison, a Worcester maths graduate from the 1970s, values it as a way of giving thanks and “acknowledging the lucky position we’re in. [For younger generations] who have less pomp and circumstance in their lives, these rituals have even more significance,” he says. Most importantly, the meal times are designed to prompt conversation and help students interact with more social ease. Prior to coming to Worcester, Ruby Steele, an undergraduate in classics and modern languages, “had never had the experience of sitting next to someone I didn’t know and making small talk before. Nor had I ever sat at a meal with more than one pair of cutlery.” It’s one of the many formalities the provost makes a point of “demystifying” for the fresh intake each year. “You learn how to speak with people who are considerably more senior,” adds Worcester MCR president and current postgraduate Georgia Neilson. “How to ask good questions and listen; how to bring others into conversation. [The specialness of the occasion] prepares you to be open-minded.” You might also get to meet some of the world’s great thinkers and doers. Moore remembers being introduced to English civil servant Oliver Franks, “who was a complete hero – to have access to such interesting people was a thrill”. The lure of the dining halls means visiting guests can be eclectic. “Recently Mick Jagger was at a formal hall at Oriel College,” says Steele. “That was very cool.” “I’m always surprised at how – despite coming from a wide range of backgrounds – our students enjoy Oxford traditions and dressing up for dinner,” Isaac says. “They reject the Waugh image of Brideshead privilege, but perhaps because they grew up on Harry Potter, they wholeheartedly embrace formal hall by making it their own.” Comments
