item.title: Turn Eggs Into Dinner With This Salsa de Chorizo Recipe
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 3.53
Advertisement In the sun-washed kitchen of Hacienda San Lorenzo at Casa Madero Winery in Parras, Mexico, Mari Medina places two eggs in an oil-slicked pan and turns the heat on low. As the whites slowly set, she ladles a chunky, brick-red sauce that smells of roasted tomatoes, toasted chiles and its rich, smoky main ingredient: chorizo. Recipe: Salsa de Chorizo Ms. Medina, who has cooked at the hacienda in the state of Coahuila for more than 18 years, and whose family has lived in Coahuila for six generations, said that guests travel great distances. They’ll have the salsa de chorizo for the first time and request it again the next morning. Coahuila, the vast Mexican state that stretches from the Texas border to deep into the Sierra Madre, is one of Mexico’s underrepresented culinary regions. Its most famous dish, nachos, was invented in the border city of Piedras Negras in the 1940s and went on to conquer the world. Salsa de chorizo, on the other hand, has been nourishing Coahuila for generations — Ms. Medina learned to make it from her mother, who learned from hers, who learned from hers — but almost no one outside the state knows its name. Whether you call it salsa de chorizo or caldillo de chorizo, which is technically soupier, the idea is the same: chorizo as the base of a stellar sauce, scooped with torn pieces of warm corn or flour tortilla. Though it’s often served alongside eggs or a small bowl of frijoles de olla, the dish began as a meal on its own. Coahuila is an arid place, settled by miners and ranchers who needed food that was nutritious, would not spoil and, above all, rendidor, a word that means yielding, or able to feed many from a little. Cooking the chorizo into a salsa meant that a family could eat well from only a modest amount of meat. The chorizo that cooks in Coahuila seek out above any other comes from a town tucked into a remote corner of the state: Ciudad Melchor Múzquiz. Múzquiz, as everyone there calls it, was founded in 1739 by Basque soldiers looking for silver and gold, and it was shaped by those mining and ranching families. Yolanda Elizondo Maltos, the city’s official historian and chronicler, who was born there and traces her roots to the first Spanish settlers who arrived in Coahuila about 450 years ago, describes the town as “un rincón en el mapa de Coahuila.” A nook on the map of Coahuila. That isolation, she said, further necessitated smart ways to preserve food. “The chorizo has been made here for centuries because it is a way to conserve meat,” Ms. Elizondo Maltos said. “With the spices and the vinegar, it holds for long periods without refrigeration.” Families in Múzquiz follow closely guarded recipes. There’s no one single way to make chorizo, but the common denominators are quality pork butt, as well as dried chiles that are toasted, rehydrated and puréed with fresh garlic, oregano, cumin, black pepper and vinegar. The mixture is then oreada, left to air under a fine cloth to marinate deeply before being packed into casings. People buy their chorizo from the same butcher their entire lives, the one their mothers and grandmothers used. When they cook it, it tastes like home. The chorizo of Múzquiz is so prized that chefs and restaurants across northern Mexico are starting to call it out on their menus. “Rather than make our own chorizo at our butcher shops, I realized it was better to source it from a place that really knows how to make it,” said Anuar Yutani Morales, the owner of Super Carnes Coahuila in the neighboring town of Sabinas, who runs the state’s Festival de la Carne Asada. “The artisanship is incomparable.” In 2019, Múzquiz held its first Festival del Chorizo, which brought together about 30 chorizo-making families. Ms. Elizondo Maltos, who helped organize the event, wants to bring it back. “It marks the city as unique,” she said. At the hacienda, Ms. Medina makes her salsa with chorizo, tomatoes, onion, garlic and jalapeño. She roasts everything until deeply charred. That is, she said, the secret. “It is very homey food,” she said. Once salsa de chorizo enters a kitchen, it tends to stay. Pair it with sunny-side-up eggs, or scramble the eggs directly into the salsa. Poach it like a smokier and meatier shakshuka. Use it to sauce crispy tacos and tacos sudados, filled with mashed potato or shredded beef. Pair it with quesadillas, rice and beans. With potatoes, it becomes an even more filling guisado. Or, pair two of the region’s classic dishes and use it to top nachos. Asked what it would mean if salsa de chorizo were to reach the fame of nachos, Ms. Elizondo Maltos did not hesitate. “Nuestra identidad reconocida,” she said. Our identity, finally recognized. After a pause, almost teary-eyed, she said: “Mucho orgullo.” A lot of pride. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. item.title: The Quick Sauce That Changed How I Cook Fish
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 2.58
Advertisement Friends often ask me how to cook more fish at home — not salmon, they’ve figured that one out — but the white fish their doctors recommend for its lean protein. They know it cooks quickly and like how it tastes, but worry about preparing it. Recipe: Caramelized Garlic Fish That’s how I felt when I first started cooking professionally, and for myself. It was one thing to learn how to sear flaky white fish on the line in a restaurant, another to make it at home. I was on a tight budget, but even if I hadn’t been, I wouldn’t have been able to find fish as fresh as the kind available at restaurants or the Asian markets of my childhood. Then I made a fish recipe that changed my kitchen life. In her 2001 cookbook, “Pleasures of the Vietnamese Table,” the chef Mai Pham shared her recipe for cá kho tộ and described it as the “one dish that best represents Vietnamese home cooking.” Originally from the south of the country, freshwater snakehead fish (cá lóc) is braised (kho) in a clay pot (tộ) until it becomes deeply savory and a little sticky. Bright with cilantro and black pepper, it begs to be spooned over rice and shoveled. It’s all comfort and still light, punchy but delicate with nuance. And the whole dish comes together in less than 20 minutes. The first time I tried it, I couldn’t believe how easy it was for how good it tasted. I didn’t have a clay pot, but it was, as Ms. Pham promised, “also delicious cooked in a regular pot.” It starts with melting sugar past golden, and then stirring in oil and garlic. As the garlic sizzles and softens, it releases its fragrance into the dark amber caramel. Adding fish sauce and water stops the sugar from going over its bittersweet cliff to burned and turns it into a funky sauce to soak into the fish, and then glaze it with a mahogany shine. This sauce is unbelievable with fish and just as good with tofu, chicken, beef, pork, duck and all kinds of vegetables and seafood. Sometimes known as nước sốt (or kho sauce in English), there are countless variations in Vietnam and its diaspora. Some melt the sugar with oil or vinegar; others add shallots, coconut water or both. As the dish became part of my rotation, I stopped flipping open Ms. Pham’s book and started adjusting it to my taste. I throw in a lot more garlic, splash in less water and skip the scallions in favor of more cilantro. She called for catfish fillets, which are earthy like snakehead fish, but cod, fresh and frozen, is always at my market and its mildness benefits from the big flavors. (Using crosscut fish steaks hews more closely to the dish’s origins, and the bones give the sauce even more body.) It takes only one go to get the rhythm of this sauce. Once you have its pantry ingredients (and stock your freezer with frozen fish fillets), you’ll be able to pull together this one-pot meal any night. item.title: Theo James Shares His Restaurant’s Burro e Parmigiano Recipe
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 2.45
Advertisement Theo James loves to cook based on vibes.“I don’t do it with exactitude because I’m too impatient,” Mr. James said. He extends that approach to burro e parmigiano, a simple Northern Italian dish that happens to be one of his favorites. (It’s also a recipe he makes for his kids, he told Cathy Lo, a New York Times Cooking editor.) Recipe: Theo James’s Burro e Parmigiano While he may not be one for measurements, when he makes his version, which is adapted from Ornella, a restaurant he owns with Naz Hassan and Ed Templeton in East London, he does make sure the ingredients are the best they can be: deeply flavored dark chicken stock, aged Parmesan, fresh tagliatelle. When simplicity and incredible ingredients meet, he said, “those things bound together create something incredibly delicious.” You can watch him cook the dish alongside Kaya Scodelario, his co-star in Guy Ritchie’s comedy-drama series “The Gentlemen” and another passionate cook, in the video below (or on YouTube). Here are excerpts from the interview and the outtakes, which have been edited and condensed. Have you ever cooked with each other before today? THEO JAMES No, but you keep threatening to cook me Brazilian. KAYA SCODELARIO I want to cook dinner for you, but you don’t ever answer my calls. JAMES Kaya’s a great Brazilian chef. What’s your favorite thing to cook? SCODELARIO I just like home comfort food. When I’m working, I really miss cooking — when I’m away in hotels and stuff and traveling. So when I get home, it’s the first thing I want to do: spend four hours in the kitchen just cooking. Podcast, glass of wine, no one disturbing me and, yeah, cooking for people. It’s my love language. I like to feed. Have either of you ever worked in the food service industry? JAMES Yes. SCODELARIO Did you? JAMES Yeah. God, yeah. I was a waiter in multiple pubs. I even did one of those things where you had to turn up to catering venues — SCODELARIO Silver service? JAMES No. God, no. You turn up as kind of a teenager. I’ll always remember — I had all of the pinnies on — and I leant over to pour someone some coffee, and I had another coffee pot in my left hand, and I poured the coffee all over the guy’s crotch, basically. I got instantly fired. Cheers! SCODELARIO I’ve never worked in the service industry. JAMES Have you not? SCODELARIO No, I never. But I played a waitress, and I was really bad at it. I couldn’t carry the [tray]. What’s the best or worst food you’ve ever had to do a scene with? SCODELARIO We, on “Maze Runner,” had to do a scene where we hadn’t had food for ages, and we walk in a room, and there’s every kind of food imaginable. They let us choose, and I wanted deep-fried Oreos. But I got really sick because I had about seven of them straight away. So that was great but also awful. How do you feel about eating food in bed? SCODELARIO I’m down for eating food in bed. JAMES Really? I’ve always felt kind of repulsed by the idea of it. SCODELARIO OK. [Both laugh] SCODELARIO I think it’s always a better idea than the reality of it. Like, you know, on Mother’s Day or Father’s Day, where they’re like, “Oh, we’ll do Mummy’s breakfast in bed.” And you’re like, This is actually annoying because now I’m stuck in the bed, and there’s orange juice everywhere. JAMES That’s cute. Yeah, but I don’t like the idea of scoffing sandwiches while you’re asleep. SCODELARIO What about in a hotel? JAMES Hotel, you’re allowed to do for breakfast, but that’s it. SCODELARIO OK. What about a midday club sandwich? You wouldn’t eat that on the bed? JAMES Maybe near the bed, or adjacent to the bed, but never in the bed. If the cast of “The Gentlemen” owned a restaurant, what would everyone’s roles be? SCODELARIO I’d like you as the angry chef in the background. You don’t ever want to come out and see people, but you’re really stressed all the time. JAMES What would Joely [Richardson] — what would her role be? SCODELARIO Front of house. JAMES What would your role be? Manager. SCODELARIO No. JAMES It’s a bit boring. SCODELARIO I’d be … I don’t know. Keep the books. In your family, do you have any specific traditions around food? JAMES You have good traditions from your mother in your family about food, right? SCODELARIO Kind of. We do Christmas on Christmas Eve instead of Christmas Day. We eat, like, I think, three or four times a week Brazilian food. JAMES What are the classics? SCODELARIO Rice and beans. But proper beans. JAMES What’s the most complex Brazilian dish to make? SCODELARIO Feijoada takes a good few hours. JAMES What is that? SCODELARIO It’s really good, and I’ll do it for you when we get back. It’s got, like, pork trotters and pig ear and everything —— JAMES Aw, poor piggy. SCODELARIO My son is a pescatarian, so I’ve been learning more vegetarian meals. But I don’t like bell peppers or chickpeas, and I think everything vegetarian is that. So I need better veggie recipes. Do you do Sunday dinners? Do you make the kids sit at the table with you? JAMES No. God, no, no, no. Growing up, it was pretty English. We had Sunday roasts. The Greek side, my grandfather’s side, we did a bit of Greek-y style but he wasn’t a big cook. SCODELARIO Do you ever have bacalhau? It’s salt cod. We do that for Easter, always. JAMES Do your kids — do they feel connected to the Brazilian part of you? SCODELARIO Yeah, I think food is a really great way of introducing kids to their culture and heritage and stuff. Because it’s something they can taste and see and be included in. He’s very proud of that. Both the kids are. Whenever we travel the world, the first thing I’ll do is find the local Brazilian restaurant. And luckily Brazilians are everywhere. What’s the biggest difference between craft service on a British film set versus an American one? JAMES We often talk about this. Basically, in England, craft doesn’t exist. SCODELARIO It doesn’t exist. They don’t feed us. JAMES It’s like a table with a kettle. And some terrible biscuits. SCODELARIO Crappy biscuits. Off brand. The cheap ones. JAMES A molding orange or something. Whereas here, in America, craft service is an art. SCODELARIO Incredible. It’s a whole truck, and anything you want they can just make. My favorite thing about working in America is the food on set. JAMES Not the work? SCODELARIO Not the work. [Both laugh] What are you eating, Kaya? On an American set? SCODELARIO Breakfast burrito, because that’s not a thing in England. I love a breakfast burrito. JAMES We should get one after this. SCODELARIO Yes, that’s exactly what we need. Jambalaya. I had that recently on a job, and I was like, that’s fun. Never had that before, that was great. It’s just that, every three hours, they will make sure there’s a hot meal for everyone. And we just don’t do that in the U.K. JAMES There’s a slight culture of Britishness where they’re like, “Oh, you don’t need — stop moaning!” It’s like a 14-hour day, and they’re like, “You can have a cup of tea!” SCODELARIO “Have a biscuit! You’re OK!” But we always, don’t we — we get for the crew, we’ll get, like, an ice cream truck or coffee. JAMES We’re good like that. SCODELARIO We’re good people. If you were a food dish, what would you be? Can you answer for each other? JAMES You would be — SCODELARIO A dehydrated mango. JAMES No, you would be six chicken nuggets. [Laughs] JAMES No, you would be something exotic with a simmering undertone of vermouth. SCODELARIO Ooh. All right, I’ll take it. You would be—— JAMES Some chips. SCODELARIO No, you would be something simple but delicious. Genuinely! Like this [burro e parmigiano]. You would be this. JAMES That’s what my ex-girlfriends used to say. SCODELARIO Easy, not overcomplicated. JAMES Simple but delicious. SCODELARIO A bit dumb but pretty. [Both laugh] Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. item.title: The Vegetarian Dinner Menu You Have to Make Before Summer Ends
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 2.24
Advertisement It’s a true joy to cook straight from the farmers’ market, and this is the perfect time to do so. During this period, the sweet spot between the end of summer and the beginning of fall, there is bounty at every stall. Want corn, melon, zucchini, green beans or tomatoes? Help yourself. Fresh herbs? In spades. Stone fruit? Peaches, nectarines and plums are piled high. But, I’ll admit, it’s the sweet peppers that really excite me. This includes the standard bell peppers (red, yellow or orange), an interesting fleshy variety called corno di toro, or bull’s horn, (red or yellow) and the cultish Jimmy Nardello, a slender, thin-skinned Italian “frying” pepper. The rest of the year, sweet peppers are apt to be hothouse or hydroponically raised. Field-grown peppers are usually more flavorful. This is their moment. A quick tour of the market decides the menu for me. Rather than feature everything available in one dish, I divvy up my favorites for a three-course meal. This means a tender green salad from the herb sellers, paired with fresh mozzarella; a hearty risotto of roasted peppers; and a simple dessert of roasted plums. Recipe: Fresh Herb and Mozzarella Salad For the mozzarella herb salad — a delicate, delicious pairing — freshness is everything. Look for super-fresh, soft domestic mozzarella (also called fior di latte, made from cows’ milk), and serve it at cool room temperature, not straight from the fridge. You can cut slices from a half-pound piece or opt for smaller ovolini (egg-size), ciliegini (cherry-size) or bocconcini (bite-size). Or choose more expensive imported Italian mozzarella di bufala, with its distinctive tanginess. For an herb salad, I prefer a varied assortment, which can contain parsley, dill, watercress, chervil, basil, mint, tarragon, shiso, sunflower sprouts, small red sorrel and purslane. But I add some slightly larger leaves, like baby arugula, to bolster the mixture and make it easier to dress. The most important thing is to wait until the very last minute to dress the tender herbs — just barely — so they maintain their shape. You can drizzle more vinaigrette over the mozzarella. Advertisement I love to make risotto, and the technique I recommend is fairly foolproof. With practice, any cook can confidently achieve success. Most cooks go wrong with how much liquid they add, drowning the rice instead of allowing it to gradually absorb the hot broth. Keeping a brisk heat below the pot is also crucial. You want to let the rice go nearly dry. Look for little sinkholes on the surface before adding more broth. Yes, you do need to stir throughout the process, but not every second. It should take 20 to 25 minutes, start to finish. This risotto is quite flavorful, full of smoky roasted and peeled sweet peppers. With a touch of saffron and a dash of cayenne, it feels a little bit Spanish. I’d serve it as a main course for lunch, perhaps accompanied by grilled zucchini or sautéed cherry tomatoes, or alongside grilled fish or roasted chicken for a more substantial meal. Fruit for dessert is my go-to whenever possible. Lately, I’ve been quite enamored of roasting fruit — especially stone fruit — and letting it caramelize. Here, nearly any variety of plum will do. Choose slightly underripe fruit, then cut it into fat wedges and toss them with a bit of sugar. A quick stint in a hot oven transforms them. To serve, they are placed in a shallow pool of a sauce that’s similar to crème anglaise but is made with cardamom-infused coconut milk instead of dairy cream. It’s not fancy, but it is heavenly.
