item.title: 5 Workouts to Build Serious Uphill Hiking Strength
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.96
(Photo: Peter Amend/Getty) The first time I ever went backpacking abroad, I was so unprepared for the climbs that I couldn’t complete my planned itinerary. The route in question should have been a dream loop through the Italian Dolomites. But instead of frolicking through alpine passes, I found myself two days in, on the verge of tears, staring down yet another 6,000-foot climb. The sun was about to set, and my quads were Jell-O. I couldn’t do it. I booked a room in an inn I couldn’t afford, climbed the pass the next morning, and then took a bus to my endpoint. While there’s no shame in calling a trip early, it’s a bummer to miss out on miles of beauty just because your hiking fitness isn’t where you thought it was. And while it’s relatively easy to train for a route if you have similar terrain close to home, it can be tough to prep for truly enormous climbs—like the kind you’ll find in the Colorado Rockies, the Italian Dolomites, or the French Alps. “It’s especially hard to train in America for stuff like the Alps or the Dolomites because those mountains are so steep,” explains Alexa Hasman, a mountain athlete, personal trainer, and founder of Rise Ultra Coaching. The trick, she says, is to combine endurance training with hill repeats and gym time to build serious muscular power. Here are a few of her favorite hill workouts. Your first order of business is to build a strong endurance base. For this, Hasman recommends finding the longest hill you can (or setting your treadmill to its maximum incline) and climbing at a consistent pace for one to two hours. Ideally, you’ll carry a little weight: Hasman suggests starting with ten percent of your bodyweight and hiking for 60 minutes. Add 15 minutes each week. You can also play with weight, adding about five pounds per week until you’re at 20 percent of your bodyweight. Hasman cautions against carrying any more than that. Upwards of 20 percent, the likelihood of injury outweighs the diminishing strength gains. (Also avoid increasing weight and distance in the same week—up one or the other, but not both.) Throughout, stick to a pace that’s engaged but sustainable. “You should be conversational,” Hasman says. “If you can say three sentences at a time without gasping for breath, that’s where I want you.” A single long hike is great, but it doesn’t quite simulate the back-to-back days of serious vert that you’ll encounter on a backpacking trip. To prepare, Hasman recommends doing two endurance workouts per week on consecutive days. “Cumulative fatigue is really important there,” Hasman says. “It teaches your body to work on tired legs. You might feel stiff, sore, or heavy the next day, but that’s normal. This is just as much about mental training as it is physical.” Once you have a strong endurance base—i.e., you can reliably hike uphill for 90 to 120 minutes while carrying 15 to 20 percent of your bodyweight—it’s time to start building speed and power. Find a steep hill and charge up it at close to your max effort for ten seconds. Walk slowly down to the base of the hill, then do it again. Your goal is four total reps. Over time, build up to reps of 30 seconds, then 60 seconds, then two minutes, then three minutes. If you live near a hill that’s long enough for a three-minute interval, great. If not, do this on a treadmill at its maximum incline setting. “If you’re an uphill athlete, then you’re also by nature a downhill athlete,” Hasman says. And if you’ve ever done a long descent with weight on your back, you’re probably aware that downhills are the real quad-killers. To avoid jellified quads during your trip, Hasman recommends training downhills specifically. One way to do this is to reverse the above workout. Walk slowly up a hill, then charge down it as fast as you can go without being reckless. Do this for four reps. You can also combine these two workouts: Book it up the hill, then book it down, and take your rest at the bottom. Welcome to the least-fun workout on this list—but perhaps the most effective. “Wall sits are my secret sauce for downhill,” Hasman says. They’re great because they hold you in an exaggerated, active downhill-hiking position for an extended period. “I start my athletes with one-minute wall sits a couple of times a week. After a few weeks, we go until failure. Then we add weight.” Once you can sit with a ten-pound plate on your lap for a minute or two, you’re ready for boss level: single-leg wall sits. “Most people can only hold them for a second or two—it’s almost like marching while sitting against a wall,” Hasman says. “If you can hold it for 30 seconds, you’re an absolute beast.” Nothing beats single-leg exercises for building uphill strength and stability. To this end, Hasman recommends getting into the gym at least twice a week during the meat of your training. Focus on your glutes, quads, hamstrings, and core. While there are tons of relevant exercises, Hasman says step-ups are a particular must-do. “Do 15 to 30 reps on one leg, then switch,” she recommends. Start with three sets. Every week, either add a set or add five pounds of additional weight to make it harder. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Buried in 2 Feet of Snow With No Overnight Gear, a Hike in the Enchantments Just Turned Deadly
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.79
Two people in the Enchantments at the summit of Asgard Pass in the Cascade Mountains (Photo: Tegra Stone Nuess/Getty Images) An Oklahoma woman died of hypothermia while attempting a thru-hike of the Enchantments, a renowned high-alpine region in Washington state’s Cascade Mountain Range. Sybil Claborn, 45, was hiking with her husband on September 13 when an early-season snowstorm struck the trail, according to the Chelan County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO). Several feet of snow buried the couple, both of whom suffered severe hypothermia. Claborn succumbed to the cold. “The area the couple was at is approximately 7,000 to 8,000 feet in elevation, with either trailhead approximately eight to ten miles away,” CCSO Chief Ryan Moody said in a statement sent to Outside. “Storms had persisted throughout the day, producing significant snowfall in the area. The male reported that both individuals’ clothing was soaked and that they did not have overnight gear.” Authorities have not released the man’s name, age, or condition. The Enchantments is a coveted alpine hiking area known for mountain goats, turquoise lakes, and jagged peaks. The Washington Trail Association (WTA) categorizes the 18-mile one-way hike as being “hard,” with 4,500 feet of elevation gain and a high point of 7,800 feet. The couple was in the so-called “core zone” of the Enchantments, which is a high plateau filled with lakes, authorities say. A high-alpine basin forms the centerpiece of the Enchantments traverse. Camping along the Enchantments traverse is only allowed by securing a competitive permit. Some hikers will attempt the entire trek in a day to avoid one, but weather conditions can turn violent quickly, especially at high elevations, putting unprepared mountaineers at an extreme risk of rapid hypothermia. Although large amounts of snow don’t typically accumulate until November, variable weather is common through these alpine peaks. “Those undertaking the Enchantments thru-traverse in September should be aware of variable conditions brought by the onset of autumn in the alpine,” WTA writes on its website. “Conditions can vary greatly this time of year—it is not uncommon for 30-plus degree temperature swings to occur in a single day.” September 13, 5:30 P.M. The husband placed the initial SOS call, reporting his wife was unable to move. 5:50 P.M. A second call confirmed the couple was buried in one to two feet of snow under an emergency blanket. Air rescue was grounded due to severe weather. 8:00 to 10:50 P.M. Army helicopter pilots make multiple attempts from Yakima, Washington, to reach the couple but fail due to storm conditions. September 14, 3:30 A.M. Ground rescuers from Chelan County Mountain Rescue reach the site on foot, finding Claborn deceased and her husband suffering from severe hypothermia. 9:00 A.M. Air evacuation clears, transporting the surviving hiker to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth. CCSO provided Outside with a detailed timeline of the rescue. Just before 5:30 P.M. on September 13, authorities say they received an initial emergency call from a man who reported his wife was unable to move, and that he couldn’t carry her out on the trail. Twenty minutes later, the man called again to say the woman was under an emergency blanket and the couple was buried between one and two feet of snow. Weather conditions were quickly deteriorating, and responders determined that it wasn’t safe to fly a helicopter in to evacuate the couple. “At that point, the only other option was to get a ground team in as quickly as possible to try to warm her up,” Moody said. “A ground rescue team was requested from Chelan County Mountain Rescue (CCMR). They provide the quickest ground response possible.” CCSO requested a hoist-capable helicopter before 7 P.M. if weather conditions improved. An hour later, an Army helicopter launched from Yakima, Washington, located about 100 miles away. Weather again prevented responders from reaching the pair. Throughout the evening, CCSO said that the man continued to communicate about his wife’s condition and the possibility that she may die. The Army again tried to fly a helicopter into the area at 10:50 P.M., but the weather was still too dangerous. At 3:30 A.M. on September 14, two CCMR personnel reached the couple on foot. At this point, the woman had died, and the man was suffering from severe hypothermia. Responders warmed the man in a tent rescuers brought, the Sheriff’s office said. Later that morning, a helicopter arrived to transport the man and two CCMR rescuers. They landed at the Leavenworth Fish Hatchery, about ten miles from the trailhead, around 9:00 A.M. Officials transported the man by ambulance to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth for treatment. By 10 A.M., the sheriff’s office sent in a recovery flight to recover the deceased woman. She was transported to the Chelan County Coroner’s office Additional information regarding the cause and manner of her death is under investigation, authorities say.

item.title: A New Approach to Disaster Relief
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.53
Participants carrying Amazon’s portable rapid response technology systems during their disaster relief training exercise. (Photo: Pete Kiehart) From this summer’s intense wildfires to back-to-back earthquakes to a brewing Super El Niño, one thing is clear: The growing threat of natural disasters is hard to ignore. Supercharged by climate change, events like wildfires, earthquakes, hurricanes, and floods now occur more regularly, often in places that aren’t prepared for them. This reality means billions of people worldwide need stronger preparedness and resilience measures. This new era of heightened risk requires a new era of heightened response, from innovative tools to strong relationships to advanced preparation. Enter Amazon. “When I spoke with first responders, I kept hearing the same failures repeat over and over—disasters affecting their ability to communicate, provide relief quickly, or even access resources as basic as clean water,” said Jeffrey Schweitzer, Amazon’s disaster relief innovation lead. Along with nonprofit partners, Schweitzer and his team developed new, customizable rapid response technology systems to restore critical services, all in suitcase-sized packages that one person can carry and set up in just a few minutes. “During disasters, responders need to understand the landscape, the impact, where survivors are, and who needs help,” said Rodney Cooper, who serves as national director for technology and programs with the Information Technology Disaster Resource Center (ITDRC). “During Hurricane Helene, everything was dark. Survivors could not reach out to each other.” That’s exactly the kind of situation this new tech is made for: restoring services within hours, so communities don’t have to wait weeks to call loved ones or turn the lights back on. Amazon’s rapid response tech includes 10-plus configurations that relief personnel can set up: solar microgrids, satellite Wi-Fi, water purification devices, even terrain-mapping drones. The drone systems alone can cost up to $250,000, but Amazon provides them to partners at no cost. And the tech is reusable: After a disaster response ends, nonprofits ship the systems back to Amazon for inspection, refurbishment, and restocking. Meaning one system can serve multiple communities, across multiple disasters. The systems can power hospitals, emergency shelters, fire departments, and community centers. A single system can keep a 50-bed hospital running for 72 hours or serve more than 2,600 hot meals—and they’ve already been crucial for restoring communities after recent disasters. Following the recent twin earthquakes in Venezuela, where telecommunications were completely severed near the epicenter in La Guaira, Amazon worked with nonprofit partners on the ground to deliver portable Wi-Fi systems to connect clinics, shelters, and community hubs. One system was placed on a car roof to create a movie night for kids. And in Jamaica, after Hurricane Melissa, portable solar batteries and satellite Wi-Fi units restored power and communications within minutes so doctors could coordinate patient care. Solar systems even allowed World Central Kitchen to power its food trucks and serve hot meals after dark. “For Amazon, preparedness means prepositioning. It’s having the people trained. It’s having everything from pallets of diapers to satellite communications ready to go,” said Abe Diaz, senior manager for disaster relief at Amazon. “That means the time it takes for the community to get back on their feet is shorter, and ultimately that means recovery time is shorter.” Amazon will make 2,000 of these systems available to nonprofit partners in 2027, with 800 ready to ship from the company’s disaster relief hub in Tennessee this hurricane season. Preparation also requires coordination and practice. At a recent training exercise in a small Maryland town, Amazon brought together two dozen organizations—including local fire and rescue, nonprofit partners, and government agencies—to practice how people, technology, and partnerships can work together to strengthen disaster response. Participants launched into a series of hands-on missions, including a river crossing into an isolated flood-affected community, a simulated search-and-rescue mission, and helicopter-assisted aid delivery. Each mission was designed to put Amazon’s rapid response technology to the test in real-world conditions and allow local communities, companies, and government agencies to get hands-on experience with both the tech and each other. “You don’t want everyone exchanging business cards and meeting each other in the middle of a disaster itself,” said Civil Affairs Major Alex Haseley, an emergency management specialist with the U.S. Army. “Events like this, we’re getting to meet each other, we’re building some trust, we’re figuring out how to contact each other on relatively short notice. Emergency management is such a magical mission: When people feel what it’s like to truly help a survivor, it’s like a drug and you want to keep doing it.” During a disaster, hot meals do more than sustain people—they restore dignity and normalcy when communities need it most. For the training exercise, nonprofit organization Operation BBQ Relief used Amazon’s technology systems to power hot-meal preparation for dozens of people, including police officers and firefighters who serve the town daily. “A lot of times, the last thing you’re thinking about is nourishing yourself—you’re worried about your home, belongings,” said Chris Huggins, head of logistics and inventory for Operation BBQ Relief. “Barbecue brings hope and comfort—you’ve never sat down to a plate of barbecue and been sad, y’know? Taking five minutes to share a hot meal with a loved one is like saying, ‘Hey, there’s gonna be a better tomorrow. You’re not alone, and we’re here for you.’ This groundbreaking tech is a natural evolution of Amazon’s commitment to aid global communities threatened by sudden disaster. Since 2017, Amazon has donated and delivered over 30 million emergency supplies to support communities impacted by more than 200 disasters globally. Amazon leverages the same logistics network, aviation capabilities, and cloud technology that power its day-to-day operations to deliver rapid aid to communities facing crisis. “When a major disaster strikes, every minute a community spends without power, clean water, or connectivity is critical,” Schweitzer said. “Amazon is uniquely positioned to repurpose our existing delivery network, fulfillment hubs, and tech capabilities to get essential aid where it’s needed in hours, so even when infrastructures fail, recovery can start sooner.” When disasters strike, Amazon uses the same strengths that get packages to doorsteps to bring critical aid where it’s needed, fast. Since 2017, Amazon has donated and delivered more than 30 million relief items to support communities impacted by 200-plus disasters worldwide. For more information, visit AboutAmazon.com.

item.title: Runners Have Been Analyzing Their Gaits For Decades to Manage Chronic Pain. Could It Help Hikers, Too?
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.60
(Photo: Corey Buhay) I often feel like my legs are screwed on wrong. Any time I hike, especially with heavy weight, I get aches and pains in my right hip and ankle—but never in my left. I’ve tried almost everything to fix my crooked body: single-leg exercises, physical therapy, foam-rolling, and massage. I even had a somewhat new-age doctor hammer my hips back into place with a mallet. My friends call her the Bone Carpenter. Then a physical therapist suggested I do something far less medieval: Get a gait analysis. Maybe strength wasn’t my issue, they suggested. Maybe it was the way I was walking. Gait is the particular movement pattern you use to hike or run. It’s sort of like handwriting—it’s uniquely yours and shaped by years of practice, learned shortcuts, and old habits. And, like handwriting, it can get sloppy with age. All our gaits have idiosyncrasies. For most people, those idiosyncrasies don’t cause any particular problems, especially over short distances. But over thousands and thousands of steps, little asymmetries can add up. If you tend to favor one side or tilt a little too far in any direction, you could end up with chronic pain in your hips, lower back, or knees over time, says Dr. Steve Brown, an athletic trainer, chiropractor, and co-owner of the Boulder Sports Clinic, a chiropractic and physical therapy practice. “The number-one predictor of injury is previous injury,” he says. “But the number-two predictor is asymmetry.” Think of it like your car being out of alignment. It probably feels pretty normal when you’re driving. But over a few thousand miles, you’ll start to see major wear and tear on your tires and, eventually, on your suspension. To belabor the metaphor, getting a gait analysis is like taking your body to the mechanic. A trainer or physical therapist makes sure everything is working smoothly and helps you realign anything that’s come out of place. It’s a popular tool among runners, but I wondered—could it help me with my hiking problems? To find out, I visited Brown in his Colorado office. He said he was going to put a motion-capture sensor on me. I asked him if it was built into a suit like the one Andy Serkis used to create Gollum’s movements in The Lord of the Rings. Brown gave me a weird look. “It’s not quite as cool as that,” he said. He handed me a small belt with a single sensor sewn into the back. I tried to hide my disappointment. I strapped on the belt and started hiking on the treadmill at a ten-percent grade. The sensor—which was connected to a gait analysis software platform called Runeasi—measured how well and how evenly my legs pistoned up and down and how much my hips swiveled in space. I trudged on the treadmill while Brown held a tablet up for me to see. Various bars and graphs lit up and jumped around on the screen. After a few minutes, he stopped me, and we looked at my data. I felt validated: my body was, indeed, crooked. To be more specific, my right hip was locked up. That tightness was pulling my torso into a slight, right-leaning curve. Because I was bent over sideways, I was hammering more force into my right leg than into my left with every stride. Over time, asymmetries like this can cause chronic injury. In my case, the repeated, outsized impact forces had likely caused the plantar fasciitis and hip pain that I’d already been dealing with on that side. It’s hard to say where gait issues come from, Brown says. Sometimes, gait imbalances come from an injury or some other clear incident that leaves one side weaker than the other. “Other times, it’s a cascade of smaller things,” he says. Say you overwork one hip in the gym one day. It’s sore, so you favor it. That puts more force on the knee on that side, which causes it to twist slightly. You start favoring that, which both makes the hip worse and gives you an ankle problem. On and on it goes, often without you noticing. “We’re hard-wired to avoid pain,” Brown says. In other words, our bodies will shut off certain muscles or press others into double-time service to protect perceived injuries. All that happens without our conscious say-so. Small, repetitive activities can also throw your body out of whack. “Maybe you’re always pressing down through the right foot on the gas pedal, or always holding your baby on your right leg instead of your left,” Brown says. “Symmetry is obviously ideal, but it’s not something that’s baked into society.” If you’re a professional athlete or otherwise diligent about hitting the gym, you’re constantly hammering your body back into symmetrical strength. If not, those little things build up over time. The resulting biomechanical asymmetry can be as visible as a limp or as subtle as a slight lean. That’s why using a professional trainer or physical therapist—especially one with fancy sensors—is so helpful. Gait analysis is for anyone who moves their body long distances, says Brown. If you have asymmetrical pain—i.e., frequent soreness in one hip, one knee, or one ankle—your gait could be the cause. Heel pain, arch pain, and lower-back pain can also be symptoms of a faulty gait. So, if your aches and pains fall into those categories and regular strength training hasn’t fixed them, a gait analysis might be worth the expense. The answer will depend on your particular asymmetries. You might be over-flexible in some places or too stiff in others. “Physical therapy is all about figuring out what’s not moving enough and making it move—and figuring out what’s moving too much and reeling it in,” says Brown. In my case, my tight right hip was the issue. Brown did some (extremely painful) massage to loosen it up and then put me back on the treadmill. Sure enough, I was running more evenly. The changes won’t stick without a regular stretching and strengthening routine, which means I’ve got my work cut out for me. But for the first time in a long time, I had a concrete issue to work on—and hope for getting back to hiking pain-free. You can get a rudimentary gait analysis for free at some running stores. Most offer a visual analysis without any special sensors or software. That said, it’s a great place to start if you’re new to biomechanical detective work and don’t want to spend a ton of money out of pocket. If you’re looking for more detailed data, you’ll need the help of a trainer or physical therapist. PTs who specialize in runners and endurance athletes tend to offer more advanced analyses for anywhere from $100 to $400, depending on the complexity of the analysis. Mine was somewhere in between—$280 for a 60-minute session. Overall, it’s worth it. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: 10 Best Down Jackets for Backpacking | 2026 Recomendations
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 3.71
A down jacket has multiple uses on a hiking or backpacking gear list. It can be used as an insulating midlayer on its own or under a shell, as a warm outer jacket when you're less active in camp, or as an adjunct to your sleeping bag/quilt at night. For hiking or backpacking, some down jackets better meet hikers' needs than others in terms of warmth-to-weight ratio, hood design, durability, and cost. With these factors in mind, here are the best three-season down jackets that we recommend across a variety of price points. Be sure to check out our feature recommendations below, so you can choose the right jacket for your needs. | Make / Model | Gender | Weight | Fill Power | |---|---|---|---| | Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie | M \| F | 14.8 oz/420g | 800 | | Feathered Friends EOS Jacket | M \| F | 11.8 oz/335g | 900 | | Arcteryx Cerium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 11.9 oz/335g | 850 | | Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket | M \| F | 10.6 oz/303g | 850 | | REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie | M \| F | 13.1 oz/354g | 850 | | Mtn Hardware Ghost Whisperer | M \| F | 8.8 oz/249g | 800 | | Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 15.4 oz/459g | 800 | | Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak | Unisex | 7.6 oz/215g | 900 | | LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket | M \| F | 16 oz/450g | 850 | | Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket | M \| F | 13 oz/367g | 800 | 1. Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie 2. Feathered Friends EOS Jacket 3. Arc’teryx Cerium Down Hoodie 4. Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket 5. REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie 6. Mountain Hardwear Ghost Whisperer Down Hoody 7. Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie 8. Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak 9. LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket 10. Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket Down Hoodie and Jacket Buying Guide Down Hoodies, Jackets, Sweaters, Anoraks, and Parkas Manufacturer product names are applied inconsistently to lighter-weight down hoodies and jackets. In general, hoodies, sweaters, and anoraks weigh under one pound. Look for ones with hoods, as they provide the most head and neck insulation. When it comes to jackets, some are lightweight and some are heavier, designed for winter use in harsh conditions. You really have to look at the overall jacket weight to determine which is which. Anything up to or slightly over 16 oz will be good for transitional weather in spring or autumn down to freezing by itself or layered under a shell, while heavier jackets will be more appropriate for winter use. Parkas are almost always intended for very cold winter conditions and are too warm for active use when hiking. Sewn Thru vs Baffled Construction With very few exceptions, lightweight down jackets and hoodies use sewn-through construction rather than box-baffled construction because it is less expensive and labor-intensive to manufacture. With sewn-through construction, the front and back of the jacket are sewn together, creating a pocket that prevents the down insulation from shifting. However, warm air can leak through the needle holes, making the jacket slightly cooler. This is not the case with a box-baffled design, which is more prevalent on premium down parkas intended for colder temperatures. Hood Adjustment The hoods on many lightweight or ultralight down hoodies and jackets are quite rudimentary, with elasticized hood openings that may be too large to prevent cold drafts from entering around your ears. It depends on your head size and the specific jacket. Hoods that are 1-way adjustable have volume controls in the back that let you shrink the size of the hood to provide a better fit. Hoods with 2-way adjustability go a step further and add neck cords that let you size the opening to fit your face and block out drafts. Two-way adjustability is pretty rare on lightweight down jackets and hoodies, but it's a premium feature worth looking for. Down Fill Power Down fill powers, such as 700, 800, 850, or 900, measure the effectiveness and compressibility of down insulation – the higher the better. Now, 900- or 950-fill-power down is primo stuff and can add a lot of cost to a jacket while keeping it very lightweight, since it takes less down by weight to keep you warm. You can get the same warmth with a lower grade of down, like 800 or 850, but it takes more of it to keep you warm and adds a bit of weight to the jacket. However, don't dismiss 700 fill-power down jackets, especially if they include synthetic insulation in moisture-prone areas. The warmth difference isn't that significant, and while they'll be a bit heavier, they're ideal in wet climates. Down Fill Weight The fill weight of a down jacket or hoodie measures the amount of down it has, by weight. While this can be informative, a jacket's actual warmth depends on both the amount of insulation and its design, which makes it hard to compare jackets with different styles. Most lightweight jacket manufacturers don't document the amount of down in their jackets, which can make it hard to tell which will be warmer in active use. Waterproof Down Some manufacturers use down in their jackets that has been coated with a chemical formulation, called DownTek or Nikwax, to make it more moisture-resistant and help it dry faster when it gets damp or wet. Honestly, the jury is still out on whether these treatments make any difference to the insulation performance of the down. Some manufacturers believe it degrades insulation value, and others use it because it's considered a desirable feature by prospective customers. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. I have a Patagonia down sweater. I wish it were a bit warmer sitting around at camp when it gets down to 20-30F. Is there a jacket you think would perform better for those situations? I think the REI magma 850, the Katabatic gear Tarn of FF Eos will get you down to 20. Thanks, Philip. Those are ones that seemed like they might fit the bill from warmth standpoint to me. FF and Katabatic are impossible to try on without ordering. I’m on the husky side. The EOS seems like it might be too athletic cut for me. I’ve tried on a Magma. 2XL is a bit big, but XL is snug. It looks like the Tarn XXL might be kind of in between from the size charts. Does that sound about right based on your experience I’m a large – no idea about how those other sizes fit As a jacket nerd, I think that down has really been overtaken by synthetic at this point. Anything sewn through will be far colder than continuous sheets of Primaloft/Polartec that you can sweat in and throw in the wash without concern. For deep cold, baffles + the compressibility of down starts to shine again. But 1) I wouldn’t wear any of these jackets for activities where I might sweat through them. Use fleece and a wind shirt or soft shell instead. 2) Polartec/Primaloft is still only equivalent to 550 down fill power in heat retention so jackets with it have to be heavier to compensate for the lack of heat retaining loft compared to down. 3) If you’re worried about sewn through pin holes buy box baffled jackets. But I’d worry a lot more about #2 above. EX down anorak is pretty much impossible to find. And discontinued. Why would you include that? What are you talking about? Montbell has them in stock . Based on the buying guide’s point about two-way hood adjustability being a rare premium feature, I’m curious how much it actually matters compared with a good one-way hood on a jacket like the Feathered Friends EOS. The commenter asking about staying warm at camp around 20-30F seems like the exact use case where that neck adjustment and overall fill weight would matter most. Many fixed-size hoods are simply sized too large, largely because the outdoor industry thinks that there are more climbers or downhill skiers who buy gear than hikers. Without two-way adjustability (neck cords) you might as well not be wearing the hood.

item.title: How to Clean, Sanitize, and Store a Water Filter in the Off-season
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 3.34
It's important to clean and sanitize your backcountry water filter or purifier before storing it during the off-season and winter months. A simple three-stage process involves cleaning the filter to improve flow rate, sanitizing it to kill microorganisms, and drying it before storing it until you're ready to use it again. Step 1: Backflush Your Water Filter or Purifier Many backcountry water filters and purifiers can be backflushed, meaning you reverse the normal flow of water through the filter element. This unclogs debris or contaminants stuck in the filter, flushes them out, and improves the filter's flow rate. Many filters and purifiers come with a hose or a syringe, like the Sawyer Squeeze that you can use to perform this backflushing operation. to clean it. If you've used your water filter or purifier recently, you only need to backflush/clean it a few times. If you haven't used it recently and the filter element is “dry”, it's best to run water through the filter in the normal direction to wet it out before commencing the backflushing operation. Try not to apply extra pressure when you backflush the filter element because it can rip or deform the internal element, which may be paper, depending on the product you use. Sawyer claims their filters are pretty tough, but others are not, and I think it's prudent to be firm but gentle during the backflushing process. Step 2: Sanitize the Filter Element In this next stage, you need to sanitize the filter/purification element and kill any microorganisms that may remain inside. You don't want these to keep growing over the winter because they can permanently clog or damage the filter element. Different manufacturers suggest slightly different procedures, so check their website recommendations. The two most common ways people sanitize their water filter/purification element are to flush it with a diluted bleach solution made with one capful of fragrance-free bleach per Liter of tap water. A few liters should do the trick. Filter these as you would in the field with raw water. Once finished, filter a quart or two of plain tap water through to remove any remaining chemicals so you don't get a mouthful when you start using the filter next season. Alternatively, you can treat a liter or two of water with Aquamira drops or Katadyn Micropur tablets to sanitize your filter. These contain chlorine dioxide, which is an ultralight way to purify backcountry water sources without filtering. If you use one, you don't need to rinse your filter afterward, as the water you'll backflush or clean your filter with is completely potable. In fact, many city and town water supplies use chlorine dioxide to treat their tap water. Step 3: Drying and Storage Let your filter/purifier dry slowly and naturally by placing it in a warm, well-ventilated location, out of direct sunlight. After a week, move it to a drawer or closet in the heated part of your home. Come next season, it will be ready to use. Note: Some manufacturers suggest slightly different procedures, so check their website recommendations. For instance, rather than letting your filter dry, some recommend storing it wet after sanitizing. That's all there is to it! Updated September 2026. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Some municipalities have enough metals in their water that flushing with your tap water as a final step may lead to a stubborn clog in the spring. It generally requires some sort of acidic flush to get those minerals about. Citric acid is recommended by some manufacturers for this. This happened to me. We live on an island so all our water is comes from a well; lots of metals. Last year filter worked great. It is 12 years old. I used the same backwash and storage procedure as usual. When I took it out this year, no flow at all. I tried backwashing and letting many bags of water through it. Still very slow flow. I soaked it in hot, but not too hot to touch, vinegar. Now it flows like a champ. I am curious why this never happened before. I will argue against the step 3 recommendation. In my experience allowing a sawyer (or similar technology) filter to dry out and remain that way during storage can lead to a permanently under performing filter. Instead, I suggest storing the filter full of distilled water. I have had great luck doing this over the past few years. It may also be a good idea to repeat step 2 prior to use next season if you are a ‘’belt and suspenders” person. Regardless, always thoroughly test your filter before each trip to verify proper function. I’m going to offer Too Much Information here. But hey, it’s the Internet. Better to have TMI (that you can ignore/discard) than not enough information (to make an informed decision). In no particular order: – LifeStraw recommends storing their units (at least their v1 units) wet with a mild vinegar solution. (I carry a LifeStraw as a backup to my Sawyer.) This addresses JCH’s concern about letting the hollow fibers dry out. And it addresses Mr. Mann’s concern about hard water minerals clogging the fibers. But it’s not just that hard municipal water can clog the filter while cleaning. There can be hard water blockage from use in the field. (Here in Arizona.) So using vinegar to clean will dissolve the calcium. The downside of storage wet is that the vinegar solution inevitably weeps during storage. So store in a zip lock bag to hold the leak. (Altough this time around, I’m storing my filters dry. Now I’m concerned that they might not come back fully to life.) – I’m on a chlorine dioxide health kick lately, where I drink a 3x normal concentration of Aquamira water daily. I though “Since CLO2 is a disinfectant, why not store my Sawyer wet with a CLO2 solution?” So I did. A few months later, while preparing for a trip, I flushed the filter and checked for prime. (A lesson that takes only one time to learn after I used my unflushed LifeStraw in the backcountry and sucked in a mouthful of vinegar.) A brownish colored liquid came out, similar in color to the body of the Sawyer. Yikes! I’ve since found that chlorine dioxide is rated “Unsatisfactory” for long term exposure (more than a 48-hour) to ABS, the plastic used for the body of the Sawyer. (Also there’s some debate about compatibility with polysulfone, the material used for the fibers.) So now I use CLO2 only as a first flush/20 minute soak to killl any really bad stuff. – Some on the net warn about using non-chlorinated bleach/hydrogen peroxide in Sawyer filters. (I didn’t know there was such a thing as “unchlorinated” bleach.) They claim that “the Sawyer team warn[ed] that hydrogen peroxide ‘can damage the hollow fibers’ of the filter.” (I can supply links for my source material later if allowed.) – Regarding “shaking” a filter to clear it vs. “banging” a filter: Years ago, on my 2nd backpack trip ever, I became lost and desperate for water, I used my Sawyer to filter a very small, very muddy puddle of a spring. It clogged immediately. Backflushing at home never brought it back fully to life. Then I saw a video by a “Dixie” chick banging her Sawyer against the edge of a sink to dislodge dirt. Wow, what a shock when I did that to mine. It took two hours before all the dirt came out. It now backflushes easily. (Which Sawyer says is the test if the filter is clear.) But I’ve since read that banging can break the fibers. (I was banging against a towel to soften the impact.) I’ve used it for a few years since in the backcountry without any ill effects. Still, I wonder. Good stuff! Im a Be Free guy so no Sawyer pumps, hoses and other do dads to lose and break. After every trip I’ll put a few drops of bleach in a glass of water and filter that. Bleach is very corrosive so I’m not sure of long term storage. I wonder how it affects the Tubules inside? I’ve found it’s almost impossible to get the inner parts dry unless you take it apart which of course would ruin it. Before heading out on a trip I test the flow. If its medium slow then its good to go. So far so good. Hope this helps My understanding is that the core technology in the Befree, the Quickdraw, and the Sawyer is the same: hollow tubes. The only difference is the material quality and durability. Sawyer seems to have that advantage, hands down. I have not been out hiking in 5 years, cleaned and stored my Sawyer Mini Squeeze Water Filter properly. Think it will still work well? Define work. Mine didn’t, but that was before reading these ideas. I’m pretty sure the vinegar soak and ‘fonzarelli fix’ would have restored the bugger, which reminds me that i’d watched a ‘Miranda Outdoors’ video where Water Women / Water Angels were using the Squeeze for residential supply — and keeping the viable for 10 yrs — using ‘tap, tap’ and backflush. This week i bought the Quick Connect Cap for my P.QuickDraw off the MSR website … they sent a 15% coupon as a bonus. I’m thinking about switching to the HydraPak filter cap for my chest strap since I have those bottles on my bike. Also recommend not drying out the filter. One can restore the flow but it takes time and, for me, needed to use chelating solution like lactic acid (ie CLR) to get all the pores open again. This is in soft water area. I have had luck submerging filters in tap water and 5% citric acid solution long term. Vinegar tends to eat into the plastic for some reason, and distilled water along is not biostatic enough to stop microorganism growths.

item.title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 4.18
‘You’re going to Samobor? You must try kremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north. “But I’ve already had kremšnita in Zagreb,” I told them. They do it better in Samobor, they insisted. I wasn’t about to get embroiled in a battle of the cream cakes in a region where Croatians, Slovenes and Austrians all like to celebrate their own versions of this decadently thick, fat custard slice topped with puff pastry and icing sugar. But I was more than willing – happy, even – to follow everyone’s suggestions to try kremšnita in Hotel Livadić’s Kavana Livadić, in Samobor’s main King Tomislav Square, a mere half-hour drive west of Zagreb. It lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, in Zagreb County’s prettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter. The lush green Samobor Hills overlook the medieval town, through which the Gradna – part river, part stream – flows and ripples under wooden bridges adorned with flowers. One of these bridges led to the onion-domed church of Saint Anastasia; another, with a fairytale wooden roof, took me to one of Samobor’s many green spaces, dotted with free red deckchairs, which had the slogan “Volim Samobor” (“I love Samobor”) written in white. In front of them, the stately former home (now the town’s museum) of one of Croatia’s foremost 19th-century composers, Ferdo Livadić, added to the air of gentle refinement, of culture worn lightly. It was easy to visualise Livadić entertaining his artistic friends, including Franz Liszt, in this august setting. As well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within the Žumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last. Closer to Samobor, the hilltop ruins of Okić castle rose to nearly 500m above sea level, one of the best-preserved romanesque fortifications in the country. The Mongols couldn’t defeat it, nor could the Ottoman Turks. Sadly, it defeated me when I attempted to hike to the top. Not realising there was a newer, easier path, I ended up on one that was little else but vertical tree roots. With a newly healed ankle and no phone signal, I thought it unwise to continue. But it’s on my list for next time. A much easier path to take was along the Plešivica wine road, where more than three dozen wineries were scattered on a heart-shaped route between the village of Plešivica (10 miles south-west of Samobor) and the town of Jastrebarsko. In a harmonious landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany, vineyards clung to steep slopes between forested hills, many producing the sparkling wine Plešivica is renowned for. I met Martina and Krešimir Ivančić, whose ancestors were given a noble title and coat of arms by the Austrian empress Maria Theresa in 1759. The griffin on the family crest inspired the name of the Griffin Winery, which came about when a Hungarian count gave them a licence to plant a vineyard in 1773. Martina took me to the covered patio of a wooden hut above the vineyards, a suitably bucolic place to taste an elegant and lightly fruity sparkling rose made from red portugieser grapes. We carried on in the extremely stylish tasting room, where plates of cured meats and cheeses accompanied glasses of full-bodied chardonnay. I was also offered copanjek, a thin savoury pastry pie of cheese and greens. “They’re very portable, so workers would take them to the vineyard,” Martina told me. This looked like the winemaker’s version of rudarska greblica, which I had tasted that morning in the village of Rude, about a 10-minute drive west of Samobor, and liked so much I had to have two. Filled with cheese and walnuts, carrots or greens, these used to be made by the wives of Rude’s long-gone miners. They’re such an integral part of the region that they have their own festival every July and have been given EU protected status. At Pekarnica Nikl, in Rude, I met Jelena and Andrejas Nikl, the only authorised bakers of this much adored speciality. Jelena acknowledged the responsibility of keeping up this tradition of rudarska greblica, especially with the paperwork that came with legal protection – but, she said, it was worth it. All around the Samobor Hills, people were holding fast to their heritage and infusing it with life. The Korak family is one of the most illustrious, with its Michelin-starred Korak winery and restaurant in Plešivica. Not a whiff of Michelin stuffiness or pretentiousness here, just the fourth and fifth generations of a family producing superb wine and making beautiful food in a serene setting facing the vineyards. Brother Bernard is chef (and has worked with Massimo Bottura of Italy’s Osteria Francescana and Ana Roš of Slovenia’s Hiša Franko); sister Vera is front of house; and parents Velimir and Mirjana tend the vines – even the siblings’ grandparents are still making cheese and pršut (prosciutto) for the restaurant. Bernard grows as much as he can – the rest comes from local producers, including the farmer whose pigs are fed on scraps from Bernard’s kitchen. And if it’s not in season, it’s not on the plate. My June visit rewarded me with a truffle tagliatelle, and clams and green beans in a caviar sauce, among other delicious dishes in a five-course tasting menu at €118 (a very reasonable price, and in keeping with the region’s overall lower prices). I could only imagine what delights autumn will bring, especially during the annual Wine Days festival in Jastrebarsko from 25-27 September. The Samobor Hills will be teeming with autumn truffles and mushrooms, and welcoming the change in season the best way they know – on the plate. Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: 10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomie
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.51
Cabaña Verónica, Spain A good mountain hut, I reckon, should be small and only accessible on foot after considerable effort. Throw in a bit of historical interest and I’m bound to be happy. In which case, Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa is a fine start to this list. It sleeps six, and at 2,325 metres requires a two-hour trek from the nearest cable car station, never mind road. It has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order. Yet the real attraction is that this place was formerly a gun turret of a US navy battleship that was scrapped in Bilbao in 1960. An enterprising engineer, Conrado Senties, had it carried up on horseback and reassembled on a plug of rock in the middle of nowhere. Don’t ask why, just enjoy the eccentricity. €15, reservarefugios.com Låktatjåkko, Sweden An absolute gem just over 100 miles north of the Arctic Circle and 1,228 metres up a mountain, Låktatjåkko is well placed to deliver that other essential experience of a decent hut: cosy conviviality while surrounded by frequently hostile conditions. When I visited, it was hard to find the hut because it was coated in thick ice and half-buried in snow. The snug timber-clad lounge is the perfect spot to sit in front of the fire and read old accounts of Arctic explorers such as Fridtjof Nansen (there is no phone coverage). The kitchen bangs out endless plates of waffles with cloudberry jam and cream as well as more substantial fare. Be warned, however: in winter the chances of being marooned are quite high and the skiing can be a serious challenge due to extreme cold and fast-changing mountain weather. From 515 Swedish kronor (£40), laktatjakko.se Gaustatoppen, Norway Like many other huts belonging to the wonderful Norwegian Trekking Association, this place is small, well-run and traditional. It’s the route up to it that is astounding. You enter a mountainside, take a thundering old-school funicular railway one kilometre inside the granite, then wander through tunnels of military-grade concrete, before exiting through a blast-proof steel door and climbing down a short way to the hut. All that startling infrastructure is the cold war relic of a Nato communications station now doubling up as a museum and underground route to the hut, which dates back to 1893. This unique means of access gives the hut an advantage: you can stay in winter (weekends only) on the summit of the highest peak in Telemark province, Gaustatoppen, a popular ski resort, and then ski down. When I was there, the view was about 10 metres into thick mist. On a clear day, however, they say you can see one-sixth of Norway. From 1,550 Norwegian kroner (£122), dnt.no Chata pod Rysmi, Slovakia The Tatra mountains have some excellent huts, but this is my pick. Close enough to the summit of Rysy (2,501 metres) for an early start to catch dawn on the top, it is traditional, well-run and basic. The weather here can take a brutal turn at any time of year and, like all the best huts, this is in precisely the right position to be a genuine bolthole. If it looks younger than its 1933 start date, that is because it has been destroyed several times by avalanches and rock falls, which is also why it only opens 1 June to 31 October. €65, chatapodrysmi.kst.sk Kredarica on Triglav, Slovenia This is, in many ways, a standard, old-fashioned mountain refuge, but Kredarica has the great advantage of being the last potential stop en route to the summit of Slovenia’s highest peak, Triglav (2,864 metres). Given that every Slovene feels compelled to visit the summit at least once in their lifetime, this can be a busy place in summer, especially as the views are magnificent. The hardcore, however, savour its spartan winter comforts, when the dormitories are unheated bunkholes for those about to tackle the final, rather tricky ascent to the top (ice axe and crampons essential). €30 half-board, triglavskidom.si Le Refuge de Ciottulu di Mori, Corsica One of the attractions of Corsica’s epic GR20 long-distance footpath is its unapologetically old-fashioned mountain huts. No emergency helicopters swooping in when the G&Ts run out: this is gruff, mule-supplied, mountain hospitality. Ciottulu is a good example of the genre: bare bones dining room and a dormitory with communal sleeping benches for 26. Its ambience is more like a bothy set at 2,000 metres in a vast stony panorama with a slightly unpredictable caretaker. €15, le-gr20.fr Breiðuvik, Iceland The east of Iceland is home to a scattering of superb huts like this one. Breiðvik is actually on the coast and has the usual bunk rooms and well-appointed kitchen. The location is the big attraction: a wild, desolate coastline of volcanic sand beaches and abandoned villages. Together with 39 other locations, Brieðvik is part of a useful network run by the Icelandic Touring Association. 11,500 Icelandic kronur (£70), ferdaf.is Scotland’s mountain bothies The UK has always remained aloof from the continental urge to build something cosy on a mountain top. We are much happier sitting inside our leaky waterproofs eating soggy sandwiches. The Mountain Bothy Association is doing a little to encourage us away from such Spartanism, but not too much. Most are former cottages for miners or shepherds; many now have a fireplace or even a wood burner. In some, there are a few supplies left on a shelf by previous guests. I have a soft spot for the hard charms of the least comfortable, where you may find only a stone bench and an open doorway. A few have become over-used and afflicted by visitors who don’t understand the ethos of mucking in, sharing out and cleaning up. For that reason, I’m not sure it’s worthwhile picking out any particular bothy (pictured is the Elphin Bothy in the Assynt region of Sutherland), suffice to say that the roster contains some absolute classics. Go and find them. mountainbothies.org.uk Rifugio Nuvolau, Italy The Dolomites are so blessed with exceptional huts and Nuvolau is one of the best. Only accessible on foot, it was originally built in 1883 as a bequest from the Baron Richard von Meerheimb, the man who coined the term “psychodrama”, something he may have dreamed up while watching a Nuvolau sunset. The impeccable location is famous for its stunning shifts in light and colour. Inside is a dining room that serves excellent food, including a three-course dinner; upstairs is a small dormitory. €51 B&B, rifugionuvolau.it Rifugio Lagazuoi, Italy Many huts in the Dolomites have learned that economic survival is via tourists rather than hikers and climbers. Lagazuoi is one of them. Built as a climbers’ refuge, it has expanded over the years and been connected to the road by cable car, which enables coach parties to stay. And yet, it remains magnificent. The south-facing terrace is lovely and there are fantastic walks all around, not least through the tunnels and terraces of the first world war frontline that lie on the cliff face below. Mount Lagazuoi (2,835 metres) was one location where the Austro-Hungarian empire faced off against Italians. Many years later, in 1965, Ugo Pompanin, a local Alpine guide and rock-climbing pioneer, recognised the potential and built the first hut, which, several additions later, is still run in great style by his son Guido. From €85 with breakfast, rifugiolagazuoi.com

item.title: Leaf-peeping season is almost here: Where to see spectacular fall foliage across the US in 2026
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.24
Leaf-peeping season is almost here: Where to see spectacular fall foliage across the US in 2026 Editor's Note Autumn officially begins on Sept. 22, and that means leaf-peeping season will soon be here. Where and when the foliage will be most dramatic depends on location, altitude and weather. Leaves turn earlier in places with higher elevations and lower temperatures, so some parts of the northern and western U.S. are starting to see some color, while other destinations may not kick off their leaf-peeping seasons until October. If you'd like to plan a leaf-peeping trip this year, we've got you covered. Here are the best destinations you can visit over the coming weeks to see spectacular foliage. Related: Fall foliage cruises in New England, Canada and beyond When and where can we see fall foliage at its peak? Each fall, various forecast tools aim to predict the arrival of autumn foliage across the U.S. using precipitation and temperature statistics, historic trends for peak leaf peeping, local observations, and model outputs from previous years. Our favorites include The Old Farmer's Almanac and the Smoky Mountains Fall Foliage Prediction Map. Plus, camping app Hipcamp launched an interactive map to help you find campgrounds for leaf-peeping trips. Even with these tools, no one can guarantee exactly where and when foliage will peak — especially with unusual weather patterns on the rise. "Of course, past results do not necessarily indicate what will happen this year, but it should give you a fairly good idea of how fall leaves typically progress," an Old Farmer's Almanac representative said. Here, we'll cover the country's top destinations for leaf peeping, and when to visit each for your best chance at seeing spectacular fall colors. Best places in the US to see fall foliage Northeast For travelers on the East Coast, the foliage is just beginning to turn in New England's most popular leaf-peeping states. Prime destinations include the Vermont ski town of Stowe, the Berkshires mountain range in Massachusetts and Acadia National Park in Maine. You can expect mountainous regions to reach maximum color toward the end of September and early October. Lower-elevation areas, like the Hudson Valley in New York and Bar Harbor, Maine, may peak a little later. However, unexpected weather can shift these dates. Last year, a flash drought caused Vermont's leaves to drop early, while unseasonably warm weather in Pennsylvania delayed the leaf-peeping season. To stay updated on your destination, check local reports. Many states and regions offer fall foliage reports with predictions and regular updates throughout the season; Maine and the Poconos have already launched theirs for 2026. You can even sign up for local leaf-peeping newsletters to get updates in your inbox. Related: My first all-inclusive experience at a super-luxe upstate New York resort West The mountains of Colorado — known for their glorious gold and crimson aspen forests — are changing color earlier this year due to the state's prolonged drought. Peak foliage is expected to start in mid-September in the northern part of the state and travel south over the following weeks. The aptly named mountain town of Aspen is a great option, but there are plenty of brilliantly colored areas closer to Denver, such as Guanella Pass near Georgetown and Golden Gate Canyon State Park outside Golden. Utah's unearthly landscapes may be best known for their sandstone cliffs and gravity-defying arches, but they're also great places to enjoy the fall foliage of canyon maple, scrub oak and more come early to mid-October. Plus, the autumnal light illuminates the red rocks spectacularly. On the West Coast, Oregon's wild landscapes explode with color every fall. This year, Portland's foliage is expected to peak in mid- to late October. Take a steamboat ride to admire the changing leaves from the river, or drive the Columbia River Highway, a stretch of interstate designed specifically for its scenic vistas. Related: A points-fueled autumn road trip through Oregon's natural wonders Midwest Due to the Great Lakes' insulating effect, Michigan enjoys a long leaf-peeping season. This year's is already starting, with peak color forecast for early October in northern parts of the state and progressing south through late October. The famous M-119 road, also known as "Tunnel of Trees," recently reopened some sections after devastating floods earlier this year. Parts of Missouri, such as Lake of the Ozarks, are great candidates for a leaf-peeping trip as well. By Nov. 1, the maple, oak, hickory and ash trees along the lake's 1,150 miles of shoreline will be a riot of painterly hues. However, the American smoke tree, which turns an almost electric shade of pink, tends to peak much earlier. For a change of scenery, consider Lexington, Kentucky, where you can experience fall foliage from the water with a paddling tour along the Kentucky River or Elkhorn Creek. The leaves are expected to peak in the middle of November. Related: 5 stunning fall foliage road trips in the Midwest Mid-Atlantic and Southeast For endless views this fall, plan a road trip along the Blue Ridge Parkway or the North Carolina coast. The state boasts a long leaf-peeping season thanks to a wide range of elevations. You can see spectacular color in the Great Smoky Mountains on the state's western side starting in early October, and that peak will shift east over the coming weeks, hitting the coast in early November. Virginia's plentiful deciduous trees and varied landscape provide a long fall foliage season as well. The season should start in earnest toward the end of September, at which point the Virginia Department of Forestry will start updating its fall foliage report weekly. For thinner crowds, consider Columbia, South Carolina. This hidden gem will be packed with color in late October and early November, whether you stay in town to explore Riverbanks Zoo and Three Rivers Greenway or head to nearby Congaree National Park — home to some of the country's oldest and tallest deciduous trees. Related: The best national parks for a weekend getaway South The farther south you go, the later leaf-peeping season starts, giving you a few extra weeks to plan a trip. Plus, you may not have to contend with as many crowds in these colorful Southern destinations. For example, Louisiana has plenty of top spots for leaf peeping from late October through mid-November, including Chemin-A-Haut State Park, Lake Claiborne State Park and Jimmie Davis State Park. Experience the vibrant red leaves of the bigtooth maple trees in Lost Maples State Natural Area outside San Antonio. The leaves likely won't start to change until late October; check back here for updates. Or try Garner State Park in southern Texas, where you can explore 11 miles of hiking trails and take in the varied hues of cypress, oak, mesquite and persimmon trees. The town of Eureka Springs, Arkansas, is surrounded by enough blazing mountainsides to rival northern leaf-peeping spots — and it offers preserved Victorian buildings and therapeutic natural hot springs. Mid-October through early November is the best time to go. Related: Air Canada will return to San Antonio in 3-route expansion Bottom line If you're dreaming of a leaf-peeping trip, now is the time to book it. Even better, it doesn't have to eat up your travel budget or vacation days — with so many stellar destinations in the U.S., you can experience the magic of the season while staying close to home. Though tools like the ones we mentioned can't make any guarantees, they are useful guides for determining where and when to travel for optimal fall colors. This is especially true for the maps, which update based on real-world user data gathered as the season unfolds. But remember, any weather changes over the coming weeks could adjust the predicted peak timing for any of these places, so try to be as flexible as possible with your plans. We recommend booking changeable flights and hotel stays whenever possible.
