item.title: The ultimate guide to Delta One Suites
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.10
The ultimate guide to Delta One Suites It's hard to believe it has been 10 years since Delta wowed the travel industry as the first airline in the world to unveil an all-suite business-class cabin with each seat having its own closing door for privacy. Since then, Delta One Suites has won the TPG Award for best U.S. airline business class several times as well. No wonder these enclosed pod styles have become more popular with airlines, including Qatar Airways, British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, All Nippon Airways and Air France, among others. Here's what you need to know about Delta One Suites, where you can find them and how you can use miles to book them. Aircraft with Delta One Suites You can find Delta One Suites aboard the following planes in Delta's fleet (and you can check out our reviews of each): Although the product on the 767 is not technically a true Delta One Suite due to the lack of a sliding door, we'll include it for the purposes of this article, since these seats' footprint matches that of the suites aboard the A350 and A330-900neo. These are the long-haul jets that do not have Delta One Suites: - Airbus A330-300 - Airbus A330-200 - Boeing 767-300ER However, Delta will begin retrofitting its aging A330s with Delta One Suites starting later this year. We do not yet know how long this rollout will take altogether, though. The airline also recently announced that it will introduce all-new Delta One Suites aboard its forthcoming Airbus A350-1000s, which it plans to take delivery of starting in 2027, so be on the lookout for those. That's a lot of information, so it's important to pay attention to what kind of jet is operating your flight. According to Airfleets.net, the airline has the following numbers of each jet, and this is the total number of Delta One suites you'll find aboard each. | Aircraft type | Number in fleet | Number of seats | |---|---|---| | Airbus A350-900 | 41 | 32-40 depending on configuration | | Airbus A330-900neo | 39 | 29 | | Boeing 767-400ER | 21 | 34 | | Airbus A330-330 (refit project) | 11 | Being refitted | | Airbus A330-200 (refit project) | 31 | Being refitted | | Airbus A350-1000 | 20 on order, deliveries begin 2027 | 53 | While seat counts vary on the A350, all the A330-900neos have 29 Delta One Suites and all retrofitted 767s have 34 suites. On all of them except the A350-900s with 40 seats, Delta One is in a single cabin at the front of the aircraft, so your experience should be pretty similar from plane to plane. For those interested, the forthcoming A350-1000s will also have a large front cabin with 45 of the new Delta One Suites as well as a small back section with just eight of them. Delta primarily flies the A350, A330-900neo to an array of destinations in Africa, Asia, Europe and Australia from its various hubs, including: - Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) It tends to operate the 767-400 on shorter transatlantic routes between the East Coast and Europe. What to expect with Delta One Suites What makes the Delta One Suites so special? These are staggered Vantage XL seats, so each has a large footprint and plenty of privacy, especially those with closing doors aboard the A350 and A330-900neo. Each is around 20 1/2 inches wide and up to 77 inches long in bed mode on the A350. On the A330-900neo, they are 22 1/2 inches wide and up to 80 inches long. The 767 has the smallest seats, with only 20 inches in width, and a bed that's 77 inches long. All recline to fully lie-flat beds with memory foam cushions. The suites on the A350 and A330-900neo are very similar, though there are some slight design differences that those with a keen eye will notice. Here's a quick look at the differences between these planes and their onboard features. | Plane | A350-900 | A330-900neo | 767-400 | |---|---|---|---| | Total Delta One Suites | 32-40 | 29 | 34 | | Configuration | 1-2-1 | 1-2-1 | 1-2-1 | | Seat dimensions | 20 1/2 inches wide, 76 to 77 inches lie-flat | 22 1/2 inches wide, 79 to 80 inches lie-flat | 20 inches wide, 77 inches lie-flat | | Screen size | 18 inches | 18 1/2 inches | 18 1/2 inches | We found the aisles on the A330-900neo to be a little cramped, though the Wi-Fi was fast. The A330-900neo, A350-900 with 40 seats and 767 have just two lavatories for business class, while the A350-900 with 32 Delta One seats has four lavatories. So, you might find lineups on some flights. Delta One seats on the retrofitted 767-400 do not have sliding doors, but they offer more privacy than their older counterparts on Delta's 767-300s and feature finishes that bring them in line with the newer A350s and A330-900neos. Delta One seat selection guide On all of the jets, the Delta One Suites are arranged in a staggered 1-2-1 configuration. The suites on the sides of the cabin alternate between being closer to the aisle and closer to the window. The "true window" seats have their wider armrest on the aisle side, which provides you with even more privacy. Though truth be told, I don't mind the other window seats that are closer to the aisle since the closing door offers enough privacy on its own, and it's easier to get in and out of them. The seats in the center of the cabin shift either to the right or to the left of the preceding row to maximize seat pitch. So you won't find "honeymoon" center seats that are closer together, like you'll see on some other airlines, like LATAM. Instead, there is always a wide armrest and a movable privacy screen between center seats, no matter which row you sit in. Here's a quick guide to which seats are best for which type of traveler. | Aircraft | True window seats | Best for travel companions | Seats to avoid | |---|---|---|---| | A350-900 (32 seats) | Rows 3, 5, 7 seats A and D | Any row B and C seats | 1B, 1C, 9B, 9C — near galley and lavatory | | A350-900 (40 seats) | Rows 3, 5, 7 seats A and D Row 10 seats A and D | Any row B and C seats | 1B, 1C, 9B, 9C — near galley and lavatory | | A330-900neo | Rows 2, 4, 6 seats A and J | Any row D and G seats | 8A — near galley | | 767-400ER | Rows 2, 4, 6, 8 seats A and D | Any row B and C seats | 9A, 9D — near galley and lavatory | Delta One seat features As you can see, Delta One Suites bear similar dimensions and layouts no matter which aircraft you find them on. The primary differences are the number of seats on each jet, the lavatory-to-passenger ratio, and the fact that the seats on the 767 lack actual doors. Other than that, the experience is pretty consistent. The suites have 18 to 18 1/2-inch high-resolution touchscreens, high-powered USB ports for charging your devices and universal power outlets. Passengers can illuminate "Do not disturb" indicators, adjust their own lighting and take advantage of numerous personal stowage areas. Business-class travelers can enjoy hallmark Delta soft touches, including amenity kits (the current ones are cute Missoni designs with Grown Alchemist skincare products), over-ear headphones and and Missoni bedding that includes a mattress pad, lightweight duvet and memory foam pillow. Menus created by celebrity chefs like José Andrés, which you can conveniently preorder and wines chosen by the airline's sommelier, Andrea Robinson, are all presented with the airline's Alessi glassware, plates and cutlery, lending the meal service an elevated ambience. Finding Delta One award tickets Since Delta stopped publishing award charts and switched to a dynamic pricing model for award tickets several years back, it has become harder and harder to find decently priced award tickets in Delta One. Long-haul flights can cost several hundred thousand miles in each direction. For the most part, Delta prices long-haul flights in suites at exorbitant levels, ranging from 125,000 to around 800,000 miles each way. Yes, you read that correctly. That said, you can still find some rare saver-level awards — including recent deals between various U.S. hubs and cities across Europe starting at 115,000 Delta SkyMiles. I also tend to find that awards on the airline's flights between Seattle and Taipei are priced lower than on its other transpacific routes. Delta has a few useful award-search tools that make finding award prices easier. You can use the flexible dates calendar on Delta's website to look for awards five weeks at a time. And if you're just searching routes where you know an A330-900neo, A350 or 767 with suites is in service, select the option for nonstop flights to narrow down your query quickly. You might also look at city pairs that pass through non-hubs, since some of these options will be available at lower fares and mileage prices. On dates when you see noticeably less-expensive awards than surrounding days, you might be able to book them using partner currencies like Air France-KLM Flying Blue miles or Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points. Don't forget to use tools like Seats.aero to search broad swaths of the calendar. With a paid subscription, you can even use search filters like operating airline (Delta) and program you want to use miles from, including Delta's own SkyMiles frequent flyer program and those of its partners. Using points and miles to book Delta One Suites If you want to use miles to book Delta One Suites, you have a few choices. Delta SkyMiles First, you could use Delta's own SkyMiles. The program is a 1:1 transfer partner of American Express Membership Rewards if you have a card like American Express Platinum Card® or the American Express® Gold Card. Or, consider applying for one of Delta's cobranded credit cards to rack up award miles quickly both on welcome offers and everyday spending (terms apply): Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a Delta partner and uses dynamic pricing, so it's harder to find bargains using Flying Club points for Delta One award tickets. However, it's easy to rack up Virgin Atlantic points since Flying Club is a transfer partner of every major transferable points program, including: - American Express Membership Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Bilt (at a 1:1 ratio) - Capital One (at a 1:1 ratio) - Chase Ultimate Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Citi ThankYou Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Wells Fargo Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Marriott Bonvoy (at a 3:1 ratio, with a 5,000-point bonus for transferring 60,000 points; expect a 48-hour transfer time) That said, you'll likely have to redeem well over 100,000 points in each direction (and sometimes much more than that), depending on where you want to fly. Air France-KLM Flying Blue Another good option is Flying Blue. This program is a transfer partner of: - American Express Membership Rewards - Bilt - Chase Ultimate Rewards - Capital One - Citi ThankYou Rewards - Wells Fargo Rewards There are two major caveats, though. First, availability for awards booked through partners is very scarce. Second, you will typically pay more taxes and surcharges on these tickets than you will when using Delta SkyMiles. Downsides to Delta One Delta One has won the TPG Award for best U.S. airline business class several times, but there are a few drawbacks to be aware of before you actually fly: - Award availability at affordable mileage levels is extremely limited. - The suites are consistent but do vary slightly by aircraft type. - Many Europe and South America routes are operated by planes without suite-style seats. - The food, while elevated, does not always impress. - The number of lavatories does not feel sufficient for the number of passengers on some planes. - Newer suites will be coming online with the advent of the Airbus A350-1000, so you might want to wait for those. Bottom line Delta changed the game with its all-suites business class a decade ago. Closing doors (on the A350s and A330-900neos), up-to-the-minute tech and signature soft amenities all ensure a comfortable and memorable flight on the airline's newest Delta One products. However, the exorbitant award pricing of many flights with these suites means they're out of reach for most flyers looking to redeem miles to book them (except at the most inconvenient of times). Hopefully that will change, but in the meantime, the more flexible you can be with your travel plans, the better your chances of experiencing Delta One Suites for yourself. Related reading:

item.title: Hyatt goes glamping in New Mexico, an affordable Hilton in Deer Valley and other hotel news
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.61
Hyatt goes glamping in New Mexico, an affordable Hilton in Deer Valley and other hotel news For the past five years, I've had the privilege of serving as TPG's senior hotels reporter. Being the first dedicated hotel-focused reporter on staff has given me the freedom to shape our coverage in some incredible ways. I'll be frank: I have a dream job, and I don't take it for granted. Over these five years, I've had the chance to stay in the most expensive hotel in New York City, eat 10 free hotel breakfasts in three days to find the best — and even spend two nights sleeping on my hero, Dolly Parton's, tour bus. And that's just to name a few! But one of the most important things I do here is share hotel news with our readers, from new hotel openings to major changes in loyalty programs, and everything in between. For the last few years, I've written a monthly news column to consolidate some of the many news stories we want to cover but can't carve out the time for. Now, we've decided to shift that column into a weekly format that's even more digestible and timely to help keep you all even more in the know. After all, TPG readers are the best in the points and miles game. If you have questions, ideas or comments about our hotel coverage, feel free to comment on this article. Without further ado, here's the hotel news you need to know this week. Under Canvas is opening in New Mexico Upscale glamping has taken the U.S. by storm, and Under Canvas is one of the pioneers in the space with locations spanning from California's Yosemite to the White Mountains in New Hampshire. Part of World of Hyatt, the company just announced that Under Canvas will pitch its luxury tents in Santa Fe starting next April. For Under Canvas, this location will be a series of firsts: the first location in New Mexico, plus the first to offer saunas and "temperature-controlled, hard-sided cabins" (to come later). How to book: Cash rates through Under Canvas are currently available as low as $224 per night. World of Hyatt award nights are currently unavailable. An affordable lifestyle hotel opened near the slopes of Deer Valley Hilton's approachable and trendy Canopy lifestyle brand is now open at Deer Valley in Park City, Utah. Located at the base of the resort, Canopy by Hilton Deer Valley is "steps from the Jordanelle Express Gondola and minutes from Deer Valley East Village," according to a statement from Hilton. The hotel features 180 rooms, four bars and restaurants, a sauna, a steam room and a fitness center. Plus, it's not far from some of the most popular ski slopes in the country. How to book: Cash rates from $181 during the off-season and upwards of $600 per night during ski season. Hilton Honors members can book from 58,000 points per night off-season and 85,000 points per night during ski season. Wyndham Rewards updated award chart goes live Earlier this summer, Wyndham Rewards announced it was shifting its fixed award chart to include four award tiers. As of Sept. 15, those changes are now live with the lowest tier shifting down from 7,500 points to 5,000 points per night, and a new top level of 45,000 points. When the changes were announced, a Wyndham Rewards spokesperson told TPG that the 45,000-point tier will be "for a small number of our most elevated hotels." A California Marriott will rebrand as a JW In Southern California, the Laguna Cliffs Marriott Resort & Spa will undergo a multi-million dollar renovation and reopen as The Ocean Cliffs at Dana Point, a JW Marriott Resort. Located in Dana Point in Orange County, the nearly forty-year-old resort will see its 371 rooms refreshed, alongside a new pool, an expanded lawn, enhanced meeting spaces, a new 6,000-square-foot ballroom, a new signature restaurant and other refreshed or new amenities. The resort will remain open during renovations, and work will happen "in stages to limit any disruption and keep the guest experience as seamless as possible," according to the hotel's website. No formal finish date has been announced at this time. Crowne Plaza opened its new flagship property in NYC In the glow of New York City's bustling Times Square, IHG's Crowne Plaza brand just opened the doors to its new flagship property. Originally built for the 1964 New York World's Fair, the hotel has been reimagined with 685 rooms and the Fifty-First Street Social bar and restaurant, offering all-day dining. Guests can also check into "Manhattan Level" rooms, "an elevated stay experience featuring expansive suites and thoughtfully designed guestrooms with sweeping skyline views," according to a press release from IHG. How to book: Cash rates start as low as $194 per night. IHG One Rewards members can book from 30,000 points per night.

item.title: Capital One Lounge is reopening after months-long closure
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.32
Capital One Lounge is reopening after months-long closure For the last few months, the Capital One Lounge at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) has operated with limited service while Capital One completed infrastructure and ventilation upgrades. Now, the good news is Capital One has told TPG that full-service lounge operations are about to resume. Beginning Sept. 18 at 11 a.m. ET, Capital One's Dulles lounge will reopen for full-service operations following upgrades designed to improve temperature consistency and maintain a comfortable environment year-round. The lounge's physical space and design remain unchanged. During the closure of the main portion of the lounge, Capital One offered eligible visitors a dedicated food service counter with some hot food options, grab-and-go items and a limited amount of cafe-style seating located just outside of the lounge. But with the full reopening, eligible guests can once again enjoy the 8,500-square-foot lounge and its seating, coffee bar, grab-and-go section, full bar and buffet featuring a mix of hot and cold items. How to access the Capital One Lounge As before, Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Business cardholders can access Capital One Lounges when they have a departing flight within three hours. Guests cost $45 per adult and $25 per child ages 2 to 17; children under 2 are free. However, primary cardholders who spend at least $75,000 on their Venture X or Venture X Business in a calendar year can bring two complimentary guests per Capital One Lounge visit for the remainder of that year and the following calendar year. Authorized users can also receive lounge access for an additional fee. Venture X cardholders can pay $125 per year to unlock lounge access for up to four authorized users, while Venture X Business cardholders pay $125 per authorized user per year. Alternatively, Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card cardholders and their guests can access the lounge for $45 per person or $25 for those 17 and under. Bottom line With full-service operations returning Sept. 18, eligible travelers at Dulles will once again have access to the complete Capital One Lounge experience after several months of limited service. The Dulles reopening comes as Capital One continues to expand its airport lounge network. The issuer opened the Capital One Landing at LaGuardia earlier in 2026 and has announced a 14,000-square-foot lounge in Charlotte, which will become its eighth Capital One location. Related: Guide to Capital One Lounges

item.title: Delta adds another new city from LAX, bolsters 7 others as hub battle intensifies
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.71
Delta adds another new city from LAX, bolsters 7 others as hub battle intensifies For the second time in less than a week, Delta Air Lines announced it's adding a service to Los Angeles. The Atlanta-based carrier on Friday announced a new nonstop route from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) to Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). The daily flight will launch next summer. That news comes just days after TPG reported that Delta planned to launch a new route from LA to California's Central Coast, where it will return after a 19-year hiatus. It's part of a larger buildup the carrier is undertaking in Southern California. Additional daily flights on 7 existing routes In addition to the new service to Philly and Monterey unveiled this week, Delta on Friday also announced plans to bolster schedules on seven existing routes. Beginning next spring, the carrier will add additional daily flights on its LA routes to seven cities: Boston, Cincinnati, Houston, Raleigh, San Antonio, San Diego and Seattle. All told, Delta expects to fly its biggest schedule ever in LA next year, the carrier told TPG. "We're creating more opportunities for customers to connect to the places they want to go while building on our long-term commitment to Los Angeles and the West," Amy Martin, vice president of network planning, said in a statement. Delta's largest schedule yet in Los Angeles Even prior to Friday's expansion, the carrier had been on pace to grow its total departures at LAX by roughly 9% during the first half of next year, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. It has been a busy year for Delta at its Southern California hub. Since last winter, the carrier has launched new long-haul services to Hong Kong and Melbourne. In July, Delta announced a new route to Manila, Philippines. In November, it'll bring back LA service to Vancouver for the first time in eight years. And the carrier just opened its second business-class-only Delta One Lounge at LAX, following massive terminal investments at the airport in recent years. Hub battle heats up Still, Los Angeles remains one of America's most competitive cities when it comes to air travel. Each of the "Big Three" U.S. carriers (Delta, along with American Airlines and United Airlines) has a hub at LAX. Delta will offer more flights from LAX than any other carrier this year, per Cirium. But United has a bigger Pacific schedule from the airport — and will grow its long-haul offerings at LAX in 2027 with new service to Osaka, Japan. "It's a very competitive marketplace, and we're in it to win it as well," United chief commercial officer Andrew Nocella said on the airline's July earnings call. "But I suspect it will be very competitive for the foreseeable future." | Airline | Total 2025 departures | Total 2025 scheduled seats offered | |---|---|---| | Delta | 53,600 | 8.6 million | | United | 49,000 | 8.1 million | | American | 48,000 | 7.3 million | Source: Cirium Bottom line Delta's new route to Philadelphia will launch June 7, 2027. The carrier plans to operate its daily service with an Airbus A321neo. With its additional daily flights on more than half a dozen other LAX routes, the carrier plans to reach more than 200 daily departures at the peak of next summer. I also wouldn't be surprised if you see the airline add more transpacific service from the airport in the near future. Delta executives have made it clear: Asia is where the company sees the most growth opportunity going forward. Related reading:

item.title: Can you earn a Citi / AAdvantage Executive Mastercard welcome bonus more than once?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.50
Can you earn a Citi / AAdvantage Executive Mastercard welcome bonus more than once? Editor's Note Credit card welcome bonuses are one of the quickest ways to earn valuable travel rewards. You can often pick up 100,000 points or more in a single bonus, which can be worth thousands of dollars in travel. Right now, American Airlines' top-tier card, the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (see rates and fees), is offering new cardholders a best-ever, limited-time bonus to earn 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. Based on September 2026 valuations, this offer is worth $1,813. But what if you already have the card or have held it before? Can you earn the welcome bonus on it again? To answer this question, it's important to understand Citi's application rules and identify the exact date when you last earned the welcome bonus on this card. Let me walk you through it. Related: Is the Citi / AA Executive Mastercard worth it? Understanding Citi's application rules On most of its cobranded cards, Citi restricts earning the welcome bonus to once every 48 months. This rule applies to the Citi / AAdvantage Executive. The best way to find out this date is to call Citi at 888-766-2484. Alternatively, you could also call AAdvantage at 800-882-8880. (You can only see your account activity through your AAdvantage online account for the past two years.) Timing is important The 48-month period starts on the date the previous bonus was received, not on the date the account was opened or closed. That's important because a few months will probably have passed between when you were approved for the card and when you met the minimum spending requirement and, thus, received the welcome bonus. Product changes You can earn the welcome bonus on each of Citi's AAdvantage cards once every 48 months — each product is treated separately. In the past three years, I have applied for the following three Citi / AAdvantage cards and earned the welcome bonus on each: However, suppose I had earned the bonus on my Platinum Select and then the product changed (or upgraded) it to the Executive. In that case, I would need to wait 48 months from the date I received the Platinum Select welcome bonus to earn the Executive welcome bonus. The information for the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Strategies to maximize bonus opportunities Here are some of my top tips for quickly earning a lot of AAdvantage miles by applying for cobranded American Airlines credit cards. Work out your application strategy If you are confident that you received the welcome bonus on your Executive card more than four years ago and don't currently hold the card, you're good to apply for it again. If you currently have the card, first, you'll want to downgrade or cancel it. My recommendation would be to downgrade it to the no-annual-fee American Airlines AAdvantage® MileUp® card by calling Citi at the number on the back of your card. However, note that downgrading will make you ineligible for the MileUp card's (small) welcome bonus. The upside is that you will protect your credit score as there will be no change to your credit report. The information for the AAdvantage MileUp card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Alternatively, you can cancel your Executive card. While this may temporarily hurt your credit score due to an increase in your credit utilization ratio, you may be eligible to earn the welcome bonus on the MileUp should you choose to apply for it in the future. Bottom line Citi's 48-month rule makes timing critical when applying for its AAdvantage credit cards. By tracking when you last earned a welcome bonus and understanding how product changes affect your eligibility, you can ensure you maximize your chances of approval. If you're an AA loyalist sitting on an old bonus, now's the time to reapply — but track that 48-month window carefully or you'll miss out. To learn more about the card, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Executive. Apply here: Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard TPG featured card | 4X | Earn 4X Membership Rewards® points per dollar spent on purchases at restaurants worldwide, on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1X points for the rest of the year. | | 4X | Earn 4X Membership Rewards® points per dollar spent at US supermarkets, on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1X points for the rest of the year. | | 5X | Earn 5X Membership Rewards® points on prepaid hotel stays booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™. | | 3X | Earn 3X Membership Rewards® points on flights booked through AmexTravel.com, the Amex Travel App™, or purchased directly from airlines. | | 2X | Earn 2X Membership Rewards® points on prepaid car rentals booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™ and cruises booked and paid through AmexTravel.com. | | 1X | Earn 1X Membership Rewards® point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases. |

item.title: Elite status, hotel nights and more: Your guide to the Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.33
Elite status, hotel nights and more: Your guide to the Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard Editor's Note The Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard®* may have flown under your radar, especially if you don't often fly Virgin Atlantic. But with some useful perks that can easily offset the annual fee, this card is worth a look even for casual Virgin travelers. With a wide range of spending categories that earn bonus rewards, a fast track to status and no foreign transaction fees, this is a card that can be well worth having in your wallet. Read on to learn how to make the most of this card and decide if it's right for you. What is the Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard? The Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard,* issued by Synchrony Bank, is a cobranded card affiliated with Virgin's family of travel programs. It rewards cardholders not only on Virgin Atlantic flights, but also on stays booked through the Virgin Hotels platform and cruises booked through Virgin Voyages. The card technically earns Virgin Points, but these are interchangeable with Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points because your balance shows up in both programs. TPG values Virgin points at 1.45 cents apiece based on our August 2026 estimates, making them one of the more valuable airline currencies on the market. The card carries a $99 annual fee,* but Virgin flyers will find the rewards and benefits more than make up for this. Let's dive in. Related: What's the difference between Virgin Atlantic Flying Club and Virgin Red? Earning points First off, the Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard has a welcome offer of 60,000 bonus points, earned when you spend $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. According to the card page, that's "enough for a reward flight" — but considering that Virgin redemptions start as low as 6,000 points each way, you could potentially book several award flights with a single welcome bonus.* As you might expect, the card earns bonus points on Virgin purchases: 3 points per dollar spent on Virgin Atlantic, Virgin Hotels and Virgin Voyages. It also awards 2 points per dollar spent in several other common categories — grocery stores, dining out, select streaming services and EV charging — and 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases. That's a solid earning structure, considering many cobranded airline cards offer bonus rewards on purchases with the airline but not on other travel categories. Plus, the elevated earn rate on staples like groceries makes it more rewarding to focus your spending on this card (I'll get into why you may want to do that later). Cardholders also receive 5,000 bonus points on their anniversary each year when they renew the card. That's worth roughly $73 by TPG's valuations, almost enough to offset the card's annual fee. And you can earn 2,500 bonus points each time you add an authorized user (on up to four users). Since there is no fee to add an authorized user, you could maximize this benefit to score 10,000 bonus points (worth $145) right off the bat.* Since you can transfer any of the major credit card currencies to either Virgin Atlantic Flying Club or Virgin Red at a 1:1 ratio, this card could be a perfect complement to another travel rewards credit card of your choice. Plus, all Virgin Atlantic Flying Club members have the ability to pool points with loved ones in a household account, which could make it easier to accrue the points you need for your next trip. Related: Your guide to credit card transfer partners Elite status acceleration Unlike many airline credit cards, the Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard doesn't offer much in the way of day-of-travel benefits like free checked bags and priority boarding. However, the card can help you access these perks if you leverage it to earn Virgin Atlantic Flying Club elite status. You'll earn 25 tier points for every $2,500 of qualifying spend on the card, up to 50 Tier Points per month. That means you could reach Silver status (which requires 400 points in a calendar year) in as little as eight months with spending alone. Or you could get more than halfway to Gold (which requires 1,000 points) if you maximize the tier points on this card over the course of a year.* Tier points are primarily earned by taking Virgin Atlantic flights and spending on the Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard. So, if you want to reap the benefits of elite status but don't fly Virgin often enough to reach it, this card could be a no-brainer. Other perks The card comes with no foreign transaction fees,* an important feature for anyone who travels internationally. Another notable perk is the annual third-night-free benefit: Once a year, cardholders can add a third night for free when booking two nights at participating Virgin Hotels.* These include properties in popular destinations like New York City, New Orleans and London-Shoreditch. Although the list of participating destinations is fairly short, if you travel to one of them, this perk could save you hundreds of dollars, which can help offset the card's annual fee. You can access additional benefits if you hit certain spending thresholds. Cardholders who spend $15,000 on the card in a cardholder year can choose one of six Personal Perks, while those who spend $30,000 in a cardholder year can choose up to two: - Round-trip companion award: Book a companion for no extra points on a Virgin Atlantic flight redemption (taxes and fees apply). - Round-trip cabin upgrade: Upgrade one passenger round-trip on a Virgin Atlantic flight redemption. - Virgin Hotels free night award: Book one free night at a participating Virgin Hotels property in the U.S. or U.K. - Virgin Hotels suite upgrade: Upgrade to a suite at a participating Virgin Hotels property in the U.S. or U.K. - Virgin Voyages bar credit: Save up to $300 on your bar tab on a Virgin Voyages cruise of seven nights or more, or up to $150 on a cruise under seven nights - Virgin Voyages upgrade: Upgrade your sailing to the Blue Extras tier, which includes perks like a Sailing Club cocktail event, $10 daily specialty coffee credit, laundry service and Sailing Club Services Support. These customizable perks can add significant value, and the minimum spend required to earn them should be attainable for many travelers if they put most of their monthly expenses on the card. How to maximize redemptions You can redeem Virgin Points for a wide variety of purchases, including stays through Virgin Hotels, cruises through Virgin Voyages, gym classes through Virgin Active and gift cards at popular brands through Virgin Red. However, you'll generally get the most value from your points when you spend them on reward flights through Virgin Atlantic. According to Virgin's site, "every seat onboard, on any date, can be paid for with Virgin Points."* Award rates can vary widely due to Flying Club's dynamic pricing; you can use tools like Seats.aero or Virgin's Reward Seat Checker to find the best deals. Redemptions are not limited to Virgin-operated flights; you can also redeem points for seat upgrades and partner flights. Virgin has a long list of both SkyTeam and other partner airlines, including Delta, KLM, Air New Zealand and All Nippon Airways (ANA). A few examples of the best ways to maximize your Virgin points include: - Saver fares from the East Coast to London, which start at just 6,000 points each way in economy. - Delta partner fares as low as 7,500 Virgin points each way. - Air France economy tickets to Europe from the West Coast from 15,000 points one-way. - Premium cabin seats to Japan on ANA, which start from 105,000 Virgin points round-trip in business class or 145,000 points roundtrip in a first-class suite seat. Of course, you will still have to pay taxes, fees and surcharges on award tickets. Virgin is known for tacking hefty surcharges onto its own award fares, especially in premium cabins, though partner fares tend to have more reasonable taxes and fees. The Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard could help you maximize your earnings on these charges.* Related: Which Virgin Atlantic Flying Club partner redemptions can be booked online? Bottom line As with many travel rewards cards, the Virgin Red Rewards Mastercard is designed to encourage cardholders to stay within the Virgin ecosystem. You will get the most out of it if you book other travel through Virgin's platforms, or if you fly Virgin Atlantic enough to value Flying Club elite status. However, this card could make a good addition to your wallet even if you're a casual Virgin reward traveler. (And with the program's many transfer partners and low award rates, who isn't?) The card's welcome bonus alone makes it worth considering, and between the yearly third-night-free hotel benefit and 5,000-point anniversary bonus, most travelers should be able to recoup their annual fee. item.title: Maintenance delay? Airlines may soon have fewer reasons to compensate you
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.13
Maintenance delay? Airlines may soon have fewer reasons to compensate you Flight delayed or canceled? For airline passengers, it's already an uphill battle to get any sort of compensation. Soon, travelers may have even fewer protections. The U.S. Department of Transportation just finalized a rule that could make it harder for flyers to get a free meal or a hotel voucher when their travel plans get upended by a dreaded maintenance issue. The change, which alters how the government views maintenance delays, was ordered by a federal law passed in 2024. It's set to take effect in October. Once it does, airlines could face less pressure to pay up when flights are delayed due to mechanical problems. That means passengers could be on the hook to pay for whatever expenses pile up while they're stuck. Let's take a look at what's changing, why this is happening, and how you can protect your wallet when you fly in the future. It's already a hurdle to get compensated for flight delays Already, passengers are often out of luck when flight delays and cancellations pop up. Airlines typically don't pay for stranded flyers' expenses when bad weather or air traffic control problmes lead to flight woes. Those disruptions are typically considered outside the airline's control. Maintenance has historically been different. Up until now, the DOT has generally counted those delays and cancellations as within the airline's control. And when it's the airline's "fault," carriers will often pay for passengers' costs like meals, hotel accommodations and ground transportation. But will airlines be as generous in the future? That's the big question. Rule change in October Next month, the DOT will change its approach to aircraft maintenance delays and cancellations. Starting Oct. 19, unexpected maintenance that can't wait until after the flight will generally not count as "controllable." That means airlines could be free to stop offering meals and hotel accommodations for some flight delays — even if the delay is due to maintenance. In its final rule, the Trump administration was clear on what this shift will likely mean for passengers: "The number of delays and cancellations for which air carriers provide amenities and compensation to consumers is expected to be reduced," the DOT said. Not just maintenance The changes don't only apply to maintenance-related disruptions, by the way. Several other types of flight delays and cancellations will no longer count as something within the airline's "control." Some examples include when a plane has to be cleaned because a passenger has died on board, when an unruly flyer has to be removed, and cyber attacks (as long as the airline has been up to date with all cybersecurity regulations). Why is this happening? This new rule was actually mandated by the 2024 Federal Aviation Administration Reauthorization, which was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden. Ironically, that bill was notable for strengthening some consumer protections, beefing up airline refund rules. Those policies will remain as-is. Read more: Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight: What to know in 2026 But passengers will likely be less enthusiastic about this latest shift, which could leave travelers with fewer options for reimbursement when they are stranded. Not all maintenance delays Airlines won't be off the hook for all maintenance disruptions. These changes would only apply to unexpected mechanical problems that pop up outside carriers' scheduled maintenance programs. Essentially, we're talking about issues that must be fixed before departure, often for safety reasons. Airlines would still be considered responsible for more routine maintenance disruptions, the DOT tells TPG. And when those snafus happen, carriers would still have to meet their customer service promises listed at FlightRights.gov. What airlines are saying We should also note: Airlines haven't technically said they will scale back on paying for hotels and meals. But it appears they'll have much more flexibility in deciding whether to compensate passengers. Airline industry officials argue that carriers aggressively compete for customers, and continue to offer customer service policies that go beyond what the government requires. Another point Supporters also argue these changes will improve government data on flight disruptions. In the future, federal regulators — and consumers — will get a clearer picture of why flights are delayed or canceled. What should travelers do? Going forward, the best way for passengers to protect themselves is likely to keep a travel insurance policy or use a credit card with built-in protections. Certain cards, for instance, carry trip delay policies that can help flyers recoup unexpected costs when they run into flight woes. Just keep in mind that to make a successful claim, you typically have to book your whole trip with that card. Oh, and of course, keep all your receipts. Bottom line This is the latest blow to airline consumer protections. Last year, the Trump administration scuttled a Biden-era proposal that would have required carriers to offer cash compensation to flyers when "controllable" flight issues occur. Now, under this congressionally mandated change, passengers may find it harder to even get a free meal when they're delayed. Related reading: FAQ Yes. The airline may (or may not) give you anything, but you can always ask. Keep in mind that some maintenance delays will still be considered "controllable." And in those cases, your carrier may still owe you special accommodations, such as a meal or a hotel room. Yes. Federal refund rules aren't changing. Airlines must offer a full refund if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed. The catch: You're only owed a refund if you don't actually fly. Here's more on how refunds work. No. Every airline has different "guarantees" they offer to stranded passengers. You can find those promises at the U.S. Department of Transportation's FlightRights.gov dashboard. Keep in mind, those guarantees only apply when the cancellation or delay is within the airline's "control. And with these changes in October, fewer flight disruptions will be considered "controllable."

item.title: 9 great ways to use Bilt Cash — from bonus points to helicopter rides
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.62
9 great ways to use Bilt Cash — from bonus points to helicopter rides Editor's Note When the revamped Bilt program launched in early 2026, one of the biggest additions was Bilt Cash. Only $100 of Bilt Cash rolls forward per calendar year, with the rest expiring on Dec. 31. That means you don't want to let it sit for too long. With Bilt, you can earn both redeemable Bilt Points and Bilt Cash. And with the Bilt credit cards, you can earn both types of rewards at the very same time. Most of us are probably at least somewhat familiar with how to use traditional points, but Bilt Cash is a newer part of the program with a growing list of redemption options. If you've been racking up 4% in Bilt Cash on every dollar charged to a Bilt credit card and planning to figure out how to use it "one day," let me encourage you to make that day now. The good news is that there are now lots of great ways to use it, so here are some of our favorite ways to use Bilt Cash here at TPG, starting with the options that can potentially stretch it the furthest. How to earn Bilt Cash First, a quick overview of how you earn Bilt Cash. You earn some Bilt Cash when you reach certain milestones within Bilt, such as for every 25,000 Bilt points you earn toward your status. If you choose to earn Bilt Cash instead of housing-only rewards, you'll earn 4% in Bilt Cash on eligible nonhousing purchases with the three Bilt credit cards. New cardholders can also receive a chunk of Bilt Cash upon approval, depending on the card: - Bilt Blue Card (see rates and fees): Receive $100 in Bilt Cash when you apply and are approved and can earn 4% in Bilt Cash on non-housing purchases on the card. - Bilt Obsidian Card (see rates and fees): Receive $200 in Bilt Cash when you apply and are approved, plus you can earn 4% in Bilt Cash on non-housing purchases. - Bilt Palladium Card (see rates and fees): Earn 50,000 bonus points and Bilt Gold status (through the rest of the calendar year in which it was earned and the following calendar year) after spending $4,000 on everyday purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. Additionally, cardholders receive $300 in Bilt Cash upon approval and can earn 4% in Bilt Cash on non-housing purchases on the card. Related: TPG Bilt calculator helps you choose how to earn the most rewards with Bilt Best ways to use Bilt Cash There isn't one universally best redemption, but some options can earn more Bilt points or more value than others. Earn Bilt points on your rent or mortgage payment One of the ways to redeem Bilt Cash is to cash it in to earn transaction-fee-free points while paying your rent or mortgage via Bilt. This costs $30 in Bilt Cash for every $1,000 in housing payments that you want to earn points on via Bilt. For example, if your monthly housing payment is $3,000, it would cost you $90 in Bilt Cash to earn 1 point per dollar on that full amount for a total of 3,000 points. There is a setting in Bilt to automatically use your Bilt Cash this way each month. From a pure points-earning perspective, this is one of the stronger standing uses of Bilt Cash. And Bilt members appear to agree. Bilt told TPG that unlocking points on rent and mortgage payments accounts for a significant portion of Bilt Cash usage. Beyond housing, the company said members have also shown strong engagement with local restaurants and fitness studios. If you want to earn points on your housing payment but don't earn enough Bilt Cash to fully utilize both this option and the Points Accelerator, know that the housing option is mathematically a bit more generous. So, I'd recommend prioritizing earning points on your housing payment if you have to choose between the two. Use Bilt Cash to unlock better transfer bonuses Sometimes, on the first of the month, during what Bilt calls 'Rent Day,' there are transfer bonuses to one of Bilt's hotel or airline partners, with those with higher Bilt elite status often receiving larger bonuses. In some cases, you can use Bilt Cash to "buy up" one status level and unlock a larger transfer bonus. For example, on a recent Rent Day, Bilt Gold members received a 45% transfer bonus to Virgin Red. But those same Gold members could spend $200 in Bilt Cash to upgrade to the Bilt Platinum bonus tier, which offered a 75% transfer bonus. If you were transferring 100,000 Bilt points to Virgin Red, spending that $200 in Bilt Cash would get you an additional 30,000 Virgin points compared with the standard Gold transfer bonus. That's a fantastic return on $200 in Bilt Cash — and, in that specific example, far better mathematically than using the same amount of Bilt Cash for the Points Accelerator or even earning points on your housing payment. Earn more points with the Points Accelerator Whether you pay your housing via Bilt or not, one valuable use of Bilt Cash is to earn an extra point per dollar on everyday purchases with the Bilt Obsidian Card or Bilt Palladium Card via what Bilt calls its Points Accelerator. This option isn't available with the Bilt Blue Card. For $200 in Bilt Cash, you can activate the Points Accelerator in your Bilt app to earn an extra point per dollar on the next $5,000 in non-housing purchases on your Obsidian or Palladium Card through the end of the year. You can do this up to five times per calendar year. When this Points Accelerator option is activated, these cards earn: - Obsidian: 4 points per dollar spent on grocery (up to $25,000 spent each year, then 1 point per dollar) or dining, 3 points per dollar spent on travel, 2 points per dollar on everyday spend - Palladium: 3 points per dollar spent on non-housing everyday spending You need to manually go into your Bilt account and activate the Points Accelerator option each time — there's no setting that auto-renews it when the $5,000 is fully utilized, though there is a tracker to show your progress toward spending the full $5,000. Max out the full $5,000 in spending, and your $200 in Bilt Cash will have earned you an additional 5,000 Bilt points. Put another way, the Points Accelerator costs $40 in Bilt Cash per 1,000 additional points, compared with $30 per 1,000 points when using Bilt Cash toward housing. That's why I'd generally prioritize housing first if you have to choose between the two. That said, being able to turn the Palladium Card into a 3-points-per-dollar-on-virtually-everything card with the click of a button and $200 in Bilt Cash is absolutely phenomenal, if you ask me. Related: My Bilt Palladium mid-year update: What's changed since January Use Bilt Cash toward hotel stays Another popular use of Bilt Cash is toward hotel stays booked through Bilt Travel. You can redeem up to $100 in Bilt Cash (depending on your elite status tier) toward hotel stays of two nights or longer booked through Bilt Travel, up to once per calendar month. What's really cool about this option is that you can stack it with the Bilt Palladium Card's up to $400 in annual hotel credits, for hotel bookings made through the Bilt Travel portal (up to $200 biannual statement credits from January through June and July through December). You must book a minimum stay of two nights. Stacked together, you can essentially save up to $300 on two two-night hotel stays per year using Bilt Cash and the Palladium Card's credits. That's exactly how I saved $300 on a stay at The Villas at Disneyland Hotel that I booked via Bilt earlier this year. Other ways to use Bilt Cash Not every Bilt Cash redemption needs to maximize your theoretical return. If you have a balance to use before Dec. 31, several lifestyle options can provide straightforward savings. Use Bilt Cash on Blade helicopter rides A newer way to use Bilt Cash is on up to two Blade helicopter seats per calendar year, at a rate of up to $350 in Bilt Cash per seat. Blade operates between Manhattan and both John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), as well as to some farther-afield spots such as the Hamptons, making this a pretty fun way to spend down a bunch of Bilt Cash in a hurry. Use Bilt Cash on Blacklane car service Another newer way to use Bilt Cash is on Blacklane car service. If you aren't familiar, Blacklane is a service with professional chauffeurs in high-end cars. You can redeem up to $150 in Bilt Cash per year toward Blacklane in one transaction, with the exact amount tied to your Bilt elite status level. - Up to $150 annually for Bilt Platinum members - Up to $100 annually for Bilt Gold members - Up to $50 annually for Bilt Blue and Silver members Use Bilt Cash to pay for fitness classes You can redeem up to $40 a month in Bilt Cash toward workout classes bookable via Bilt. Some big-name fitness options include Barry's and SoulCycle, but there are more local options available, too. One bonus perk of booking with a Bilt partner such as Barry's is that you also get a smoothie from the Barry's Fuel Bar after class when you book your workout through the Bilt app. Use Bilt Cash on Lyft If you regularly use Lyft to get around, an easy money-saving use of Bilt Cash is to redeem $10 per month for Lyft ride credits. TPG Tip: You can also earn 2 Bilt points per dollar when using Lyft, even if you aren't paying with a Bilt credit card, as long as you have linked your Lyft and Bilt accounts and have the card you use to pay for your Lyft rides in your Bilt wallet. To link your Bilt and Lyft accounts, open your Bilt account and navigate to the Neighborhood Benefits section. Once there, select "Rideshare" and follow the prompts. After you link your Bilt and Lyft accounts, open the Lyft app and ensure Bilt is selected as your preferred travel partner. Use Bilt Cash at Walgreens A final popular use of Bilt Cash for some in the TPG offices is at Walgreens, where you can use $10 of Bilt Cash each month toward Walgreens purchases. When you redeem $10 in Bilt Cash, you'll get a $10 Walgreens gift card that's stored in the gift card tab of your Bilt app. You can then use it in-store or online for Walgreens purchases. Bottom line As the year has gone by, Bilt Cash has only gotten better and better as more uses have been introduced. Personally, I use my Bilt Cash first to earn points on my mortgage each and every month, and I'm now on my fourth Points Accelerator option for the year so that I earn 3 points per dollar on everyday spending on my Bilt Palladium Card. I've also used $100 in Bilt Cash twice this year towards hotel stays booked via Bilt Travel — both times in connection with using one of the biannual $200 hotel credits (total of $400 each year) that come with my Bilt Palladium Card. I've made a few smaller Bilt Cash redemptions, too, such as using it for Lyft rides when I'm in New York City. Now I'm running a little low on Bilt Cash, so I probably won't have much trouble using the rest before Dec. 31, when all but $100 of my balance will expire. Luckily, the clock starts all over again on Jan. 1. As a Palladium cardholder, I'll get another $200 in Bilt Cash beginning on January 1, and all those annual redemption limits will reset for another year. To learn more, check out our reviews for the Bilt Palladium, Bilt Obsidian and Bilt Blue cards. Apply here: Bilt Palladium Card Apply here: Bilt Obsidian Card Apply here: Bilt Blue Card

item.title: How El Nino will impact travel in the coming year
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.55
How El Nino will impact travel in the coming year El Nino has officially arrived, and this one is a doozy. What does that mean for travelers? This powerful natural phenomenon could make some destinations more enjoyable this year — while you may want to reconsider visiting others. It also increases the risk of severe weather events and travel disruptions. The good news is: you can prepare yourself. Read on to learn exactly what El Nino means for various destinations and how to plan your trip accordingly. Related: Travel mistakes that can ruin your next trip What is El Nino? El Nino is a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years. In general, El Nino forms in the northern hemisphere's summer months and lasts through the following spring, with its effects peaking in winter. The most recent El Ninos occurred in 2023-2024 and 2018-2019. El Nino weakens, or even reverses, the trade winds that typically blow east to west across the Pacific Ocean, pushing warm water east toward the Americas. The changing water temperature affects the Pacific jet stream, a powerful wind channel that flows from west to east across North America. During El Nino, the Pacific jet stream splits into two streams: a weaker polar jet stream that brings warmer, drier conditions to the northern U.S. and Canada, and a stronger subtropical jet stream that brings more rain to the Southern U.S. and Gulf Coast. But while North America is typically at the center of El Nino, this climate phenomenon can have much more far-reaching impacts — especially this year. That's because the World Meteorological Organization expects the current El Nino to reach "very strong" (aka "super") status by the end of 2026. Based on how these temperatures compare to past El Nino events, some forecasters think this one is on track to become the most extreme El Nino on record. El Nino's effects around the world El Nino has the capacity to change weather patterns worldwide, making some destinations less ideal for travel while making others more desirable. El Nino also puts some areas at higher risk of natural disasters and disease outbreaks. And while WMO predicts the current El Nino will end around February, it could have ripple effects further into 2027 — especially if this year's event turns out to be as strong as predicted. Here's what you need to know to plan your travels during this potentially historic El Nino year. North America While strong and super El Ninos can impact the whole planet, the biggest impacts — both good and bad — tend to be centered around North America. On the northern side, Canada and the upper U.S. will likely experience a warmer, drier winter than usual. This could make it a good time to visit these areas, as temperatures should be milder and precipitation lower. City trips could be more pleasant in places like Chicago and Montreal, and you can probably score deep discounts on off-season flights and hotels. The same goes for the historically rainy Pacific Northwest, where drier El Nino conditions could make it easier to enjoy outdoor pursuits during the (usually wet) winter. On the other hand, reduced snowfall and increased rain could potentially put a damper on a ski trip to the northern U.S. or Canada. Snowsports enthusiasts may prefer to head west, as El Nino stands to bring above-average snowfall to Colorado and California's slopes. Lake Tahoe ski resorts have been known to extend their seasons into June or July following an El Nino cycle. Related: Epic Passes on sale now for this year's ski season — with a new Gen Z discount That's because, while the northern part of the country tends to get warmer and drier during El Nino, areas farther south will likely get cooler and wetter. The Gulf and Southeastern U.S., in particular, will likely experience more precipitation. This could make it a less desirable time to travel, but more importantly, it increases the risk of severe weather. El Nino sets the stage for severe thunderstorms, flooding, snowfall, freezing rain and even tornadoes in the South — potentially leading to flight delays and trip disruptions. On the other hand, parts of the southwestern U.S. that tend to be dry, dusty and brown in spring — like Joshua Tree National Park in California — often burst into bloom following El Nino rains. Death Valley's 2016 spring superbloom was the direct result of winter downpours brought on by El Nino. While spring could be a great time to see the desert erupt in color, moving into summer 2027, northern areas that experienced a drier winter thanks to El Nino will be at heightened risk of wildfire and drought. The Caribbean and Pacific Islands Hurricane season is underway, and this year's powerful El Nino has the potential to flip the script. In the Atlantic, El Nino has put a damper on hurricane season with powerful wind shear, which can break up storms before they develop into hurricanes. Now, over 100 days into hurricane season and around the season's statistical peak, we are still waiting for the first one of 2026 to blow in. That could make this fall a great time to snag off-season deals in Atlantic beach destinations, or to take a Caribbean cruise. Just remember that while the risk of hurricanes is significantly lower, it still isn't zero, so stay alert. On the flip side, El Nino has spiked sea surface temperatures and brought low wind shear to the Pacific, creating ideal hurricane conditions. Hawaii, where storms are rare — only six hurricanes have come within 50 miles of the islands in the last 75 years — has already experienced three hurricanes in 2026. As a result, a fall trip to a Pacific island or Mexican Riviera cruise may carry greater risks than usual. You may want to consider rebooking your beach vacation to a different locale or postponing it until after hurricane season, which usually ends Nov. 30. Related: The 12 best secret beaches in the Caribbean South America As with the southern U.S., El Nino is expected to bring wetter conditions to parts of South America. In particular, coastal Ecuador and northern Peru are at risk of heavy rains and flooding. During the 1997-98 El Niño, Peru's arid northern coast — which is accustomed to less than one inch of average rainfall per year — saw roads washed out and bridges destroyed by over 100 inches of rain. Even Lima and Machu Picchu, much farther south, have already seen disruptions due to flooding and landslides brought on by this year's super El Nino. You may want to avoid traveling to these regions in the coming months. If you do visit, be aware of the risks — I'll discuss how to prepare yourself in a later section. Related: We visited the New 7 Wonders of the World on 1 ticket — here's how Asia El Nino generally brings weaker monsoons to South and Southeast Asia. This can lead to more sunshine and ideal beach-going conditions in places like Bali, Thailand and the Philippines — tempered by more frequent wildfires, hazy skies and low air quality. The super El Nino of 2015-16 contributed to devastating fires in Indonesia, as well as one of Thailand's worsts droughts in decades. Similarly, Japan is likely to get less snowfall than usual this year, while Korea may experience a warmer and wetter winter — so keep that in mind if you're considering a ski trip. Related: Delta plans major Asia growth, confirms Singapore flights are coming Africa If you're planning a safari, El Nino could impact your trip in multiple ways. El Nino is known for bringing heavier short rains across East Africa between October and December, potentially making roads impassable and shutting down bush airstrips — though travelers who risk it will be rewarded with breathtaking emerald-green grasslands and vast flocks of migratory birds. Some of Africa's most popular safari destinations have already seen these effects firsthand. The super El Nino of 1997-98 left parts of Kenya cut off from the rest of the country, while the strong El Nino in 2023-2024 damaged hundreds of miles of road and dozens of bridges in Tanzania. Conversely, the southern part of the continent, including tourist hotspots South Africa and Botswana, is likely to get drier. This could make Victoria Falls along the Zimbabwe-Zambia border less impressive and even lead to water restrictions at safari lodges. At the same time, drought could be good news for safari-goers, as animals can be easier to spot when they concentrate around scarce water sources. Related: Marriott's new rhino-focused luxury safari lodge is now taking reservations Australia Since a spike in ocean temperatures is a hallmark of El Nino, it's no surprise that this event can lead to mass coral reef die-offs. The historic 1997-98 event triggered the first documented global coral bleaching event, while the super El Nino in 2015-2016 ushered in the longest global coral bleaching event on record. By spring and summer 2027, areas like the Great Barrier Reef will likely be feeling the effects of this year's event. It could be a good idea to postpone a visit until the coral has had a chance to (hopefully) recover somewhat — both to ensure better underwater views and to minimize additional strain on an already stressed reef. Australia's underwater crown jewel isn't the only area at risk. El Nino typically brings drought conditions to New South Wales, Queensland and other parts of inland Australia. This increases the risk of bushfires, particularly in the continent's summer months (December to February). Travelers are more likely to face hazy skies, low air quality and travel disruptions as a result. Europe Besides warming the surface of the Pacific, El Nino also contributes to higher air temperatures around the globe by releasing heat from the ocean into the atmosphere. This year's event has already had a hand in sky-high temperatures this summer, and that trend will likely continue into 2027. While Europe tends to be far enough removed from the Pacific to be spared most of El Nino's effects, the continent has become increasingly prone to heatwaves. The most recent was in summer 2026, which broke temperature records in France, Germany and more. If you want to beat the heat — and the dangers it poses — consider visiting Europe outside the peak summer months. (You'll enjoy the added benefit of lower prices and thinner crowds.) Or, consider booking a coolcation elsewhere. Related: 8 European destinations that are better in spring than summer How to prepare El Nino doesn't guarantee any of the above conditions; it just increases their likelihood. Knowing how El Nino has historically affected different parts of the world can help you determine where and when to travel in the coming months. But the key takeaway? Expect the unexpected. El Nino significantly raises the odds of severe and unpredictable weather events, which could lead to serious disruptions for unlucky travelers. Your best bet is to prepare yourself. We always recommend traveling with trip insurance. The right coverage can protect you from financial loss if you are forced to cancel your trip, and even help you get home safely if disaster strikes. Adding a cancel-for-any-reason clause to your policy is a great idea during El Nino years. Just keep in mind that this type of coverage must usually be purchased within a short time (anywhere from 24 hours to 21 days) after you make your first trip purchase. Also remember to stay alert while traveling and prepare a contingency plan in case of emergency. Be sure to enroll your trip in STEP to be notified of weather events and other need-to-know updates. Lastly, El Nino's impacts can extend beyond the weather, as changing temperatures and rainfall can exacerbate the spread of water- and mosquito-borne diseases. For example, dengue fever cases surged across Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands in the wake of the 2015-16 super event. That makes it more important than ever to see a travel health specialist before your trip and get any vaccines or prophylactic medications you may need. Related: The complete travel health checklist: How to stay safe abroad Bottom line This year's El Nino is primed to impact countries around the world — but that doesn't mean you should put travel in hold. Knowing how El Nino will likely influence weather patterns in your destination can help you plan your best trip. That being said, super El Nino conditions make it more important than ever to prepare for the unexpected. Following the steps above can help you rest easy and stay safe. Plus, don't miss these other practical tips:

September 20, 2026 • 10 min read The cards we feature here are from partners who compensate us when you are approved through our site, and this may impact how or where these products appear. Related stories Quick summary A student-oriented cash-back card offers a simple way to build credit and earn rewards, with elevated rates at gas stations and restaurants up to a quarterly cap. The card features an automatic first-year cash-back match, effectively doubling rewards earned in the first 12 months. No activation is needed for bonus categories, and the card provides tools to help monitor credit and spending. Long-term earning potential is limited after the first year, making it best suited as a starter card rather than a primary rewards card. What to consider Quarterly caps apply to elevated cash-back earnings at select merchants, with all other purchases earning a lower rate. Eligibility requires at least part-time college enrollment and sufficient income or savings to make payments. Account terms remain the same after graduation, which may help maintain credit history length. What you'll miss from the article A detailed comparison of alternative student and cash-back cards, including options with higher flat-rate rewards or rotating bonus categories. Generated by AI with support from our editorial team. If you're a student looking for a no-annual-fee cash-back card that can help you build credit, the Discover it® Student Chrome is a straightforward option. While it may not offer the strongest long-term earning potential, it can be a solid starter card for students who are new to credit cards. Card rating*: ⭐⭐½ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. Discover it Student Chrome: The basics The Discover it Student Chrome is a no-annual-fee cash-back card for students who want to earn rewards while building credit. You'll earn 2% cash back at gas stations and restaurants on up to $1,000 in combined purchases each quarter, automatically. All other purchases earn 1% cash back. The card's biggest draw is its first-year cash-back match. Discover will automatically match all the cash back you've earned during your first year, with no limit on the amount it will match. While the benefits are limited, I appreciate how the card can help newer credit card users. Discover says you don't need a credit score to apply, and responsible use of the card can help build credit because Discover reports your payment history to all three major credit bureaus. Through 2027, Capital One ismerging all of Discover's card products into its system. If you're a current cardholder, your account should transition at some point over the next year. New cardholders will immediately be put on Capital One's network. Certain perks covered in this review may be unavailable for current cardholders until their account is migrated to Capital One. Keep an eye out for an email about your account migration. Discover it Student Chrome pros and cons Pros Cons Elevated cash-back earnings on gas stations and restaurants The Discover it Student Chrome offers a relatively simple set of benefits geared toward students who are new to managing credit. Discover provides cardmembers with a free FICO Score, and checking your score doesn't hurt your credit. The issuer also provides tools that can help you monitor your spending and manage your account. If you misplace your card, you can quickly freeze your account through Discover's website or mobile app to prevent new purchases and cash advances. The card also includes $0 fraud liability for unauthorized purchases. Other useful features include free Social Security number alerts, account alerts, a recurring-charges dashboard, a spend analyzer and digital wallet support. New cardholders are automatically placed on Capital One's network, while existing cardholders will gain access as their accounts are migrated. Once your account is on Capital One's network, you'll also receive access to Capital One Offers, which can provide up to 15% cash back on eligible purchases with select merchants. These aren't benefits that will make the Student Chrome stand out among rewards cards, but they can be useful for students who are learning how to manage a credit card and monitor their credit. You also don't have to give up the Student Chrome once you graduate. According to Discover, your account's terms, conditions, rewards and features remain the same after graduation, so you can continue using the card even when you're no longer a student. Keeping the account open may also be beneficial if it's one of your oldest credit accounts, since the age of your accounts is one factor that affects your credit score. *These earning rates are only available once your account is on Capital One's network. The 2% rate applies automatically, so there's no need to remember to activate quarterly bonus categories. Purchases in those categories after you hit the $1,000 quarterly capearn 1% cash back. For a student who regularly spends on gas and dining, that's a useful perk. While the quarterly cap limits how much you can earn at the elevated rate, most students likely won't find the cap particularly restrictive. If you spend the full $1,000 each quarter in those categories, you'd earn $20 in cash back each quarter before factoring in the first-year Cashback Match. The card's first-year match can make those earnings considerably more valuable during your first year. After the match ends, though, the Student Chrome's 1% base earning rate isn't especially competitive. You can redeem cash back for a statement credit or an electronic deposit. You can also use rewards with select merchants, purchase gift cards or make a charitable donation. Your cash back doesn't expire while your account remains open. There is no minimum redemption amount, so you don't have to wait to accumulate a certain amount of cash back before using your rewards. I appreciate that the redemption system is straightforward for students who may prefer simple, flexible cash-back rewards over a more complicated points system. The biggest drawback of the Discover it Student Chrome is that the card's benefits are relatively limited once the first-year Cashback Match ends. The 2% rate at gas stations and restaurants is useful, but it's capped at $1,000 in combined purchases each quarter. While cardholders on Capital One's network can also earn elevated rates through Capital One Travel and Capital One Entertainment, most everyday purchases outside the card's bonus categories earn just 1% cash back. Depending on your spending habits, you may earn more with a different card. The card's cash-back rewards may also feel limiting if you eventually want to use your rewards for travel. Unlike cards that earn transferable points or miles, the Student Chrome doesn't give you access to airline or hotel transfer partners, which can potentially provide more value from your rewards. The Student Chrome's first-year Cashback Match makes it particularly attractive as a starter card. But after the first year, its earning rates become less compelling, especially as your credit history improves and you become eligible for a broader range of rewards cards. Is the Discover it Student Chrome worth it? The Discover it Student Chrome is worth considering if you're a student looking for a straightforward way to earn cash back while building credit. There's no annual fee, the 2% categories require no activation and the first-year Cashback Match can significantly boost your rewards. For long-term everyday spending, though, you may eventually find better options as your credit profile develops. The Student Chrome makes the most sense as a simple starter card rather than a card you'll necessarily want to keep as your primary rewards card indefinitely. When to apply for the Discover it Student Chrome The best time to consider the Discover it Student Chrome is when you can take advantage of its first-year Cashback Match. There's no limit to how much you can earn with the cash-back match at the end of your first year, which means your earnings are effectively doubled for 12 months. This can be a solid offer if you plan to use the card frequently in your first year. Keep in mind that you'll need to meet the card's eligibility requirements. You must be enrolled at least part-time at a college or university and have sufficient income or savings to make your monthly payments. If you meet those requirements and are looking for your first credit card, applying while you're still a student can give you an opportunity to build your credit history while earning cash-back rewards. If you want higher rewards on rotating categories: TheDiscover it® Student Cash Back earns 5% cash back on rotating categories each quarter, up to the quarterly maximum when activated, plus at least 1% on other purchases. It also offers a first-year Cashback Match. To learn more, read our full review of the Discover it Cash Back. If you want straightforward 2% cash rewards: The (see rates and fees) earns 2% cash rewards on purchases with no annual fee. It’s a good fit if you’d rather earn at a consistent rate without having to track bonus categories or spending caps. To learn more, read our full review of the Wells Fargo Active Cash Card. If you spend more on dining and groceries: The Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card earns unlimited 3% cash back at grocery stores (excluding superstores like Walmart and Target) and on dining, entertainment and popular streaming services, all for no annual fee. To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Savor Cash. The Discover it Student Chrome is a solid starter card for students who want to earn cash back without paying an annual fee. The automatic 2% rate on gas and dining is easy to understand (subject to a quarterly spending cap), while the first-year Cashback Match can make the card particularly rewarding during its first year. I think the card is a strong starter option for students who value simplicity and don't want to keep track of rotating bonus categories. Its long-term earning potential is more limited, but for students who are focused on building credit and want a straightforward rewards structure, the Student Chrome is a worthwhile option.
